We use ~5,000 of the ~5,000 generated (all pass a fluency/parse filter); fewer only if a model's closed-book consistency filter drops an item for that model. Each claim carries an evidence SEQUENCE of k pieces (k up to 6) each with a stipulated strength; two matched sweeps are built per claim holding per-piece strengths and total magnitude identical but mirrored: INSTALL (neutral → k pieces FOR → k matched pieces AGAINST) and UNINSTALL (neutral → k AGAINST → k FOR). Prior-plausibility (prior-consistent vs prior-contradicting) is crossed in. Each item also carries a behavioral ASSERTION probe at every step, comprehension checks ("restate the latest evidence"), and 3 paraphrase/order perturbations. A human validates 200 sampled items for matched strength.

Models. Frozen open-weight Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B (base and instruct). Nothing in the transformer is trainable; the only trained objects are linear probes (L2-regularized logistic/linear regression, one per layer) fit on frozen residual-stream activations. Probes: 80/20 item-disjoint train/test split, 5-fold CV for the L2 penalty, 3 seeds {0,1,2}; report mean±sd. Steering uses contrastive activation addition (difference-of-means direction) with coefficient α ∈ {±2,±4,±8} × per-layer activation std.

Experiment 1 (H1 — hysteresis loop area). For each item, read the internal belief probe at every evidence step of the up-then-down INSTALL sweep, plot belief vs cumulative signed evidence, and compute LOOP AREA and the residual belief at sweep end (should be ≈ the neutral start if updating is reversible). Systems compared: observed loop vs the Bayesian-symmetric oracle trajectory (synthetic track) / a reversible-null bootstrap (real track). Decisive metric: mean loop area, normalized to the probe's belief range, tested > 0 per model/track. Convincing: normalized loop area ≥ 0.10 with 95% CI excluding 0 in ≥3 of 4 models. Indecision band: normalized loop area in [0.03, 0.10] or CI touching 0 — cannot distinguish hysteresis from probe noise; we then withhold the H1 claim and report the bound. Negative (area ≤ 0.03, CI includes 0): LLMs update reversibly — H1 rejected, a reassuring result reported as such.

Experiment 2 (H2 — install/uninstall threshold gap, graded by plausibility). Define per-item INSTALL THRESHOLD (evidence to cross a "believed" criterion of probe belief = 0.5→0.75) and UNINSTALL THRESHOLD (counter-evidence to drop back below 0.5 once believed), matched in per-piece strength. Decisive metric: (uninstall − install) threshold gap in units of stipulated log-likelihood-ratio, tested > 0 and larger for prior-consistent than prior-contradicting claims (interaction term). Convincing: mean gap ≥ 0.5 LLR units, CI excludes 0, and plausibility interaction significant (p<0.01) in ≥3 models. Indecision band: gap in [0.15, 0.5] LLR — report as weak/graded evidence, no strong claim. Negative (gap ≤ 0.15 or plausibility interaction absent): asymmetry is not graded — the H2 portion is rejected while H1 may still hold.

Experiment 3 (H3 — internal asymmetry predicts sticky errors). Collect behavioral "sticky" errors: after the counter-evidence half of the sweep, does the model still assert the original claim (LLM-judge scored on open output, 300 items human-validated, target κ ≥ 0.7)? Decisive metric first: AUROC of per-item loop area / uninstall-threshold predicting sticky error, compared against a closed-book log-prob baseline. Convincing: probe-based AUROC ≥ 0.70 and ≥ 0.05 above the log-prob baseline in ≥3 models. Indecision band: AUROC 0.60–0.70 or within 0.05 of baseline — internal signal is present but not clearly the driver. Negative (AUROC ≤ 0.60): internal hysteresis does not track behavior — H3 rejected.

Experiment 4 (H4 — localization and causal symmetrization). Use activation patching / causal mediation, patching UNINSTALL-phase activations against a fresh no-prior-belief run to find the minimal head/layer set that resists the belief drop; compare to truth/belief heads. Then derive a contrastive stubbornness/hysteresis steering direction (high- vs low-hysteresis states) and test: (a) subtracting it drives loop area → 0 and uninstall-threshold → install-threshold and lowers sticky errors; (b) adding it exaggerates hysteresis; (c) specificity — random-direction and truth-direction steering do not selectively symmetrize; (d) collateral — MMLU (1k-item subset) and perplexity on WikiText-103 (2k lines). Decisive metric: reduction in normalized loop area under subtraction. Convincing: ≥50% loop-area reduction with <2% absolute MMLU drop and <5% perplexity increase, and random/truth baselines showing <15% reduction. Indecision band: 20–50% reduction, or collateral MMLU drop 2–5% — a partial/contaminated effect, reported without a clean causal claim. Negative (<20% reduction or effect matched by control directions): no identifiable symmetrizing component — H4 rejected. All effects are planned, not yet measured.


Formal definitions (pre-specified). For an item, let b(e) be the probe-decoded belief at cumulative signed evidence e; the up-then-down sweep traces b over e ascending to +E then descending to -E. LOOP AREA = the signed area enclosed by the up and down branches, normalised by the probe's belief range; the Bayesian-symmetric NULL sets b_rational(e)=sigma(e) (logistic in the stipulated cumulative log-likelihood-ratio), whose loop area is 0. THRESHOLD GAP = uninstall-threshold minus install-threshold in stipulated LLR units. Added baselines (all experiments): behavioural conclusion-probability, a recency/primacy-only model (predicts from evidence order alone), and hidden-state CCA alignment to the oracle trajectory, in addition to the closed-book log-prob baseline. Downstream task: a RAG-style correction benchmark where a retrieved document contradicts an installed claim — we report end-task retraction rate and its correlation with loop area, so the effect is shown to matter for system behaviour, not only probe trajectories.

Statistical analysis plan. The unit of analysis is the item; we report bootstrap 95% CIs over items and over seeds {0,1,2}, fit mixed-effects models with random intercepts for item and fixed effects for model family and plausibility, and apply Benjamini-Hochberg correction across the layer/head/model comparisons. A power analysis fixes per-model/condition sample sizes to a minimum detectable normalised loop area of 0.05. The PREREGISTERED PRIMARY endpoint is the Experiment 1 (H1) normalised loop area > 0; all numeric thresholds above are heuristic desiderata, and inference rests on the CIs, not the bins. Minimum viable scope: H1 (loop area vs the symmetric null with the recency/primacy control) plus the H4 subtractive-steering causal demo; H2 grading and full head localisation are contingent refinements. H4 head localisation is framed as candidate circuitry unless lesion+rescue+specificity all hold.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Hysteresis could partly reflect rational asymmetry (e.g. a prior-plausible claim rationally needs more counter-evidence to dislodge); the synthetic track with explicit matched likelihood ratios and a Bayesian-symmetric oracle, plus the prior-plausibility manipulation, are designed to separate genuine order/direction-dependent stubbornness from justified prior-weighting, though full separation is hard for real claims. The apparent loop could be driven by evidence-order/primacy effects rather than an install-vs-uninstall asymmetry per se; matched reversed sweeps and order-of-piece perturbations disentangle these (both sweeps contain identical pieces in mirrored order). The effect may be absent internally (a robust negative result -- LLMs update reversibly -- is itself valuable and reassuring). Belief may not be cleanly linearly decodable at every step; we report layerwise results with control tasks and treat loop shape, not absolute values, as the object of study. The stubbornness component may be distributed; we treat 'steer to symmetrize' as the causal test rather than pinning an exact head. Steering could degrade fluency or make the model indiscriminately gullible/labile; we use small magnitudes, random/truth-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity, non-swept accuracy, and general benchmarks. Sticky-error scoring on open-ended output needs an LLM-judge plus human validation. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

Name: internal_belief_coherence_gap
Title: Rational Inside, Fallacious Out: Is the Conjunction Fallacy a Readout Bug in LLM Belief Representations?
Short Hypothesis: The conjunction fallacy and related probabilistic incoherence in LLMs are largely a *verbalization/readout* failure rather than a failure of the model's internal belief representation: a linearly-decoded internal belief-strength readout for conjunctions (P(A∧B)) respects probability-theory monotonicity (≤ P(A) and ≤ P(B)) far more often than the model's stated probability judgments do. The internal representation is thus more coherent than the output, the residual internal incoherence is carried by an identifiable component, and steering it can bring stated judgments back into coherence.
Related Work: Behavioral work shows LLMs produce incoherent probability judgments mirroring human systematic deviations (Incoherent Probability Judgments in LLMs, Zhu et al. 2024) and commit the conjunction fallacy driven by token bias (A Peek into Token Bias, 2024; Thinking Fast and Slow in LLMs, 2022). Others attempt to *recover* coherent probabilities from embeddings by imposing axiomatic constraints via a trained VAE (Recovering Event Probabilities from LLM Embeddings, 2025) or find LLMs fail to give rational probabilistic beliefs at the output (Exploring the Potential..., 2025). Interpretability work isolates linear truth/belief directions (Geometry of Truth 2023; Truth-value judgment 2024), plausibility/modal-category vectors (Is This Just Fantasy? 2025), and belief-state geometry (Constrained Belief Updates 2025). CRITICALLY, all prior probabilistic-coherence work is either purely behavioral or *engineers* a coherent latent via extra training; none ask whether the model's *own, natively-decoded* belief-strength representation already respects the conjunction rule while its verbal output violates it — i.e., whether the fallacy is representational or a readout artifact — nor localize/causally steer the incoherence. We reframe a canonical human-cognition bias as a decodable internal-vs-stated coherence gap and give it a mechanistic, causal treatment, distinct from all my prior single-belief attribute proposals (this concerns *coherence relations among multiple beliefs*).
Abstract: People judge 'Linda is a bank teller and a feminist' as more probable than 'Linda is a bank teller' — the conjunction fallacy, a signature violation of probability theory. LLMs reproduce this and related incoherences in their stated judgments, and prior work either documents this behaviorally or trains auxiliary models to squeeze coherent probabilities out of embeddings. We ask a sharper, mechanistic question: is the fallacy a bug in the model's internal belief representation, or a bug in how that representation is read out into words? We hypothesize that a linearly-decoded internal belief-strength readout for a conjunction P(A∧B) respects the conjunction rule (it is ≤ the readouts for P(A) and P(B)) substantially more often than the model's verbalized probability judgments do; that the internal representation is therefore more coherent than the output; that the residual internal incoherence is carried by an identifiable component; and that steering it restores coherence in the stated judgments. We construct a controlled dataset of item propositions and their conjunctions/disjunctions (Linda-style representativeness pairs, plus neutral and synthetic-entity conjunctions to control priors and token-bias confounds). On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) we train linear belief-strength probes, compute per-triple internal vs. stated conjunction-rule violation rates, geometrically relate a 'coherence-violation' direction to the truth/plausibility directions, localize the responsible heads via activation patching, and test whether steering reduces both internal and stated violations. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, internal vs. stated violation-rate gap, monotonicity error, subspace angle, patching effect sizes, post-steering coherence gains, and perplexity.
Experiments:
Setup shared by all experiments below. Models: four frozen open-weight base LLMs — Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B; model weights are never updated (frozen), the only trainable objects are lightweight linear read-out probes and difference-of-means steering vectors. Probes: L2-regularized logistic-regression classifiers (or ridge regressors for graded read-outs) fit on residual-stream activations at the named token, one probe per layer, regularization set by 5-fold cross-validation; every probe is trained and evaluated with 5 seeds {0,1,2,3,4} (mean±95% CI reported) and paired with a shuffled-label control task. A probe counts as genuinely reading the target attribute only if held-out AUROC ≥ 0.75 while its control-task AUROC ≤ 0.55; the band 0.55–0.75 (or control AUROC > 0.55) is the indecision zone — that layer/model is reported as 'representation too weak to interpret', not as evidence. Steering vectors are contrastive difference-of-means (activation-addition) directions between the two matched conditions named in each experiment; steering strength is swept over 5 magnitudes and reported as a dose-response. Collateral-damage guardrails for every causal intervention: perplexity on held-out text must rise ≤ 5% and 5-shot MMLU (1k-item subset) must drop ≤ 2 points to count as 'clean'; 5–10% perplexity or 2–4 MMLU points is the indecision band (effect real but not cleanly separable); worse than that fails the guardrail.

Data. 5,000 proposition triples (A, B, A∧B) built from scratch: (a) ~1,700 representativeness/Linda-style pairs (B typical); (b) ~1,300 neutral pairs (A,B unrelated); (c) ~1,300 synthetic-entity triples with stipulated base rates so a ground-truth coherent ordering exists; (d) ~700 disjunction triples (A, B, A∨B). Swapped-conjunct controls (which conjunct is representative), paraphrase/format/order perturbations, and comprehension checks accompany each. Because the internal read-out is graded, the belief-strength probe is a ridge regressor calibrated on a held-out set of propositions with known relative probabilities. ~4,200 triples usable; 80/20 split with no proposition shared.

Experiment 1 (H1 — the internally-decoded conjunction read-out respects monotonicity more often than the stated judgment does). Elicit the STATED probabilities/comparisons and compute the stated conjunction-rule violation rate (P(A∧B) > P(A)); separately read the graded belief-strength probe for A, B, A∧B WITHOUT the comparison question and compute the INTERNAL violation rate (read-out(A∧B) > min(read-out(A), read-out(B))). Decisive metric: internal minus stated violation-rate gap, per condition/layer. Convincing: internal violation rate is ≥ 15 percentage points BELOW the stated rate, most strongly on representativeness pairs, in ≥ 3 of 4 models, with the internal read-out preserving monotonicity on items where the verbal output flips. Indecision band: gap 5–15 points → weak; < 5 points → the representation is as incoherent as the output (a substantive negative: the fallacy is representational, not a read-out artifact).

Experiment 2 (H2 — residual internal incoherence is carried by an identifiable component that injects the representativeness pull). Compute a coherence-violation direction (violating vs. non-violating conjunctions, after controlling for representativeness) and its subspace angle to the truth/plausibility direction; localize via patching representativeness-pair↔neutral-pair runs (contrast with token-bias and plausibility heads). Decisive metric: fraction of internal violations flipped to coherent when the located component is patched out, and projected-out decodability. Convincing: patching ≤ 5% of heads flips ≥ 50% of internal violations and violation stays decodable (AUROC ≥ 0.75) after projecting out plausibility (angle > 60°). Indecision band: 20–50% flipped or angle 45–60° → partial/entangled; < 20% = distributed.

Experiment 3 (H3 — steering the coherence direction brings STATED judgments into coherence). Apply the coherence steering direction. Decisive metric first: stated conjunction/disjunction violation rate after steering; secondary: whether the internal read-out predicts, per triple, when the model will emit an incoherent stated judgment (AUROC over a log-prob baseline), then Setup guardrails; baselines random/plausibility directions. Convincing: steering cuts the stated violation rate by ≥ 50% toward the internally-implied ordering, cleanly on guardrails, while negation exaggerates the fallacy and baselines cut violations < 10%; prediction AUROC ≥ 0.70 over the log-prob baseline. Indecision band: 20–50% reduction or guardrails only in the 5–10%/2–4-point band. A negative result (no steer restores stated coherence without breaching guardrails) means the incoherence is not a modular read-out component. Generalization: transfer across representativeness/neutral/synthetic tracks, to disjunctions and simple base-rate-neglect items.

Statistical analysis (all experiments). Effects are estimated with mixed-effects models carrying random intercepts for item and for model family, so results are pooled across the four models without pseudo-replication; every rate, slope, AUROC, and effect size is reported with a bootstrap 95% CI (10,000 item-level resamples). Multiplicity across layers, heads, and steering magnitudes is controlled with Benjamini–Hochberg FDR at q = 0.05. H1 is the pre-registered primary hypothesis; H2 is secondary and the localization/steering hypothesis is confirmatory-exploratory, reported as such unless its pre-stated causal criterion is met.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The internal belief-strength probe requires a calibrated graded readout, which is harder than a binary truth probe; miscalibration could artificially inflate or deflate the internal violation rate. We mitigate by calibrating on held-out propositions with known relative probabilities, reporting layerwise results with control tasks, and focusing on the *relative* ordering (monotonicity) rather than absolute probabilities. It is possible the internal representation is *equally* incoherent as the output — a robust null (no internal-vs-stated gap) would still be a valuable, publishable finding, showing the fallacy is representational, not a readout artifact, and constraining the 'recover coherent probabilities from embeddings' program. The coherence-violation signal may be entangled with the representativeness/plausibility direction (violating conjunctions are exactly the typical ones); the swapped-conjunct controls, neutral pairs, synthetic track, and projected-out analyses are designed to dissociate representativeness pull from genuine incoherence, though full separation is difficult. Reading belief at 'matched' tokens across A, B, and A∧B is imperfect since the conjunction is longer; we anchor probes at shared conjunct tokens and use paraphrase perturbations. Localization may be distributed; we treat 'steer to restore coherence' as the causal test rather than pinning an exact head. Steering could degrade fluency or make the model indiscriminately rank conjunctions as improbable (harming cases where a conjunction is legitimately near a conjunct); we use small magnitudes, random/plausibility-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity, non-conjunction accuracy, and general benchmarks. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

Name: belief_binding_conflict
Title: One Fact, Many Faces: Do LLMs Bind Beliefs to Meaning or to Surface Form?
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM is told a fact and then queried about it, the internal belief it updates is bound to a surface-form-specific representation rather than a canonical meaning-level slot; consequently, two surface variants of the same proposition carve out *distinct* internal belief tokens that can be independently, and even contradictorily, updated. We hypothesize this 'belief binding' is localizable and that a single mechanism explains both cross-paraphrase inconsistency and the ability to hold contradictory beliefs about the same fact under different phrasings. The contribution is not 'brittleness exists' but a mechanistic account: beliefs can be independently, even contradictorily, updated under paraphrase-specific handles, tested by whether contradictory injections under two forms coexist internally rather than resolve. We report belief behaviorally (answer distributions/log-probs) alongside probe readouts so the claim does not rest on probing alone.
Related Work: Prior work shows truthfulness/belief directions are brittle to paraphrase and OOD surface form (Brittle Minds 2024; Representational Stability of Truth 2025; LLM Knowledge is Brittle 2025), that factual knowledge is cross-lingually inconsistent with a middle/final-layer bottleneck (Cross-Lingual Consistency 2025; Lost in Multilinguality 2025), and that PLMs lack factual coherency (Queen of England 2024). Belief directions are context-sensitive causal mediators (Truth-value judgment 2024). All of these *characterize* brittleness as a defect. Our proposal is different: we treat surface-form dependence as evidence of a specific mechanism—that beliefs are *bound* to form-specific internal handles rather than a shared meaning slot—and we directly test this by injecting a fact in form A and reading/steering the belief in form B, measuring belief transfer as a function of representational binding. We introduce a controllable 'belief-binding' probe and a causal test of whether a single fact occupies one slot or many, which prior descriptive work does not do. What prior brittleness papers cannot distinguish that our contradiction-coexistence test can: they show paraphrase/OOD instability of a truth readout (Brittle Minds 2024; Representational Stability of Truth 2025) but cannot say whether two forms instantiate one meaning slot updated noisily or two independently-writable handles; the coexistence test discriminates these directly. Under a meaning-bound view a contradictory second-form injection overwrites or is rejected; under our form-bound view both persist. Probing/patching are standard; the novelty is the binding hypothesis and its causal test. Released artifact: a paraphrase/translation-matched injection benchmark with comprehension controls and an ablation separating paraphrase, syntax, lexical, and cross-lingual variants (possibly distinct mechanisms). We soften 'single mechanism' to 'a shared form-invariance direction that partially accounts for both effects'.
Abstract: Large language models can be told a fact and later answer questions about it, but they are notoriously inconsistent: rephrase the query and the answer, and the model's confidence, can flip. Prior work documents this brittleness as a failure of robust knowledge. We reframe it mechanistically: we hypothesize that when an LLM ingests a novel fact stated in a particular surface form, it updates an internal belief that is *bound to that form* rather than to a canonical meaning-level representation. Under this view, two paraphrases of the same proposition instantiate two distinct internal belief handles that can be updated—and even contradicted—independently. We test this with a controlled in-context belief-injection paradigm. We construct synthetic facts (novel entity-attribute pairs, unlikely to be in pretraining) rendered in matched surface variants (paraphrases, syntactic reorderings, and translations). We inject a fact in form A and then probe the internal belief when the model reads the same proposition in form B, quantifying cross-form belief transfer with linear belief probes on frozen open-weight models (Llama-3, Qwen2.5, Gemma-2). We predict transfer is high within form and degrades systematically with surface distance, tracing a layerwise 'binding site' where form-specific and meaning-level representations converge. We then perform the critical causal test: inject *contradictory* facts under two forms and measure whether the model maintains two coexisting internal beliefs (form-bound) or resolves them (meaning-bound), and whether steering along a 'form-invariance' direction (derived contrastively from high- vs. low-transfer pairs) increases cross-form belief consistency without harming fluency. Metrics: cross-form transfer curves, layerwise binding-site localization via activation patching, contradiction-coexistence rate, post-steering consistency gains, and perplexity. So what: if beliefs are form-bound, knowledge-editing and multilingual-deployment evaluations must test cross-form coexistence, not just single-query accuracy, and editing algorithms should target the convergence layer we localize; a meaning-bound result would instead validate current single-query protocols. We validate at least one result on naturally occurring facts and externally validated edits to address the synthetic-injection concern, and release the benchmark and ablation suite.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 — an in-context injected belief is decodable and bound to a surface handle): Tests that reading a fact updates a decodable belief. Data: built from scratch, 4,000 novel synthetic facts (invented entities/attributes to exclude pretraining), each in matched surface variants: near-paraphrase, syntactic reordering, lexical substitution, and translation into 2 languages, with true/false polarity; plus a 500-item real-fact control set. Split 70/15/15 by base fact. Model: Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, frozen; trainable component only a logistic-regression belief probe P(fact holds) at the attribute token, per layer; 5 seeds. Systems compared: belief probe vs. shuffled-label control. Decisive metric first: within-form probe test AUROC after in-context injection. Convincing: >= 0.85 with control 0.50 +/- 0.05. Indecision band: 0.65-0.75 weak. Negative: < 0.65 means injected belief is not decodable and the binding test is moot.

Experiment 2 (H1 — belief is bound to form, not canonical meaning: cross-form transfer degrades with surface distance): Inject a fact in form A, read the belief probe when the same proposition is queried in form B. Decisive metric first: cross-form transfer = probe belief(A-injected) minus no-injection baseline, as a function of surface distance (edit distance, embedding cosine), summarized as a transfer matrix and a transfer-vs-distance slope. Convincing: within-form transfer >= 0.8 of the direct-injection effect while cross-form transfer falls to <= 0.4 for the most distant variants, with a monotone negative slope (bootstrap CI excludes 0). Indecision band: cross-form transfer 0.4-0.6 for distant variants is partial form-binding. Negative: transfer near-constant across forms (>= 0.7 even for distant variants) means beliefs are meaning-bound, refuting H1's binding claim.

Experiment 3 (H1 — the binding site is localizable): Activation patching of A-context activations into a B-only run; find the minimal layer set that restores the form-B belief. Decisive metric first: layer at which patched A-context first moves the B belief by >= 50% of full transfer. Convincing: a reproducible convergence layer band across seeds and models. Indecision band: a broad band is reported as gradual convergence. Negative: no patch location restores >= 20% means binding is not localizable.

Experiment 4 (H2 — contradictory facts under two forms coexist rather than resolve): The critical test of independent form-bound handles. Inject A asserting and B negating the same proposition; read both probes and query behaviorally. Decisive metric first: contradiction-coexistence rate = fraction of items where each form's probe reads its own injected value. Convincing: coexistence >= 0.6 (form-bound) vs. a meaning-bound null of near-0 (one value dominates). Indecision band: 0.3-0.6 partial. Negative: <= 0.3 means the model resolves contradictions to one belief (meaning-bound).

Experiment 5 (H1 — a single mechanism links paraphrase inconsistency and contradictory-belief holding): Derive a form-invariance CAA vector (high- minus low-transfer form pairs) and apply it during B-query, alpha at 2/4/8% residual norm. Systems compared: form-invariance steering vs. random-direction steering. Decisive metric first: increase in cross-form belief consistency; secondary: reduction in contradiction-coexistence, unrelated-fact accuracy, MMLU-subset, perplexity. Convincing: >= 15-point consistency gain and >= 10-point coexistence reduction, random steering < 5 points, perplexity rise < 10%, and symmetric-relation items unharmed. Indecision band: 5-15 point gains suggestive. Negative: < 5 points beyond random means no shared steerable mechanism.

Experiment 6 (H1 — generalization): Apply frozen probe and steering across fact domains, real-fact, and cross-lingual subsets. Decisive metric first: transfer AUROC. Convincing: >= 0.70. Indecision band: 0.60-0.70. Negative: <= 0.60.

Experiment 7 (H1 — behavioral belief and natural-fact validation): Complements probe readouts with behavior and reduces the synthetic-injection concern. Data: a 500-item real-fact subset with externally validated edits (adapted from a standard knowledge-editing benchmark) plus matched paraphrase/translation queries; comprehension of each variant is verified before injection. Decisive metric first: cross-form behavioral consistency = agreement of answer distributions (JS divergence) across forms, alongside the probe transfer of Experiment 2, compared to a standard knowledge-editing baseline and a hidden-state-similarity baseline. Convincing: probe and behavioral form-binding agree (both show the predicted cross-form drop) and comprehension is >= 90% so failures are not parsing. Indecision band: probe and behavior disagree — reported as measurement-dependent. Negative: behavior shows no cross-form drop despite probe drop means the probe effect lacks behavioral consequence.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Cross-form transfer failures could reflect comprehension failures rather than form-bound belief storage; we include comprehension checks and use matched real-fact controls. Synthetic entities may be represented differently from real knowledge; we complement with real-fact subsets. Linear belief probes may not cleanly capture the belief at every layer; we report layerwise results and use control tasks. The 'binding site' may be distributed rather than a discrete layer, weakening the clean localization story (still informative as a gradient). Form-invariance steering may degrade fluency or overwrite legitimate distinctions (e.g., subject/object asymmetric relations); we monitor perplexity, use small magnitudes, and separately analyze symmetric vs. asymmetric relations. Results may not transfer to very large closed models. Comprehension controls are first-class: each paraphrase/translation is verified as understood pre-injection so understanding failures are separated from transfer failures. E4 coexistence controls for order, recency, prompt position, and context segmentation. We report behavioral belief measures (answer distributions/log-probs) beside probe AUROC so conclusions do not rest on linear probing alone, and we keep separate the descriptive paraphrase/syntax/lexical/cross-lingual mechanisms.

Name: aleatoric_epistemic_belief_split
Title: I Don't Know vs. Nobody Can Know: Do LLMs Internally Distinguish Epistemic from Aleatoric Uncertainty in Their Beliefs?
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM is uncertain about an item's state, it internally represents not just how uncertain it is (magnitude) but WHY: whether the uncertainty is epistemic (reducible - the model lacks information but a determinate answer exists) or aleatoric (irreducible - the outcome is genuinely random/indeterminate). This uncertainty-type signal is linearly decodable, largely orthogonal to the scalar uncertainty-magnitude direction studied in prior work, and causally gates the model's information-seeking/abstention behavior (it should defer or seek evidence under epistemic uncertainty but not under aleatoric uncertainty). We narrow the novelty: not 'first to distinguish aleatoric vs. epistemic' broadly, but first to test an internal, decodable, and steerable uncertainty-TYPE representation under matched-uncertainty-magnitude controls, using a restricted operational notion (clear-case irreducible-random vs. answerable-but-unknown-to-this-model) rather than the fully general, perspective-dependent philosophical distinction.
Related Work: Prior interpretability work treats uncertainty as a scalar magnitude: verbal uncertainty is a single linear feature (Calibrating Verbal Uncertainty / MUC 2025), semantic vs. verbal uncertainty mismatch predicts hallucination, calibration is a distributed low-dimensional direction (Calibration Across Layers 2025), entropy/token-frequency neurons regulate confidence (2024), models 'know the road not taken' (2025), belief manifolds encode a posterior's mean and variance (Shape of Beliefs 2026; Transformers Represent Belief State Geometry 2024), and models can verbalize calibrated confidence (Lin et al. 2022). Neuroscience distinguishes code-driven vs. correlational representations of uncertainty. Crucially, ALL of this treats uncertainty as one axis (how confident/wide the posterior is). NONE isolate the aleatoric-vs-epistemic DISTINCTION - whether the model represents the SOURCE of uncertainty (reducible ignorance vs. irreducible randomness) as its own internal variable, or links it causally to the correct downstream policy (seek-info/abstain under epistemic uncertainty; commit/report a distribution under aleatoric). We introduce uncertainty-type as an orthogonal, decodable, steerable belief attribute and connect it to a concrete failure mode: models that abstain or over-hedge on genuinely random questions, or confidently guess on answerable-but-unknown ones. We engage prior LLM uncertainty-decomposition and caveat work directly rather than framing all prior work as scalar: some behavioral studies already separate aleatoric from epistemic uncertainty and prompt clarification-seeking. Our delta is that internal geometry plus causal steering is not implied by a behavioral decomposition — a model can act differently without representing type as a separable, manipulable internal variable. Probing/patching/steering are standard; the contribution is the matched-magnitude internal dissociation and its causal link to information-seeking. Released artifact: a matched-entropy aleatoric/epistemic benchmark with per-model ignorance verification and a clarification/abstention-policy diagnostic.
Abstract: A fair coin flip and a trivia question about an obscure fact both leave a language model unable to give a confident answer, but for fundamentally different reasons: the coin is irreducibly random (aleatoric uncertainty - no amount of information would help), while the trivia fact is merely unknown to the model (epistemic uncertainty - a determinate answer exists and could be looked up). Rational agents treat these differently: they seek information or abstain under epistemic uncertainty but simply report a distribution under aleatoric uncertainty. Prior interpretability work has thoroughly characterized uncertainty as a scalar magnitude (verbal-uncertainty features, calibration directions, entropy neurons, posterior-width manifolds) but has never asked whether LLMs internally represent WHY they are uncertain. We hypothesize that the aleatoric-vs-epistemic distinction is (i) linearly decodable from residual-stream activations, (ii) largely orthogonal to the scalar uncertainty-magnitude direction, and (iii) causally gates information-seeking/abstention behavior. We build a controlled dataset of item-state questions matched for uncertainty magnitude but varying in type: genuinely random/indeterminate (dice, coin flips, unknowable future events, ties) vs. answerable-but-unknown-to-the-model (obscure facts, redacted-but-determinate values, synthetic entity attributes withheld from context). We train linear probes on frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Pythia-2.8B) to decode uncertainty type vs. magnitude, measure their geometric relationship (subspace angle, projected-out decodability), localize responsible heads via activation patching, and test causal control: steering along the uncertainty-type direction should shift whether the model chooses to seek information/abstain vs. commit to a distribution. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, subspace angle, projected-out decodability, patching effect sizes, information-seeking/abstention-rate shifts, and perplexity. So what: today's systems conflate unknown-but-answerable with inherently indeterminate cases, wasting retrieval on coin-flips and confidently guessing on lookup-able facts; a type signal that beats scalar confidence would improve retrieval/clarification agents and abstention policies. We add a realistic downstream benchmark (retrieval/clarification-seeking agents) showing utility over scalar-confidence baselines, target measurable gains (reduced unnecessary retrieval, better abstention calibration, fewer confident guesses on answerable-but-unknown items), and release the benchmark and diagnostic.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 — uncertainty TYPE, aleatoric vs. epistemic, is linearly decodable): Data: built from scratch, 6,000 item-state questions in three groups matched for behavioral uncertainty magnitude (verified via the model's answer-distribution entropy): ALEATORIC/irreducible (fair random processes, genuine ties, no-fact-of-the-matter), EPISTEMIC-answerable-but-unknown (obscure real facts; a synthetic track where a novel entity's fixed attribute is defined but withheld), and a SETTLED-KNOWN low-uncertainty anchor; crucially includes MATCHED PAIRS of equal answer-entropy but different type; comprehension checks and paraphrase perturbations included; split 70/15/15 by item. Model: Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Pythia-2.8B, frozen; trainable only a logistic-regression probe on the item/question representation, per layer; 5 seeds. Systems compared: type probe (restricted to high-uncertainty items) vs. shuffled-label control vs. keyword baseline ('random/roll/fair'). Decisive metric first: type-probe test AUROC at best layer. Convincing: >= 0.80, control 0.50 +/- 0.05, >= 0.05 above keyword baseline, on >=3 of 4 models. Indecision band: 0.60-0.70 or within 0.05 of keyword baseline inconclusive. Negative: < 0.60 (especially on matched-entropy pairs) is an informative negative about the limits of LLM epistemic self-modeling.

Experiment 2 (H2 — type is largely orthogonal to uncertainty MAGNITUDE): Fit a magnitude probe (entropy bins) and the MUC difference-in-means verbal-uncertainty feature as baselines. Decisive metric first: type AUROC after projecting out the magnitude direction and, separately, the MUC feature, evaluated on the matched-entropy pairs; secondary: subspace angles. Convincing: >= 90% retention against both and angles > 60 degrees. Indecision band: 70-90% retention partial. Negative: < 70% retention means type is a re-description of magnitude.

Experiment 3 (H3 — the type signal causally gates information-seeking/abstention): Build a type CAA vector (aleatoric minus epistemic activations, controlling for magnitude). Data: a 1,000-item information-seeking probe offering ANSWER / SEEK-INFO / REPORT-DISTRIBUTION. Systems compared: type-direction vs. random vs. magnitude-direction steering, alpha 2/4/8% residual norm. Decisive metric first: change in information-seeking/abstention rate on aleatoric items when steered toward 'epistemic', and its decrease on epistemic items when steered toward 'aleatoric'; secondary: MMLU-subset, perplexity. Convincing: >= 15-point shift in the targeted behavior, random < 5 points, perplexity rise < 10%. Indecision band: 5-15 points suggestive. Negative: < 5 beyond random or equals magnitude steering means no distinct causal type gate.

Experiment 4 (H1 — localization): Activation patching between matched aleatoric/epistemic runs; compare heads to entropy/confidence-regulation neurons and calibration directions from prior work. Decisive metric first: fraction of the type distinction recovered by top heads. Convincing: reproducible <= 20-head set recovers >= 50%. Indecision band: diffuse = distributed. Negative: no head > 20%.

Experiment 5 (H3 — predictiveness): Decisive metric first: AUROC using the type probe to predict the model's information-seeking choice and abstention-appropriateness vs. a scalar-uncertainty baseline. Convincing: >= 0.70 and >= 0.05 above the scalar baseline. Indecision band: 0.60-0.70. Negative: <= 0.60.

Experiment 6 (H1,H3 — generalization): Apply frozen probe/steering across chance games, unknown facts, future events, synthetic withheld attributes, and synthetic-to-real. Decisive metric first: transfer AUROC and behavior-effect retention. Convincing: >= 0.70 and half retained. Indecision band: 0.60-0.70. Negative: <= 0.60.

Experiment 7 (H1,H3 — verified ignorance and an explicit agent policy task): Ensures 'epistemic' items are genuinely unknown to the model and grounds the causal claim in a real policy. Data: for epistemic items, model ignorance is verified per model by pretesting closed-book answerability, or a synthetic world with known ground truth and controlled exposure is used; the behavioral task is an explicit agent with actions ANSWER / SEEK-INFO(retrieve) / REPORT-DISTRIBUTION and a defined correct policy per item (retrieve for epistemic, distribution for aleatoric). Decisive metric first: task regret (cost-weighted wrong-policy rate) using the type probe or type-steering vs. a scalar-confidence policy and a behavioral-policy baseline; semantic-equivalence and task-performance checks confirm steering does not merely change verbosity/hedging. Convincing: >= 15% relative regret reduction over the scalar-confidence policy with unchanged task accuracy and perplexity rise < 10%. Indecision band: 5-15% reduction is suggestive. Negative: no regret reduction over scalar confidence means type adds no decision value.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Uncertainty type may be entangled with surface cues (words like 'random', 'roll', 'fair') rather than an abstract epistemic representation; we mitigate with diverse framings, paraphrases, matched-content controls, and the synthetic withheld-attribute track where 'epistemic' is inferred from a stated-but-hidden determinate value rather than a keyword. Type and magnitude may be less orthogonal than hypothesized (aleatoric items may cluster at specific magnitudes); the matched-entropy pairs are designed precisely to dissociate them, and even a characterization of entanglement is informative. The model may not actually possess a normative aleatoric/epistemic distinction, in which case a robust negative result (type is NOT decodable beyond magnitude) is itself a meaningful finding about the limits of LLM epistemic self-modeling. Information-seeking behavior depends on prompt scaffolding and may be instruction-following rather than driven by internal type representation; the matched design, comprehension checks, and predictiveness analysis relative to internal probes help disentangle these. Some 'aleatoric' items may be treated by the model as answerable and vice versa; we validate labels and use the model's own answer-entropy to define magnitude. Steering could degrade fluency (off-manifold) or overshoot into indiscriminate abstention; we use small magnitudes, random/magnitude-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity and general benchmarks. Results may not transfer to very large closed models. Labels use a restricted taxonomy of clear-case aleatoric vs. epistemic with human agreement and explicit exclusion criteria, and the perspective-dependence of the distinction is stated up front and handled by the restricted operational notion. Epistemic items are independently verified as unknown to each model. Confound controls include adversarial lexical-cue removal, balanced domains/templates, cue-free paraphrases, and transfer to unseen surface forms. Baselines go beyond keyword/shuffled to topic, template, answer-format classifiers, and scalar confidence/entropy/MUC-only models. Orthogonality is presented as approximate disentanglement with predefined partial-support criteria; the minimum viable path is E1/E2 with airtight labeling plus the single agent-policy intervention.

Name: source_independence_discounting
Title: Counting Voices, Not Sources: Do LLMs Internally Track Whether Consensus Is Independent?
Short Hypothesis: When multiple retrieved documents assert the same claim, a rational agent should update its belief more if the sources are independent than if they are copies of one origin (the 'illusion of consensus' failure in humans). We hypothesize that LLMs DO form an internal, linearly-decodable representation of source independence-vs-dependence, but that this representation is causally under-weighted: the belief-update magnitude tracks raw report COUNT far more than the internally-available independence signal. We further hypothesize an identifiable internal component gates independence-discounting, and steering it can restore appropriate discounting of redundant sources — improving RAG faithfulness on repeated-but-non-independent evidence.
Related Work: Human social-learning work shows people partially discount correlated/dependent sources and distinguish true from false consensus (Bayesian belief polarization via source-independence perceptions, 2024; belief revision sensitive to statistical dependencies, 2020; social meta-inference / evidentiary value of consensus, 2021; getting to the source of the illusion of consensus, 2021). In LLMs, behavioral RAG work finds models are 'heuristic followers': paraphrased repetition is MORE persuasive than distinct independent support, and models show primacy/repetition biases (GroupQA: Rational Synthesizers or Heuristic Followers?, 2026; DynamicQA 2024). Knowledge-conflict probing shows parametric-vs-contextual source and conflict are linearly decodable (Probing Language Models on Their Knowledge Source, 2024; ProbeRAG/CLEAR, 2025), and Belief Dynamics (2025) gives a Bayesian account of in-context evidence accumulation as sigmoidal in report count. My prior 'illusory_truth_internal' proposal studies repetition-count dose-response of a single claim's belief, and 'belief_source_tags' studies provenance (prior/context/retrieval). to our knowledge, none isolate an internal representation of source INDEPENDENCE (are these N reports genuinely distinct origins or copies of one?), nor test whether the belief-update under-weights that internally-available signal relative to raw count, nor causally restore independence-discounting. We transfer the canonical 'illusion of consensus' into LLM internals and give it a mechanistic, causal treatment.
Abstract: If ten news outlets independently confirm a claim, it is far stronger evidence than the same story copied ten times from one wire report. Humans partially honor this distinction; recent behavioral work shows LLMs largely do not, treating paraphrased repetition as more persuasive than genuinely independent support — an 'illusion of consensus' with direct consequences for retrieval-augmented generation. We ask a sharper, mechanistic question: does an LLM internally represent whether a set of agreeing sources is independent or dependent, and if so, why does it fail to use that signal? We hypothesize that (i) source independence-vs-dependence is linearly decodable from residual-stream activations at the point the model reads a group of agreeing reports, (ii) the model's internal belief-update magnitude nonetheless tracks raw report COUNT far more than this independence signal (a decodable-but-under-used representation), (iii) an identifiable internal component gates independence-discounting, and (iv) steering that component restores appropriate discounting of redundant sources. We build a controlled dataset of item-state claims each supported by N reports whose INDEPENDENCE is varied (verbatim copies, paraphrases attributed to one origin, and genuinely distinct independent sources) at matched surface repetition counts, with a synthetic-entity track to control priors. On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) we train linear probes to decode independence and to read internal belief, quantify how belief tracks count vs. independence against a Bayesian oracle, localize the gating component via activation patching, and test a contrastive steering intervention that restores discounting. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, count-vs-independence belief sensitivity, oracle-deviation, patching effect sizes, post-steering discounting restoration and RAG-faithfulness gains, and perplexity.
Experiments:
Setup shared by all experiments below. Models: four frozen open-weight base LLMs — Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B; model weights are never updated (frozen), the only trainable objects are lightweight linear read-out probes and difference-of-means steering vectors. Probes: L2-regularized logistic-regression classifiers (or ridge regressors for graded read-outs) fit on residual-stream activations at the named token, one probe per layer, regularization set by 5-fold cross-validation; every probe is trained and evaluated with 5 seeds {0,1,2,3,4} (mean±95% CI reported) and paired with a shuffled-label control task. A probe counts as genuinely reading the target attribute only if held-out AUROC ≥ 0.75 while its control-task AUROC ≤ 0.55; the band 0.55–0.75 (or control AUROC > 0.55) is the indecision zone — that layer/model is reported as 'representation too weak to interpret', not as evidence. Steering vectors are contrastive difference-of-means (activation-addition) directions between the two matched conditions named in each experiment; steering strength is swept over 5 magnitudes and reported as a dose-response. Collateral-damage guardrails for every causal intervention: perplexity on held-out text must rise ≤ 5% and 5-shot MMLU (1k-item subset) must drop ≤ 2 points to count as 'clean'; 5–10% perplexity or 2–4 MMLU points is the indecision band (effect real but not cleanly separable); worse than that fails the guardrail.

Data. 5,000 item-state claims built from scratch across news-style facts, science claims, and entity-attributes, in two tracks: (a) ~2,500 real claims; (b) ~2,500 synthetic novel-entity claims with stipulated truth and, on the synthetic track, an explicit likelihood-ratio Bayesian oracle. Each claim is supported by N ∈ {1,2,4,8} reports whose INDEPENDENCE is varied at matched N: INDEPENDENT (distinct authors/outlets/wording), DEPENDENT-VERBATIM (one report copied N times, attributed to one origin), DEPENDENT-PARAPHRASE (N paraphrases explicitly derived from one origin), crossed with true/false. A downstream belief/confidence probe, a comprehension check (restate which sources are independent), and order/length-matched controls accompany each item; ~4,000 usable; 80/20 split.

Experiment 1 (H1 — source independence-vs-dependence is linearly decodable, i.e. internally available). Train a probe to classify INDEPENDENT vs. DEPENDENT groups at matched N from activations taken after the model reads the evidence group. Decisive metric: held-out AUROC (against the Setup bar and control task). Convincing: AUROC ≥ 0.75 at some layer in ≥ 3 of 4 models, including a condition where independence must be inferred from author/wording diversity rather than an explicit 'reprinted from' tag. Indecision band: AUROC 0.55–0.75 → signal too weak to claim it is represented; ≤ 0.55 = negative (the model simply does not encode independence).

Experiment 2 (H2 — the belief-update tracks raw report count far more than the internally-available independence signal). Read the internal belief and regress belief ~ count + independence; compare standardized coefficients and the per-item deviation from the Bayesian oracle (synthetic track). Systems compared: internal belief sensitivity vs. verbal output vs. oracle. Decisive metric: ratio of the count coefficient to the independence coefficient. Convincing: count coefficient ≥ 3× the independence coefficient with the independence coefficient far below its oracle value in ≥ 3 of 4 models (under-weighting). Indecision band: ratio 1.5–3× → partial under-weighting; ≤ 1.5× with independence near oracle = negative (the model already discounts appropriately — itself an informative finding).

Experiment 3 (H3 — an identifiable component gates independence-discounting and steering it restores discounting). Localize via patching INDEPENDENT↔DEPENDENT runs at matched N (contrast with knowledge-source/conflict and copying heads); derive an independence-discounting steering direction. Decisive metric first: RAG-faithfulness/accuracy on a task where most retrieved passages are non-independent copies of a FALSE claim and a minority independent source is correct; secondary: the unwarranted belief update on DEPENDENT groups moved toward the oracle, then Setup guardrails; baselines random/truth directions. Convincing: steering raises RAG accuracy by ≥ 15 points and moves the dependent-group update ≥ 50% toward the oracle, cleanly on guardrails, while removing the direction on INDEPENDENT groups collapses the update (confirming causality) and baselines change accuracy < 5 points. Indecision band: 5–15-point gain or guardrails only in the 5–10%/2–4-point band. A negative result (no component restores discounting without breaching guardrails) means independence-discounting is not a modular, steerable mechanism. Generalization: transfer across domains, real/synthetic tracks, dependence types, and counts.

Statistical analysis (all experiments). Effects are estimated with mixed-effects models carrying random intercepts for item and for model family, so results are pooled across the four models without pseudo-replication; every rate, slope, AUROC, and effect size is reported with a bootstrap 95% CI (10,000 item-level resamples). Multiplicity across layers, heads, and steering magnitudes is controlled with Benjamini–Hochberg FDR at q = 0.05. H1 is the pre-registered primary hypothesis; H2 is secondary and the localization/steering hypothesis is confirmatory-exploratory, reported as such unless its pre-stated causal criterion is met.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The independence signal may not be internally decodable at all — a robust negative result (LLMs simply count reports and never represent independence) is itself valuable and would sharpen the 'heuristic follower' picture for RAG design. Conversely, if belief already tracks independence appropriately, the interesting finding shifts to characterizing the (smaller-than-expected) illusion — still informative. Independence might be decoded via surface cues (explicit 'reprinted from A' tags) rather than an abstract representation; we mitigate with diverse framings, paraphrase/order perturbations, comprehension checks, and a condition where independence must be inferred from author/wording diversity rather than an explicit tag. Count and independence can be partially confounded with context length and primacy; matched-N designs, length-matched fillers, and order perturbations dissociate them. The Bayesian oracle is exact only on the synthetic track; real-claim oracles are approximate. Steering could degrade fluency or make the model indiscriminately distrust all repeated evidence (harming legitimate independent consensus); we use small magnitudes, random/truth-direction baselines, monitor perplexity, independent-evidence accuracy, and general benchmarks. Downstream RAG-faithfulness scoring on open-ended answers needs automatic + human-validated judging. Localization may be distributed; we treat 'steer to restore discounting' as the causal test rather than pinning an exact head. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

Name: presupposition_failure_flag
Title: There Is No King of France: Do LLMs Internally Flag Presupposition Failure Apart From Mere Ignorance?
Short Hypothesis: LLMs maintain an internal 'presupposition-failure' flag that distinguishes questions that are unanswerable because they carry a FALSE PRESUPPOSITION (there is no fact of the matter because the question's premise is false, e.g. 'When did the King of France abdicate in 2020?') from questions that are merely unanswerable due to MISSING INFORMATION (a determinate answer exists but the model/context lacks it). This flag is linearly decodable, largely orthogonal to a generic unanswerability/abstention direction, and causally gates whether the model challenges the false premise vs. hallucinates or generically abstains.
Related Work: A rich line of work shows LLMs linearly encode (un)answerability and control abstention via a direction (Hidden States of Over-Confident LLMs 2023; Detecting (Un)answerability with Linear Directions 2025), encode question ambiguity in sparse Ambiguity-Encoding Neurons steerable to abstention (Sparse Neurons Carry Ambiguity 2025), and split abstention into knowledge-conflict vs. knowledge-insufficiency via causal inference (ABCA 2025). Critically, 'LLMs Do NOT Really Know What They Don't Know' (2025) shows internal states encode the knowledge-recall process, not truthfulness, making some hallucinations indistinguishable from facts. ALL of this treats unanswerability/ambiguity as (at most) a two-way answerable-vs-not or conflict-vs-insufficiency split. NONE isolate PRESUPPOSITION FAILURE - a question that is void because its premise is false, so the correct response is to CHALLENGE the premise, not to say 'I don't know' - as an internal axis distinct from missing-information ignorance. This is grounded in the linguistics of presupposition accommodation and 'loaded question' fallacies, and targets a distinct failure mode (models answering loaded questions as if valid, or over-generically abstaining) that the abstention/ambiguity literature does not address. It is also distinct from my prior aleatoric/epistemic proposal (randomness vs. ignorance): here both categories are 'unanswerable', but one is void-by-false-premise and the other is determinate-but-unknown. Positioning against the closest benchmarks, one line each: CREPE and FalseQA target false-premise QA behaviorally; ELOQ covers obstinate/unanswerable queries; ABCA distinguishes answerable/unanswerable classes -- none isolate an INTERNAL presupposition-failure sub-axis separable from generic ignorance/abstention. We therefore narrow the claim from 'a new internal axis' to 'a distinguishable internal SUB-AXIS within unanswerability', and add a generic-contradiction / entity-nonexistence probe as a baseline to show the signal is specifically presupposition failure, not broad semantic anomaly.
Abstract: 'When did the King of France abdicate in 2020?' has no answer - not because the information is missing, but because there is no King of France; the right move is to reject the premise, not to guess or to say 'I don't know'. Humans robustly detect such presupposition failures and repair them, yet LLMs frequently either hallucinate an answer to a loaded question or lump it in with ordinary ignorance. Prior interpretability work isolates a single (un)answerability/abstention direction and an ambiguity signal, and splits abstention into knowledge-conflict vs. knowledge-insufficiency, but never asks whether models internally represent PRESUPPOSITION FAILURE - unanswerability because the question's premise is false - as its own variable. We hypothesize that this flag is (i) linearly decodable from residual-stream activations, (ii) largely orthogonal to a generic unanswerability/abstention direction, and (iii) causally gates whether the model challenges the false premise vs. hallucinates or generically abstains. We build a controlled dataset of item-state questions in matched conditions - answerable, unanswerable-due-to-missing-info, and unanswerable-due-to-false-presupposition - holding surface form as constant as possible, plus a synthetic-entity track to control priors. We train linear probes on frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) to decode presupposition-failure vs. generic unanswerability, measure their geometry, localize responsible heads via activation patching, and test causal control: steering the presupposition-failure direction should shift the model between premise-challenging, generic abstention, and hallucination. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, subspace angle, projected-out decodability, patching effect sizes, premise-challenge/abstention/hallucination rate shifts, and perplexity. Failure mode and target: loaded-question hallucination in deployed assistants (answering 'when did X abdicate' when X never reigned). Application domains include search/QA assistants, clinical and legal intake, and customer support. Quantified target: reduce hallucinated answers on false-premise QA at fixed helpfulness, versus a generic-abstention baseline, so the gain is premise-rejection rather than blanket refusal.
Experiments: Common setup (stated once): Models — Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B-v0.3 (base + instruct); frozen weights, only linear probes trained (L2 logistic, C by CV). Activations: residual stream at question/item tokens, all layers, per-head for localization; seeds {0,1,2}; item-level splits. Dataset built from scratch: ~6k questions in three matched conditions holding surface form maximally constant — (A) ANSWERABLE, (B) UNANSWERABLE-MISSING-INFO, (C) UNANSWERABLE-FALSE-PRESUPPOSITION — using presupposition triggers with matched true-vs-false-trigger controls, in REAL and SYNTHETIC-entity tracks. We generate 6k and use all (~2k per condition). A behavioral RESPONSE probe records CHALLENGES-premise / GENERICALLY-ABSTAINS / HALLUCINATES; comprehension checks record whether the model, asked directly, can state the premise is false. Experiment 1 (H1 — a presupposition-failure flag is linearly decodable): train probe I = generic UNANSWERABILITY (A vs B+C) and probe II = PRESUPPOSITION-FAILURE (C vs B, restricted to unanswerable items). Decisive metric first: held-out AUROC of probe II vs shuffled control (0.50±0.05). Convincing H1: AUROC ≥ 0.75 on both tracks. Indecision 0.55–0.65 → weak; ≤ 0.55 refutes H1 (models lump false-premise with ordinary ignorance internally — an informative negative). Experiment 2 (H2 — the flag is largely orthogonal to a generic unanswerability/abstention direction): replicate a generic abstention direction as baseline; compute the principal angle theta between probe II and the abstention direction and projected-out decodability of II. Decisive metric first: theta, corroborated by projected-out AUROC drop < 0.05. Convincing: theta ≥ 60 degrees; indecision 30–60 degrees → partial entanglement; < 30 degrees → not a distinct axis (H2 refuted, characterize the entanglement). Experiment 3 (H3 — the flag causally gates premise-challenging vs hallucination/generic-abstention): derive a presupposition-failure steering direction (false-presupposition vs missing-info activations). Decisive metric first: (a) steering missing-info questions TOWARD 'false-presupposition' increases premise-challenging language and reduces generic abstention; (b) steering false-presupposition questions AWAY increases hallucination/generic abstention. Convincing H3: ≥ 15 pp shift in premise-challenge rate in the predicted direction for each polarity, with random-direction and generic-abstention-direction baselines < 5 pp, perplexity increase < 10%, MMLU-subset drop < 3 pp. Indecision 5–15 pp; < 5 pp means no causal gating. Experiment 4 (localization, supports H2/H3): activation patching to find heads carrying the presupposition-failure signal (logit-difference effect sizes), compared to ambiguity-encoding neurons and abstention-direction heads. Experiment 5 (predictiveness): the internal presupposition-failure readout predicts behavioral premise-challenging (vs hallucination) better than a log-prob baseline AND better than the generic-unanswerability probe (AUROC ≥ 0.70, improvement ≥ 0.05 over each). Behavioral scoring uses an LLM judge with human validation on a 200-item sample. Experiment 6 (generalization): transfer across trigger types, domains, synthetic->real (retention ≥ 0.65). Thresholds fixed pre-data. A/B/C taxonomy is stated with necessary/sufficient conditions (A answerable with a determinate answer; B unanswerable due to missing information but a fact of the matter exists; C unanswerable because a premise is false so no fact of the matter exists), with edge-case exclusion rules and ambiguous-item examples excluded. Human annotation is expanded well beyond 200 items (a stratified >= 1k subset with inter-annotator agreement; kappa >= 0.7 gate). Control datasets: contradiction WITHOUT presupposition failure, rare/unknown-entity questions, and malformed-but-answerable paraphrases; generalization is tested leave-one-trigger-family-out across 3-5 presupposition families to rule out lexical shortcuts. Orthogonality is reported layerwise/tokenwise with CCA/partialling across probe classes, not a single principal angle. A downstream intervention experiment on a realistic false-premise benchmark compares premise-rejection against standard abstention-calibration on user-visible outcomes. Because the output space is multi-behavior (challenge/abstain/hallucinate), the activation-patching target is defined as the change in the probability mass on the CHALLENGE behavior (not a single-token logit diff).
Risk Factors and Limitations: Presupposition-failure may be entangled with surface trigger words (definite descriptions, factive verbs) rather than an abstract epistemic representation; we mitigate with matched true-vs-false-trigger controls, paraphrase perturbations, and the synthetic-entity track where the false premise is established in-context rather than lexically signaled. The distinction may not be cleanly linearly separable or may be layer/model-specific; we report layerwise results with control tasks. Presupposition-failure and generic-unanswerability directions may be less orthogonal than hypothesized, in which case the finding becomes a characterization of their entanglement (still informative and safety-relevant given the recall-process finding that models poorly separate ignorance from falsehood internally). Some 'false-presupposition' items may be treated by the model as merely rare/unknown; comprehension checks and the synthetic track help disentangle premise-detection from premise-flagging, and a robust negative result (models lump false-premise questions with ordinary ignorance internally) is itself a valuable, publishable finding consistent with 'LLMs do NOT know what they don't know'. Behavioral premise-challenge vs. abstention vs. hallucination scoring on open-ended output needs an LLM-judge plus human validation on a sample. Steering could degrade fluency (off-manifold) or overshoot into indiscriminate premise-challenging; we use small magnitudes, random/abstention-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity and general benchmarks. Results may not transfer to very large closed models. We tone down universal related-work claims and state explicitly what would refute the hypothesis (presupposition failure not decodable beyond a generic unanswerability/contradiction probe) versus what would indicate entanglement (decodable but not orthogonal).

Name: belief_halo_contamination
Title: The Halo Inside: Does One Valenced Trait Silently Contaminate an LLM's Beliefs About Logically-Independent Traits?
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the human halo effect, asserting a single valenced trait about an item (e.g., a person is 'attractive', a company is 'ethical') causally shifts an LLM's internally-decoded belief about logically-independent traits of that same item in a valence-congruent direction, holding evidence for those other traits constant. We hypothesize this halo is (i) an internal belief-contamination effect visible before any query, (ii) graded with the strength/valence of the seed trait and larger for traits stereotypically associated with the seed, and (iii) mediated by a dominant valence axis, so that steering along a single valence direction reproduces and removing it abolishes the contamination.
Related Work: The halo effect - a single valenced attribute biasing judgments of unrelated attributes of the same target - is a canonical, heavily-cited human finding (attractiveness halo; 'A Constant Error, Revisited' 2024 on shared lexical context; halo-update effect 2023; confluence theory on irrelevant beliefs 2012; inferred-contagion dispositional bias 2016). In LLMs, prior work documents cognitive biases behaviorally (BiasBuster 2024) and, most relevantly, finds a single dominant 'Valence-Assent Axis' (VAA) jointly encoding 'what is good' and 'what is true' that steers reasoning (A Unified Representation Underlying the Judgment of LLMs 2025). Belief-probing work isolates truth/belief directions (Truth-value judgment 2024; Brittle Minds 2024; Shape of Beliefs 2026), and hallucination-spillover work shows learned knowledge contaminates other tasks via lexical similarity (New-Knowledge-Induced Hallucinations 2025; knowledge overshadowing 2025). CRITICALLY, none isolate the halo effect as an internal belief-contamination phenomenon: whether asserting one valenced trait shifts the internally-decoded belief about *logically-independent* traits of the same item, whether that contamination is graded/stereotype-selective, and whether it rides on the VAA valence axis or on trait-specific spreading. We transfer a canonical human bias into LLM belief internals and give it a mechanistic, causal treatment, distinct from behavioral bias benchmarks and from prior single-belief-attribute proposals.
Abstract: People who learn one good thing about someone assume other unrelated good things too - the halo effect, one of the most robust biases in social cognition. As LLMs increasingly form beliefs about entities (people, products, companies, treatments) from fragments of valenced information, we ask whether they inherit this bias at the level of their internal beliefs, and by what mechanism. We hypothesize that asserting a single valenced trait about an item causally shifts the model's internally-decoded belief about logically-independent traits of that same item in a valence-congruent direction, with the underlying evidence for those other traits held constant. We further hypothesize this halo is graded (larger for stronger/more extreme seed traits and for traits stereotypically linked to the seed) and that, consistent with recent evidence for a dominant Valence-Assent Axis, it is mediated by a single valence direction rather than trait-specific spreading. We build a controlled dataset of items each described by a seed trait (positive/negative/neutral) plus a set of logically-independent target traits, using synthetic entities to control priors. On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) we train linear belief probes to read each target-trait belief before and after the seed appears (no query), compute a per-item halo-contamination score, test stereotype-selectivity and dose-response, extract a valence direction, and test whether steering it reproduces the halo and projecting it out abolishes it, localizing the responsible heads via activation patching. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, halo-contamination magnitude, stereotype and dose modulation, valence-axis mediation share, patching effect sizes, post-intervention halo change, and perplexity.
Experiments:
Setup shared by all experiments below. Models: four frozen open-weight base LLMs — Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B; model weights are never updated (frozen), the only trainable objects are lightweight linear read-out probes and difference-of-means steering vectors. Probes: L2-regularized logistic-regression classifiers (or ridge regressors for graded read-outs) fit on residual-stream activations at the named token, one probe per layer, regularization set by 5-fold cross-validation; every probe is trained and evaluated with 5 seeds {0,1,2,3,4} (mean±95% CI reported) and paired with a shuffled-label control task. A probe counts as genuinely reading the target attribute only if held-out AUROC ≥ 0.75 while its control-task AUROC ≤ 0.55; the band 0.55–0.75 (or control AUROC > 0.55) is the indecision zone — that layer/model is reported as 'representation too weak to interpret', not as evidence. Steering vectors are contrastive difference-of-means (activation-addition) directions between the two matched conditions named in each experiment; steering strength is swept over 5 magnitudes and reported as a dose-response. Collateral-damage guardrails for every causal intervention: perplexity on held-out text must rise ≤ 5% and 5-shot MMLU (1k-item subset) must drop ≤ 2 points to count as 'clean'; 5–10% perplexity or 2–4 MMLU points is the indecision band (effect real but not cleanly separable); worse than that fails the guardrail.

Data. 5,000 items built from scratch across halo-relevant domains (people described by traits, products, companies, medical treatments), in two tracks: (a) ~2,500 real-plausible entities; (b) ~2,500 synthetic novel entities ('Zorel Corp') to remove priors. Each item has a SEED trait at five valence levels {strongly+, mildly+, neutral, mildly−, strongly−} plus a set of logically-independent TARGET traits varying in stereotype association with the seed; a NO-SEED baseline and matched EVIDENCE-controlled targets (an explicit valence-neutral fact per target trait) hold genuine target evidence constant across seed conditions. Comprehension checks and paraphrase/order perturbations included; ~4,000 usable; 80/20 split.

Experiment 1 (H1 — asserting one valenced trait shifts the internal belief about logically-independent traits, valence-congruently, with target evidence held constant). Read the belief probe at each TARGET-trait token WITHOUT querying the target, in SEED vs. NO-SEED; halo-contamination = belief(target|seed) − belief(target|no-seed), signed by seed valence. Systems compared: SEED vs. NO-SEED vs. evidence-controlled targets vs. the model's stated target judgments. Decisive metric: mean signed halo-contamination. Convincing: contamination ≥ 0.10 with CI excluding 0 in ≥ 3 of 4 models, present even when explicit neutral target evidence is supplied. Indecision band: < 0.05 or CI includes 0 → no contamination (a valuable negative: independent traits stay uncontaminated); 0.05–0.10 = suggestive.

Experiment 2 (H2 — the halo is graded with seed valence extremity and with stereotype association). Decisive metric: slope of contamination vs. seed-valence extremity, and the contrast between high- and low-association targets. Convincing: a monotonic positive valence slope (CI excluding 0) AND high-association contamination exceeding low-association by ≥ 0.05, with non-zero contamination even for low/zero-association targets (the irrelevant-belief signature). Indecision band: slope CI includes 0 or high-vs-low gap < 0.03 → grading not established (report the unconditional effect only).

Experiment 3 (H3 — the halo is mediated by a dominant valence axis: steering it reproduces the halo, projecting it out abolishes it). Extract a valence direction (positive vs. negative seed activations), compare to a Valence-Assent-Axis-style direction, and localize the transport via patching SEED→NO-SEED runs. Decisive metric first: mediation share — fraction of contamination explained by movement along the single valence direction, and whether projecting it out at the target abolishes the halo while preserving evidence-based target belief; secondary: adding the direction reproduces the halo on NO-SEED items; downstream, whether halo-reducing steering lowers biased high-stakes ratings (hiring/loan/product-safety) while preserving evidence-based accuracy; then Setup guardrails; baselines random/truth directions. Convincing: valence axis mediates ≥ 50% of contamination, projecting it out cuts the halo by ≥ 50% while evidence-based belief moves < 0.03, biased ratings drop with accuracy preserved, cleanly on guardrails, and baselines move independent targets < 0.02. Indecision band: 20–50% mediation or guardrails only in the 5–10%/2–4-point band → partially unified/partly trait-specific spreading (characterize). A negative result (valence axis explains < 20%) means the halo is distributed/trait-specific, not a single axis. Generalization: transfer across domains, real/synthetic tracks, and association levels.

Statistical analysis (all experiments). Effects are estimated with mixed-effects models carrying random intercepts for item and for model family, so results are pooled across the four models without pseudo-replication; every rate, slope, AUROC, and effect size is reported with a bootstrap 95% CI (10,000 item-level resamples). Multiplicity across layers, heads, and steering magnitudes is controlled with Benjamini–Hochberg FDR at q = 0.05. H1 is the pre-registered primary hypothesis; H2 is secondary and the localization/steering hypothesis is confirmatory-exploratory, reported as such unless its pre-stated causal criterion is met.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The halo shift could reflect rational inference from correlated real-world trait co-occurrence rather than an irrelevant-belief bias; the synthetic-entity track, the evidence-controlled targets (with explicit neutral facts), and the low/zero-association target condition are designed to isolate genuine contamination from legitimate correlational inference (though for real entities the two are hard to fully separate). The effect may be absent internally - a robust negative result (LLMs keep independent traits uncontaminated) would itself be a valuable, publishable finding contrasting with humans and with the VAA account. The contamination could arise from token-level priming/co-occurrence rather than a valence belief; paraphrase/order perturbations, comprehension checks, and reading belief at target tokens distinct from the seed mitigate this. The single-valence-axis mediation hypothesis may only partially hold; if residual trait-specific spreading dominates, the finding shifts to characterizing distributed vs. unified halo mechanisms (still informative and directly engages the VAA claim). Belief probes may not be cleanly linear at every layer; we report layerwise results with control tasks. Steering could degrade fluency or indiscriminately flatten all evaluative structure; we use small magnitudes, random/truth-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity, evidence-based accuracy, and general benchmarks. Downstream high-stakes ratings need automatic plus human-validated scoring. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

Name: transitive_belief_leakage
Title: Does Belief Survive the Chain? Probing Whether LLMs Propagate Uncertainty Across Inferential Steps or Leak Certainty Into Their Conclusions
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM internally derives a conclusion C from a chain of individually-uncertain premises (A≈p1, A→B≈p2, B→C≈p3), a rational agent's belief in C should be BOUNDED by (and roughly the product of) the link beliefs, degrading as the chain lengthens.
