We hypothesize LLMs instead exhibit 'certainty leakage': the internally-decoded belief in the conclusion is systematically HIGHER than the product of the internally-decoded link beliefs and decays far more slowly than probability theory dictates as chain length grows — an internal over-propagation of certainty that is decodable, predicts long-chain overconfidence errors, and is carried by an identifiable component that can be steered to restore proper uncertainty attenuation. (Throughout, "belief" denotes an internal, probe-decoded belief-state proxy, validated against behavior, not a claim of phenomenal belief.)
Related Work: Prior work shows LLM internal beliefs skew CoT via confirmation bias (Unveiling Confirmation Bias in CoT 2025), that internal consistency across layers signals reasoning reliability (Calibrating Reasoning with Internal Consistency 2024), that multi-hop reasoning activates a distribution of intermediate answers in middle layers (Distributional Reasoning in LLMs 2024), and that belief/truth directions are linearly decodable and context-sensitive causal mediators of in-context inference (Truth-value judgment 2024; Language Models with Rationality/REFLEX 2023 for belief-graph consistency). Behavioral work on incoherent probability judgments and the conjunction fallacy (my prior internal_belief_coherence_gap) concerns STATIC conjunctions P(A∧B) at a single query, not inferential chains. Belief-manifold work (Shape of Beliefs 2026) shows posteriors' mean/variance are encoded but studies single-distribution updating, not multi-step deductive propagation. CRITICALLY, no prior work asks whether an LLM's INTERNAL belief in a DERIVED conclusion respects the multiplicative attenuation of uncertainty across a chain of uncertain premises, whether certainty LEAKS (conclusion believed more than the weakest/product of links warrants), how this scales with CHAIN LENGTH, or whether an identifiable component can be steered to restore attenuation. We reframe long-chain reasoning overconfidence as an internal uncertainty-propagation failure and give it a mechanistic, causal treatment, distinct from static-coherence, confirmation-bias, and layerwise-consistency work. The novelty is tightened to an exact quantity: the INTERNAL conclusion-belief versus the PRODUCT of the internally-decoded link-beliefs (and versus the weakest link), across chain length — not generic calibration, layerwise consistency, or output-level uncertainty. Delta table: conjunction-fallacy work concerns a STATIC P(A and B) at one query (no inferential chain); calibration/consistency work concerns output confidence or cross-layer agreement (not a product-of-links contrast); distributional-reasoning work shows intermediate answers exist (not that certainty fails to attenuate); belief-manifold work studies single-distribution updating (not multi-step deductive propagation). If leakage is ABSENT internally while verbalised outputs are still overconfident, that is itself a new finding (attenuation is correct internally; overconfidence is a verbalisation artifact).
Abstract: A rational reasoner who is only 80% sure of each of five inferential steps should be far less than 80% sure of the final conclusion — uncertainty compounds along a chain. Yet LLMs are notorious for stating long derivations with unwarranted confidence. Prior interpretability work shows internal beliefs are linearly decodable and shape chain-of-thought, but none ask whether the model's INTERNAL belief in a derived conclusion respects the multiplicative attenuation of uncertainty across the chain that produced it. We hypothesize 'certainty leakage': the internally-decoded belief in a conclusion C is systematically higher than the product of the internally-decoded beliefs in its constituent links, and decays far more slowly than probability theory dictates as chain length grows. We further hypothesize that (i) both link-beliefs and conclusion-belief are linearly decodable, (ii) the leakage magnitude grows with chain length and predicts long-chain reasoning errors, and (iii) it is carried by an identifiable component such that steering it restores proper attenuation, improving calibration on long chains without harming short ones. We build controlled inference-chain items where each link's belief strength is stipulated (via explicit likelihood-ratio-style premises and a synthetic-entity track to control priors) and chain length is varied from 1 to 6. On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) we train linear belief probes to read each link-belief and the conclusion-belief, compute a per-item leakage score against the product baseline, trace its length-scaling, localize the responsible heads via activation patching, and test causal control by steering. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, leakage magnitude vs. product baseline, length-decay slope vs. rational, leakage–error AUROC, patching effect sizes, post-steering attenuation restoration and calibration gains, and perplexity. This matters for long tool-use and retrieval chains, where an agent that does not attenuate uncertainty across steps reports a shaky multi-hop conclusion with unwarranted confidence, changing debugging and safety decisions; we deliver a reusable leakage metric for model comparison. If confirmed, calibration and abstention should be conditioned on chain length; if internal attenuation is correct (a negative), effort moves to the verbalisation stage.
Experiments:
The hypothesis has four testable parts: H1 — both the per-link beliefs and the conclusion belief are linearly decodable, and the internally-decoded conclusion belief is systematically HIGHER than the product (and higher than the weakest link) of the internally-decoded link beliefs ("certainty leakage"); H2 — leakage grows with chain length: the internal conclusion belief decays far more slowly with the number of uncertain links than probability theory dictates; H3 — leakage magnitude predicts long-chain overconfidence errors; H4 — leakage is carried by an identifiable component such that steering it restores proper attenuation and improves long-chain calibration without harming short chains.

Data (built from scratch). ~5,000 inferential-chain items where conclusion C follows from links (A; A→B; B→C; …) of length L ∈ {1,2,3,4,5,6}, each link assigned an explicit strength (calibrated hedges "usually/probably/possibly" or explicit "80% of the time") so a rational product-of-links belief is computable. Two tracks: REAL commonsense/factual chains (~3,000) and a SYNTHETIC novel-entity track (~2,000, "Most zorbs are vantar; most vantar glow; so this zorb glows") with fully stipulated link probabilities giving an exact rational conclusion belief. We use ~5,000 of ~5,000. Matched conditions vary chain length while holding the weakest-link strength constant; a CERTAIN-CHAIN control (all links ≈1.0, conclusion should stay high) dissociates leakage from generic length/context decay. Each item carries a behavioral conclusion-confidence probe ("How confident that C? 0–100"), comprehension checks ("restate each link's strength"), and 3 paraphrase/order perturbations.

Models. Frozen open-weight Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B. No transformer weights trained; only a linear/graded BELIEF-STRENGTH probe on frozen activations (ridge/logistic regression per layer, anchored on single-premise items with known stipulated probabilities, item-disjoint 80/20, 5-fold CV, seeds {0,1,2}, shuffled-label control tasks, mean±sd). Steering via contrastive activation addition, α ∈ {±2,±4,±8} × per-layer std.

Experiment 1 (H1 — leakage vs product). Read the internal belief at each link proposition and at the conclusion (without asking the confidence question). Define per-item leakage = internal conclusion-belief − product of internal link-beliefs (also report vs the min/weakest link). Decisive metric first: mean leakage on uncertain chains, tested > 0 against the rational-attenuation null, with the CERTAIN-CHAIN control confirming no spurious decay. Convincing: mean leakage ≥ 0.15 (belief units, 0–1) with CI excluding 0 in ≥3 of 4 models, and the belief-strength probe R² ≥ 0.3 on held-out anchors. Indecision band: leakage 0.05–0.15 or probe R² 0.15–0.3 — weak/uncertain. Negative (leakage ≤ 0.05): the model attenuates appropriately — H1 rejected (a reassuring finding).

Experiment 2 (H2 — length scaling). Fit internal conclusion-belief vs chain length L (weakest-link-constant condition) and compare the decay slope to the rational product-decay slope. Decisive metric: (rational slope − internal slope), i.e. how much flatter the internal decay is. Convincing: internal decay slope < 50% of the rational slope in magnitude, CI excluding the rational slope, in ≥3 models. Indecision band: internal slope 50–80% of rational — mild over-propagation. Negative (internal slope ≥ 80% of rational): decay is roughly rational — H2 rejected.

Experiment 3 (H3 — leakage predicts errors). Collect behavioral long-chain errors (asserting a conclusion at higher confidence than warranted, or wrong on synthetic ground truth). Decisive metric: AUROC of per-item leakage (read before query) predicting the error, vs a log-prob baseline and a chain-length-only baseline. Convincing: leakage AUROC ≥ 0.70 and ≥ 0.05 over both baselines in ≥3 models. Indecision band: 0.60–0.70 or <0.05 over baselines — suggestive. Negative (≤0.60): internal leakage does not track errors — H3 rejected.

Experiment 4 (H4 — localization and causal attenuation). Via activation patching, patch short↔long-chain conclusion activations and weak-link activations into the conclusion representation to find the minimal component that inflates conclusion-belief above the product; compare to belief/truth heads and the middle-layer intermediate-answer distribution. Derive a certainty-leakage steering direction and test: (a) subtracting it lowers conclusion-belief toward the product/rational value on uncertain chains and improves calibration (ECE) and accuracy on long chains; (b) adding it exaggerates leakage; (c) specificity — random/truth directions do not selectively restore attenuation, CERTAIN-CHAIN conclusions preserved; (d) collateral — MMLU (1k subset), short-chain accuracy, WikiText perplexity (2k lines). Decisive metric first: reduction in long-chain ECE under subtractive steering, with controls. Convincing: ≥30% relative ECE reduction on L≥4 chains, short-chain accuracy unchanged (<2 pt), certain-chain belief preserved (<0.05 drop), controls <10% ECE change, <5% perplexity rise. Indecision band: 10–30% ECE reduction — partial. Negative (<10% or matched by controls): no steerable attenuation component — H4 rejected. All results are planned, not measured.


Measurement pre-registration, controls, and baselines. We pre-specify the exact probe inputs/targets, which token representations carry proposition-level belief, and how belief is extracted at matched proposition tokens across paraphrases (guarding the link-vs-conclusion position difference). Controls: a random-label probe, same-length semantically-unrelated chains, an extra-evidence control on real data (isolated by the synthetic track), and a probe-noise sensitivity analysis for the product baseline (so leakage is not an artifact of noisy per-link estimates). The hypotheses are made independently falsifiable and non-nested: leakage-absent-but-overconfidence-present, and leakage-present-but-not-predictive-of-errors, are distinct reportable outcomes.

Statistical analysis plan. Unit of analysis is the item; we report bootstrap 95% CIs over items and seeds, fit mixed-effects models with random intercepts for item and fixed effects for chain length and model family, and apply Benjamini-Hochberg correction across layers/lengths/models; a power analysis gives the minimum detectable leakage (0.05 belief units) and steering effect at the stated per-model/condition sample sizes. The PRIMARY endpoint is the Experiment 1 (H1) mean leakage vs the product null on uncertain chains, with the certain-chain control at ~0; thresholds are heuristic desiderata. Minimum viable scope: H1-H3 with the certain-chain and length controls plus a lighter causal test; full head localisation is contingent.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The graded belief-strength probe is harder to calibrate than a binary truth probe; miscalibration could bias the leakage estimate. We mitigate by anchoring on single-premise items with known stipulated probabilities, reporting layerwise results with control tasks, and focusing on the RELATIVE comparison between conclusion-belief and the product/weakest-link of internally-decoded link-beliefs (a within-representation contrast that does not require absolute calibration). Apparent leakage could reflect the model using additional valid evidence for C beyond the stated chain (real track); the SYNTHETIC novel-entity track with fully stipulated link probabilities isolates chain-only propagation. Slow decay with length could be a generic context-retention artifact rather than certainty over-propagation; the CERTAIN-CHAIN control (which should stay high) and the length-matched weakest-link-constant condition dissociate genuine leakage from length effects. The effect may be absent internally — a robust negative result (LLMs internally attenuate uncertainty appropriately, and overconfidence is only a verbalization artifact) would itself be a valuable, publishable finding. Reading belief at 'link' vs. 'conclusion' tokens is imperfect since positions differ; we anchor probes at matched proposition tokens and use paraphrase perturbations. The leakage component may be distributed rather than a discrete head; we treat 'steer to restore attenuation' as the causal test rather than pinning an exact head. Steering could degrade fluency or make the model indiscriminately under-confident on valid chains; we use small magnitudes, random/truth-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity, short-chain and certain-chain accuracy, and general benchmarks. Long-chain error scoring on open-ended output needs an LLM-judge plus human validation on a sample. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

Name: curse_of_knowledge_leakage
Title: It Can't Unknow: A Privileged-Knowledge Leak That Biases LLMs' Internal Representation of an Ignorant Belief
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the human curse of knowledge / hindsight bias, when an LLM knows the true state of an item, its internally-decoded representation of what an *ignorant* agent (a naive character, a past self, or a stipulated uninformed user) should believe is systematically biased TOWARD the true state that the model privately knows. This 'knowledge leak' is (i) linearly decodable as a shift of the ignorant-belief readout toward the true answer, (ii) graded with the plausibility/salience of the true answer, (iii) predicts egocentric false-belief errors, and (iv) is carried by an identifiable component such that ablating it restores an unbiased ignorant-belief representation.
Related Work: ToM interpretability decodes the belief status of a protagonist and an omniscient oracle from attention heads and steers ToM performance (Language Models Represent Beliefs of Self and Others 2024; Brittle Minds 2024), and identifies a 'lookback' mechanism binding character-object-state triples and updating beliefs via a visibility lookback (Language Models use Lookbacks to Track Beliefs 2025). Human cognitive science establishes the curse of knowledge / hindsight bias as a robust egocentric contamination of ignorant-perspective judgments (Are the classic false belief tasks cursed? 2021; Do Adults Show a Curse of Knowledge 2014; Hindsight Bias and Investment Performance 2008), and shows plausibility of the privileged answer modulates its size. CRITICALLY, the ToM interpretability work decodes WHETHER a model can represent a false belief, but none ask whether the model's OWN privileged knowledge of the true answer BIASES the internally-decoded ignorant/false belief toward that truth (a decodable knowledge-leak magnitude), whether that leak is graded by answer plausibility, predicts egocentric errors, or can be causally removed. We reframe the curse of knowledge as an internal representational leak from the truth channel into the ignorant-belief channel and give it a mechanistic, causal treatment, distinct from prior ToM-decoding work and from my earlier epistemic-tag proposals. Explicit novelty claims: N1 (metric) a decodable per-item KNOWLEDGE-LEAK magnitude (shift of the ignorant-belief readout toward the privately-known truth); N2 (finding) the leak is graded with the plausibility/salience of the true answer; N3 (predictiveness) it predicts egocentric false-belief errors; N4 (mechanism) an identifiable component carries it and can be ablated. Delta, one line each: 'Beliefs of Self and Others' (2024) and 'Lookbacks' (2025) decode WHETHER a false belief is representable and how belief is bound/updated, but never test whether the model's own truth channel CONTAMINATES that ignorant-belief readout; behavioral curse-of-knowledge evaluations score output errors without an internal leak estimand; generic interference/entanglement probing does not isolate an agent-specific ignorant-belief channel.
Abstract: Once you know the answer, it is hard to imagine not knowing it: people systematically project their privileged knowledge onto less-informed others and onto their own past selves — the curse of knowledge and its cousin, hindsight bias, among the most robust findings in cognitive science. LLMs are increasingly asked to reason about what an uninformed agent believes (a character in a false-belief story, a novice user, a past state of the world), tasks that require *withholding* what the model itself knows. We ask whether LLMs inherit the curse at the level of their internal beliefs: does the model's own knowledge of the true state of an item leak into, and bias, its internal representation of what an ignorant agent should believe? We hypothesize that (i) the internally-decoded ignorant-belief readout is shifted toward the true answer the model privately knows, (ii) this leak grows with the plausibility/salience of the true answer, (iii) it predicts egocentric false-belief errors when suppression is incomplete, and (iv) it is carried by an identifiable component that can be ablated to restore an unbiased ignorant-belief representation. We build controlled false-belief and hindsight scenarios in which the true state and the ignorant agent's evidence are dissociated, with matched conditions where the model is or is not itself told the truth, plus a synthetic-entity track to control priors. On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) we train linear probes to read the ignorant-belief and the true-state, quantify a per-item knowledge-leak score, test its graded structure and predictiveness, localize the responsible heads via activation patching, and test causal control by ablating/steering a leak direction. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, knowledge-leak magnitude, plausibility modulation, leak–error AUROC, patching effect sizes, post-ablation debiasing, and perplexity. Concrete stakeholders and failures: tutoring/explanation systems (over-assuming the learner knows the answer), witness-style QA, negotiation and deceptive-role simulation, and multi-agent planning all require withholding privileged knowledge; a firewall failure produces confident egocentric errors. A robust null (the model cleanly firewalls its own knowledge) is itself valuable, sharpening the ToM-representation and safety picture.
Experiments: Common setup (stated once, no external pointers): Four frozen open-weight models — Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B-v0.3 (base + instruct for behavioral runs); weights frozen, only linear probes trained (L2 logistic/ridge regression, C by 5-fold CV). Activations: residual stream at item/state tokens, all layers, per-head for localization; seeds {0,1,2}; item-level splits. Dataset built from scratch: ~6k scenarios dissociating the TRUE state of an item from an IGNORANT agent's evidence, across three framings — classic false-belief stories, hindsight scenarios, and audience-ignorance — in a REAL track and a SYNTHETIC novel-entity track; we generate 6k and use all 6k, balanced across framings (~2k each). Key manipulation, held constant across items: the model itself IS vs IS NOT told the true state (privileged-knowledge present vs absent) with the ignorant agent's evidence fixed. Labels (who-saw-what, true state) human-validated on 300 items (kappa ≥ 0.7 gate). Experiment 1 (H1 — the ignorant-belief readout is shifted toward the truth the model privately knows, i.e. a decodable leak): Train two probes on frozen activations read WITHOUT posing the belief question — probe A decodes the TRUE state, probe B decodes the IGNORANT agent's belief (which under a false belief points away from truth). Define per-item KNOWLEDGE-LEAK = shift of probe B toward the true state in privileged-present minus privileged-absent conditions. Decisive metric first: mean signed leak across items, with probe A and B held-out AUROC (each convincing at ≥ 0.75; shuffled-label control 0.50±0.05) as the precondition. Convincing H1: leak > 0 with a paired test effect size Cohen's d ≥ 0.3 in the majority of models on both tracks. Indecision band: |leak| within the ±1 s.e. of zero, or d 0.1–0.3 → leak not established; leak ≤ 0 refutes H1. Negative result = the model cleanly firewalls its own knowledge from the ignorant-belief channel (valuable for the ToM/safety picture). Experiment 2 (H2 — the leak is graded with the plausibility/salience of the true answer): vary true-answer salience (highly typical vs arbitrary state) at fixed framing. Decisive metric first: slope of leak vs salience. Convincing: significantly positive slope (bootstrap 95% CI excludes 0) in the majority of models; indecision band = CI straddling 0 with |slope| small → grading not established; negative slope refutes H2. Experiment 3 (H3 — the leak predicts egocentric false-belief errors): collect behavioral errors (model attributes the true state to the ignorant agent / hindsight-distorted prediction). Decisive metric first: AUROC of the pre-query internal leak predicting per-item egocentric error. Convincing: AUROC ≥ 0.70 AND beats a log-prob baseline and a lexical baseline by ≥ 0.05. Indecision 0.55–0.70 → weak predictiveness; ≤ 0.55 refutes H3. Experiment 4 (H4 — an identifiable component carries the leak and ablating it restores an unbiased ignorant-belief representation): activation patching of privileged-present<->absent activations to locate the minimal component transporting probe-A signal into channel B (logit-difference effect sizes), compared to belief/visibility-lookback heads and truth heads; then derive a contrastive leak direction and ablate/subtract it. Decisive metric first: reduction in leak toward 0 after ablation and reduction in egocentric-error rate. Convincing H4: leak reduced by ≥ 50% and egocentric errors reduced by ≥ 15 pp, with random-direction and truth-direction ablations not selectively debiasing, the model's OWN factual belief preserved (own-belief probe AUROC unchanged within 0.03), perplexity increase < 10%, MMLU-subset drop < 3 pp. Indecision: 20–50% leak reduction or 5–15 pp error reduction → component contributes but is not sufficient; < 20% / < 5 pp means the leak is not localized to a steerable component. Experiment 5 (generalization): transfer of probes/steering across framings, real vs synthetic tracks, and salience levels (convincing if AUROC retention ≥ 0.65). Thresholds fixed pre-data. Estimand (stated to avoid circularity): the knowledge-leak is the counterfactual difference in the ignorant-belief readout between privileged-present and privileged-absent conditions with the ignorant agent's evidence fixed; under a causal graph truth -> (own answer) and evidence -> (ignorant belief), a nonzero leak is an edge truth -> ignorant-belief that should be absent. Control datasets: (a) privileged truth varies while ignorant-evidence likelihood is held constant, and (b) ignorant-evidence varies while truth is held constant, to isolate contamination from valid inference. Primary hypotheses are H1-H3; localization/ablation (H4) is secondary. Experiment 6 (application): show that ablating the leak improves an external behavior (false-belief ToM accuracy and explanation-appropriateness), not just the internal metric (convincing if >= 10 pp behavioral improvement with own-belief preserved). Statistics: Benjamini-Hochberg FDR control across models x layers x heads x framings; power computed for d>=0.3 at the stated item counts.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The leak could reflect legitimate inference (an ignorant agent might rationally still guess the true state if it is the default); the false-belief design (where the ignorant agent has POSITIVE evidence for the old/false state), the synthetic track, and the privileged-present-vs-absent contrast are built to isolate genuine contamination from valid inference, though for highly plausible true answers the two are hard to fully separate. The effect may be absent internally — a robust negative result (LLMs cleanly firewall their own knowledge from the ignorant-belief channel) would itself be a valuable, publishable finding, refining the ToM-representation and safety picture. The leak could arise from token-level co-occurrence rather than a belief-channel contamination; comprehension checks, paraphrase/order perturbations, and reading belief at agent-specific tokens mitigate this. The two channels (true-state and ignorant-belief) may be entangled such that the 'leak' is really imperfect channel separation — still an informative characterization. Probes may not be cleanly linear at every layer; we report layerwise results with control tasks. The leak component may be distributed rather than a discrete head; we treat 'ablate to debias' as the causal test rather than pinning an exact head. Steering could degrade fluency or make the model unable to reason about true beliefs at all (over-suppression); we use small magnitudes, random/truth-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity, the model's own factual accuracy, and general benchmarks. Plausibility labels are partly subjective; we human-validate a sample. Results may not transfer to very large closed models. We apply multiplicity correction across all model/layer/head/framing comparisons and report power for the pre-registered effect sizes; localization is treated as a secondary aim so that a distributed leak still yields a valid phenomenon-level result.

Name: audience_knowledge_belief
Title: What Do You Already Know? Probing the LLM's Model of the User's Knowledge and How It Gates What Gets Said
Short Hypothesis: An LLM maintains an internal 'audience-knowledge' belief about what the current user already knows about an item, distinct from the model's own belief about that item's state, and this audience-knowledge signal is (i) linearly decodable, (ii) largely orthogonal to the model's own-belief/truth direction, and (iii) causally gates the model's pragmatic generation policy: whether it states, omits as redundant, or over-explains a piece of information. We sharpen the contribution from a broad 'internal audience model' to the narrower, strongest delta: an audience-knowledge variable that causally gates the model's OWN generation policy (state vs. omit-as-redundant vs. over-explain). 'Separate from own-belief' is held to a stronger, pre-registered criterion than mere decodability — matched pairs plus projection-out plus a causal dissociation in which steering audience-knowledge leaves own-belief unchanged.
Related Work: Interpretability of belief has focused on third-person Theory-of-Mind: decoding/steering the beliefs of story characters and an oracle (Language Models Represent Beliefs of Self and Others 2024; Language Models use Lookbacks to Track Beliefs 2025; Brittle Minds 2024; GridToM 2025; Common-ToM 2024), and on the truth-value/own-belief direction (Azaria & Mitchell 2023; Truth-value judgment 2024). Cognitive/pragmatic work (RSA-style listener/speaker modeling, common-ground benchmarks) studies inference about interlocutors behaviorally. Crucially, none isolate an internal, decodable representation of what the *current live user* already knows as a variable SEPARATE from the model's own factual belief, nor link it causally to the model's own *speaking* policy (state vs. omit-as-redundant vs. over-explain). We reframe the 'common ground' / audience model as an internal, steerable belief attribute that gates informativeness, connecting it to concrete failure modes: over-explaining to experts, condescension, unwarranted omission, and deceptive information withholding. This is not a trivial ToM extension: prior ToM decoding concerns a third party in a narrative; we concern the model's belief about its own conversational partner and how that belief controls the model's generation. Three closest lines and why each fails the dissociation test: behavioral pragmatics/RSA models listener-sensitive generation but posits no internal, manipulable audience variable; third-person ToM decoding (Beliefs of Self and Others 2024; Lookbacks 2025) recovers a story character's belief, not the model's belief about its live interlocutor gating its own speech; truth/own-belief probes (Azaria & Mitchell 2023) read what the model believes true, and would fail our matched pairs where own-belief is held constant while user-knowledge varies. The contribution is the own-generation-gating variable and its dissociation, not linear probing. Released artifact: an audience-knowledge dissociation benchmark and an explanation-calibration steering method.
Abstract: Good communicators tailor what they say to what the listener already knows: they skip the obvious, explain the unfamiliar, and avoid condescension. To do this an LLM would need an internal model of the user's knowledge, held separately from its own knowledge of the facts. We ask whether LLMs maintain such an 'audience-knowledge' belief, whether it is a distinct internal variable, and whether it causally controls what the model chooses to say. We hypothesize that (i) the model's belief about what the user knows about an item is linearly decodable from residual-stream activations, (ii) this direction is largely orthogonal to the model's own-belief/truth direction, and (iii) steering it causally shifts the model's generation between stating, omitting-as-redundant, and over-explaining information. We build a controlled dataset of item facts embedded in conversational contexts that establish the user's knowledge state (user shown to already know the fact, shown not to know it, or unspecified) while holding the underlying fact and the model's own belief constant, plus matched pairs where the model believes an item but the user does or does not. We train linear probes on frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Pythia-2.8B) to decode audience-knowledge vs. own-belief, measure their geometric relationship, localize the responsible attention heads via activation patching (comparing to known ToM belief heads), and test causal control by steering along the audience-knowledge direction and measuring shifts in redundant-restatement, omission, and over-explanation rates. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, subspace angle, projected-out decodability, patching effect sizes, informativeness-behavior rate deltas, and perplexity. So what: reliably tailoring output to the interlocutor's knowledge from an internal variable is a capability that prompt instructions and external user modeling achieve only unreliably (and not at all when the user's knowledge must be inferred from discourse). We add a downstream human evaluation showing steering reduces user-rated condescension and omission errors in a simulated tutoring/helpdesk setting, quantify failure costs for expert coding assistants, medical triage, and enterprise support, and separate scientific impact (evidence for internal common-ground tracking) from product impact (better explanation calibration).
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 — an audience-knowledge belief is linearly decodable, distinct from own-belief): Data: built from scratch, 6,000 item facts (real facts the model reliably knows, verified by >= 90% own-voice accuracy; plus synthetic entity-attribute facts to control priors), each embedded in conversations establishing the USER's knowledge state (USER-KNOWS, USER-DOESNT-KNOW, UNSPECIFIED) while holding the fact and own-belief constant; comprehension checks and paraphrase perturbations included; split 70/15/15 by fact. Model: Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Pythia-2.8B, frozen; trainable only two logistic-regression probes (own-belief, audience-knowledge) at the item token, per layer; 5 seeds. Systems compared: audience-knowledge probe vs. shuffled-label control vs. keyword baseline ('expert/novice/as you know'). Decisive metric first: audience-knowledge probe test AUROC at best layer. Convincing: >= 0.80, control 0.50 +/- 0.05, >= 0.05 above keyword baseline, on >=3 of 4 models. Indecision band: 0.60-0.70 or within 0.05 of keyword baseline inconclusive. Negative: < 0.60 is an informative negative for pragmatics/alignment (no separate audience model).

Experiment 2 (H2 — audience-knowledge is largely orthogonal to own-belief/truth): Use matched pairs where own-belief is constant but user-knowledge varies. Decisive metric first: audience-knowledge AUROC after projecting out the own-belief direction (and symmetrically); secondary: subspace angle. Convincing: >= 90% retention and angle > 60 degrees. Indecision band: 70-90% or 40-60 degrees partial. Negative: < 70% retention or < 40 degrees means audience-knowledge coincides with own-belief.

Experiment 3 (H3 — audience-knowledge causally gates the state/omit/over-explain policy): Build an audience-knowledge CAA vector (user-knows minus user-doesnt-know activations, controlling for own-belief). Data: a 1,000-item behavior probe posing a request whose ideal answer depends on user knowledge. Systems compared: audience-direction vs. random vs. own-belief-direction steering, alpha 2/4/8% residual norm. Decisive metric first: change in omission/redundancy-avoidance rate when steered toward 'user-knows', and in explanation/over-explanation when steered toward 'user-doesnt-know'; secondary: MMLU-subset, perplexity. Convincing: >= 15-point shift in the targeted behavior, random < 5 points, perplexity rise < 10%. Indecision band: 5-15 points suggestive. Negative: < 5 beyond random or equals own-belief steering means no distinct causal gate.

Experiment 4 (H1 — localization): Activation patching between user-knows and user-doesnt-know runs; compare heads to third-person ToM belief heads and own-belief/truth heads from prior work. Decisive metric first: fraction of the audience-knowledge distinction recovered by top heads. Convincing: reproducible <= 20-head set recovers >= 50%. Indecision band: diffuse = distributed. Negative: no head > 20%.

Experiment 5 (H3 — predictiveness): Decisive metric first: AUROC/accuracy using the audience-knowledge probe to predict the model's actual state/omit/explain behavior vs. a log-prob baseline. Convincing: >= 0.70 and >= 0.05 above log-prob. Indecision band: 0.60-0.70. Negative: <= 0.60.

Experiment 6 (H1,H3 — generalization): Apply frozen probe/steering across domains (geography, science, procedures), synthetic-to-real, and multi-turn dialogues where user knowledge accrues. Decisive metric first: transfer AUROC and behavior-effect retention. Convincing: >= 0.70 and half retained. Indecision band: 0.60-0.70. Negative: <= 0.60.

Experiment 7 (H1,H2,H3 — cue-conflict construct validity, competitive baselines, and human-rated gating): Data: (a) discourse-based items where audience knowledge must be inferred without explicit novice/expert phrases, plus adversarial items where lexical cues CONFLICT with the actual established knowledge (the probe/behavior must follow the latent conversation state, not the cue); (b) a 600-item simulated tutoring/helpdesk set with human ratings. Decisive metric first: audience-knowledge probe AUROC on cue-conflict items (must follow latent state, >= 0.70) and the probe's predictive value over baselines for generic verbosity, politeness, helpfulness, uncertainty, and instruction-following; plus human-rated appropriateness gains under steering via multiple intervention methods (CAA and a projection/patch-based edit) with dose-response and a specificity check that own-belief probe readout is unchanged. Convincing: cue-conflict AUROC >= 0.70 following latent state, incremental predictive value >= 0.05 over every baseline, and human-rated condescension/omission reduced with own-belief unchanged. Indecision band: cue-conflict AUROC 0.60-0.70 is partial construct validity. Negative: probe follows the cue rather than latent state, or adds nothing over verbosity/helpfulness baselines, means it is not a genuine audience-knowledge variable.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Audience-knowledge may be entangled with surface cues (words like 'expert'/'novice'/'as you know') rather than an abstract representation; we mitigate with diverse framings, paraphrases, matched-content controls, and by testing transfer to unseen cue types and to knowledge states inferred from multi-turn accrual rather than a keyword. The audience-knowledge direction may overlap with the own-belief direction or with a generic third-person ToM belief direction; the projected-out analyses and matched pairs quantify and disentangle this, and even a characterization of entanglement is informative. The model may lack a genuine separate audience model, in which case a robust negative result (audience-knowledge not decodable beyond own-belief) is itself meaningful for pragmatics and alignment. Behavioral state/omit/explain choices depend on prompt scaffolding and may be instruction-following rather than driven by the internal representation; the matched design, comprehension checks, and predictiveness analysis relative to internal probes help disentangle these. Steering could degrade fluency or overshoot into indiscriminate omission or over-explanation; we use small magnitudes, random/own-belief-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity and general benchmarks. Results may not transfer to very large closed models. Audience knowledge is operationalized without relying on explicit novice/expert phrases, including discourse-based inference and cue-conflict cases where the probe must track the latent conversation state. The causal test uses multiple intervention methods, dose-response curves, and a specificity check that own-belief is unchanged, and a human/model-graded quality evaluation confirms steering improves appropriateness rather than merely changing omission/explanation rates. Decodability, geometric separability, behavioral predictiveness, and causal control each carry explicit success/failure criteria; a watertight dissociation is prioritized over broad transfer/localization.

Name: global_self_competence_belief
Title: How Good Am I At This? A Domain-Level Self-Competence Belief That Miscalibrates and Biases LLM Per-Item Answers
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the human dissociation between local confidence (belief about a specific decision) and global self-performance estimates (belief about one's general skill in a domain), an LLM maintains an internal GLOBAL self-competence belief about a whole domain/task-type that is (i) linearly decodable and distinct from its per-item correctness signal, (ii) systematically miscalibrated against the model's true domain accuracy, and (iii) causally biases per-item answering behavior (attempt/abstain, confidence, effort), such that steering the global self-competence belief shifts per-item behavior even when the item itself is unchanged. (Throughout, "belief" denotes an internal, probe-decoded belief-state proxy, validated against behavior, not a claim of phenomenal belief.)
Related Work: Human metacognition robustly dissociates LOCAL confidence in a single decision from GLOBAL self-performance estimates (SPEs) about one's ability in a domain, with distinct cues, neural substrates, and characteristic drift when feedback is absent (Metacognition prospective vs retrospective, 2016; Formation of global self-beliefs in the human brain, 2020; Learning about Self-Performance in the Absence of Feedback, 2018; Domain-specific updating of self-beliefs, 2023). In LLM interpretability, all self-knowledge probing is LOCAL/per-item: solvability belief per problem (Confidence is Not Competence, 2025), in-advance per-question correctness directions (No Answer Needed, 2025), failure prediction (Gnosis, 2025; Language Models Can Predict Their Own Behavior, 2025), early per-trace outcome commitment (Temporal Predictors, 2025), and difficulty perception per problem (Probing Difficulty Perception, 2025). My prior proposals concern per-item behavioral commitment (behavioral_self_prediction_gap) and endowment of self-generated claims. CRITICALLY, none isolate an internal GLOBAL self-competence belief — the model's estimate of its own ability in a whole domain/task-type, abstracted over individual items — as a channel distinct from the per-item correctness signal, test whether it is miscalibrated against true domain accuracy, or show it causally biases per-item behavior independent of item content. We transfer the canonical human local/global metacognition dissociation into LLM belief internals with a mechanistic, causal treatment. Positioned against a 'no individuated metacognition' reading: a global internal self-competence channel can exist even if behavioural confidence matrices are near rank-one across models, because the claim is about an internal domain-level variable, not per-item confidence spread. Narrowed defensible novelty: we are unaware of work jointly testing (a) distinctness of a domain-level self-competence signal from the per-item correctness signal, (b) its calibration against the model's TRUE per-domain accuracy, and (c) its CAUSAL effect on per-item behaviour with item content held fixed. Closest families and one-line deltas: per-item solvability/correctness directions (local, not global), difficulty perception (item-level), failure prediction (behavioural, not a competence construct), and the authors' per-item commitment/endowment proposals (not domain-level).
Abstract: People carry two kinds of self-knowledge: fleeting confidence in a single answer, and a slower, more global sense of how good they are at a whole domain — 'I'm good at math but bad at names.' These global self-performance estimates are dissociable from local confidence, drift from reality when feedback is scarce, and steer how much effort and risk people take. As LLMs increasingly self-assess (deciding whether to attempt, abstain, or hedge), we ask whether they form an analogous internal GLOBAL self-competence belief about a domain, whether it is calibrated, and whether it biases their per-item behavior. We hypothesize that (i) an LLM's global self-competence belief for a task-type is linearly decodable from residual-stream activations and is distinct from its per-item correctness signal; (ii) this global belief is systematically miscalibrated relative to the model's true domain accuracy (over/under-confident in specific domains); and (iii) it causally biases per-item behavior — attempting vs. abstaining, expressed confidence, reasoning effort — so that steering the global belief shifts behavior on an unchanged item. We build a controlled dataset spanning many domains/task-types where the model's true per-domain accuracy is measurable, presenting items with matched framings that make the domain salient. On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) we train linear probes to decode global self-competence vs. per-item correctness, measure their geometry, quantify a calibration gap against true accuracy, localize the responsible heads via activation patching, and test causal control by steering the global-competence direction. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, subspace angle, global-competence calibration gap, per-item behavior shift under steering, patching effect sizes, and perplexity. Practical stakes are concrete: abstention thresholds, tool routing, human handoff, and safety guardrails all depend on a model's sense of its own domain competence, so systematic global miscalibration causes over-answering in weak domains and needless deferral in strong ones. If confirmed, global and local self-assessment should be calibrated separately and the global signal used as an abstention control; targets beyond the raw behaviour swing are selective-prediction AURC/ECE and reduced unsafe over-answering at fixed utility. If no distinct global channel exists (a negative), that itself bounds LLM metacognition to per-item signals.
Experiments:
The hypothesis has three testable parts: H1 — an LLM's GLOBAL self-competence belief for a task-type is linearly decodable from residual-stream activations and is distinct from its per-item correctness signal; H2 — this global belief is systematically miscalibrated relative to the model's true per-domain accuracy; H3 — the global belief causally biases per-item behavior (attempt-vs-abstain, expressed confidence, reasoning effort), such that steering it shifts behavior on an item whose content is held fixed.

Data (assembled from existing sets + a synthetic track). ~8,000 items across many domains/task-types with measurable true per-domain accuracy: MMLU by subject (public, 14k questions; sample ~4,000 across ~20 subjects), GSM8K arithmetic (~1,000), TriviaQA (~1,000), a code track from MBPP (~500), date/entity-attribute facts from CounterFact (~1,000), plus a SYNTHETIC novel-entity-domain track (~500) where true accuracy is set by construction. We use ~8,000 of the available pool (capped per domain to keep domains balanced; fewer only where a domain has too few clean items). Each item is presented in a frame that makes the domain salient ("This is a [domain] question: ..."); true per-domain accuracy is measured empirically per model. Each item carries a global self-competence elicitation ("How good are you at [domain] questions in general?"), a per-item local confidence probe, comprehension checks, and 3 framing paraphrases.

Models. Frozen open-weight Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B (instruct). No transformer weights trained; only linear probes on frozen activations (L2 logistic/linear regression per layer; item- and domain-disjoint splits so the global probe is tested on held-out domains; 5-fold CV; seeds {0,1,2}; mean±sd). Steering via contrastive activation addition, α ∈ {±2,±4,±8} × per-layer std.

Experiment 1 (H1 — decodable and distinct global-competence channel). At the domain-salient tokens, before the item is answered, train probes for (A) GLOBAL self-competence (calibrated against elicited/behavioral global estimates) and (B) per-item CORRECTNESS (the in-advance correctness direction). Then compute cosine/subspace angle between the two directions and test whether global competence remains decodable after projecting out the per-item-correctness direction, generalizing to held-out domains and the synthetic track. Decisive metric first: cross-domain global-competence probe AUROC/R² on held-out domains, and residual decodability after projecting out correctness. Convincing: held-out global-competence R² ≥ 0.3 (or AUROC ≥ 0.75 for a high/low split), subspace angle ≥ 30°, and >60% of decodability retained after projecting out correctness, in ≥3 models. Indecision band: angle 15–30° or 30–60% retained — channels partly entangled; report as such. Negative (angle <15° or <30% retained): no distinct global channel, only per-item signals — H1 rejected (a valuable limit on LLM metacognition).

Experiment 2 (H2 — calibration gap). Compare decoded global self-competence per domain to the model's measured true per-domain accuracy. Decisive metric: signed per-domain calibration gap (decoded competence − true accuracy) and its systematicity (e.g. inflated on confident-but-wrong domains). Convincing: mean |gap| ≥ 0.15 (on a 0–1 scale) with a consistent sign pattern across ≥3 models, and decoded-vs-verbal competence agreeing in direction. Indecision band: |gap| 0.05–0.15 — mild/uncertain miscalibration. Negative (|gap| < 0.05): global competence is well-calibrated — H2 rejected.

Experiment 3 (H3 — causal bias on fixed items). Localize the global-competence signal via activation patching (patch high-competence-domain activations into low-competence-domain runs on a fixed item). Derive a global-competence steering direction and, holding the item fixed, test: (a) steering "high" raises attempt rate and expressed confidence and lowers abstention/hedging; (b) steering "low" does the reverse; (c) specificity — random and per-item-correctness directions do not selectively move global behavior, and the item's actual correctness is not the driver; (d) steering toward the model's TRUE accuracy improves attempt/abstain calibration; (e) collateral — MMLU (1k held-out subset), perplexity (WikiText, 2k lines). Also test that the global readout predicts behavior beyond per-item correctness (incremental AUROC / partial regression). Decisive metric first: change in attempt/abstain rate on fixed items under ±steering, with random/correctness-direction controls. Convincing: ≥15-percentage-point behavior swing between +high and +low steering, controls <5 pt, incremental prediction AUROC ≥ 0.05 over the correctness baseline, <2 pt MMLU drop. Indecision band: 5–15 pt swing or incremental AUROC 0.02–0.05 — weak causal role. Negative (<5 pt swing or matched by controls): global competence does not gate behavior — H3 rejected. All results are planned, not measured.


Construct-validity controls and baselines. To rule out a domain-identity or difficulty alias we add within-domain difficulty stratification, adversarial domain-label swaps (identical items under different claimed domains), and synthetic manipulations that change competence without changing surface domain; the global probe must predict self-behaviour BEYOND observable difficulty and per-item correctness (incremental AUROC / partial regression). Steering baselines are matched-norm generic-confidence, refusal, and domain-identity directions. The probe's supervision target is stated unambiguously as the behaviour-inferred latent competence (with the elicited verbal self-rating and the framing label reported as secondary), since the calibration claim depends on it; 'effort' is operationalised as generated reasoning-token count at fixed decoding. We reduce dataset-family confounding by reporting within-family (subject/source/format) analyses rather than pooling.

Statistical analysis plan. Unit of analysis is the item nested in domain; we report bootstrap 95% CIs, fit mixed-effects models with random intercepts for domain and item and a fixed effect for model family, and apply Benjamini-Hochberg correction across domains/layers/models; a power analysis fixes items-per-domain to a minimum detectable calibration gap of 0.05. The PRIMARY endpoint is the Experiment 3 (H3) fixed-item attempt/abstain swing under +/- steering vs controls; thresholds (R2>=0.3, AUROC>=0.75, angle>=30deg) are heuristic desiderata pending calibration, and inference rests on CIs. Minimum viable scope: the H3 causal demo plus the cleanest H1/H2, de-emphasising head localisation unless it resolves construct validity; we explicitly distinguish 'no global channel' from 'channel present but too distributed/nonlinear for these methods.'
Risk Factors and Limitations: The 'global self-competence' probe may in fact recover a domain-identity or difficulty feature rather than a genuine self-referential competence belief; we mitigate by (i) contrasting domains matched on difficulty but differing in the model's actual accuracy, (ii) using the synthetic track where competence is manipulable independent of surface domain, and (iii) testing incremental prediction of self-behavior beyond difficulty/correctness signals — a probe that only captures difficulty would fail these controls. Global and per-item channels may be strongly entangled (the global belief may be a running average of local signals); the projected-out analyses and fixed-item steering (which holds the item and its per-item correctness constant while moving global competence) are designed to dissociate them, and even a finding of entanglement is informative. The global-competence probe requires a calibrated readout, harder than a binary probe; we calibrate against elicited/behavioral global estimates and true accuracy, report layerwise results with control tasks, and focus on relative structure. The effect may be absent internally — a robust negative result (LLMs have no distinct global self-competence representation, only per-item signals) would itself be a valuable, publishable finding about the limits of LLM metacognition. Behavioral measures (attempt/abstain, hedging) depend on prompt scaffolding and may reflect instruction-following; matched framings, comprehension checks, and the fixed-item steering test disentangle this. The competence signal may be distributed rather than a discrete head; we treat 'steer to shift behavior/improve calibration' as the causal test rather than pinning an exact component. Steering could degrade fluency or induce indiscriminate over/under-confidence; we use small magnitudes, random/per-item-correctness-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity and general benchmarks. Instruction-tuned models may show different self-competence structure than base models (an informative comparison but limits universality). Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

Name: belief_contestedness_flag
Title: Settled or Contested? Probing Whether LLMs Internally Flag Beliefs as Consensus vs. Genuinely Disputed
Short Hypothesis: LLMs maintain an internal 'contestedness' flag on beliefs about item-states that distinguishes propositions the model treats as settled/consensus (a single truth-value exists) from propositions it treats as genuinely contested (no single agreed truth-value). This contestedness signal is linearly decodable from residual-stream activations, largely orthogonal to the truth-value direction, and causally gates whether the model asserts a claim as settled fact vs. hedges/marks it as disputed. We sharpen the construct so contestedness cannot collapse into uncertainty, unverifiability, subjectivity, open-endedness, or controversial-topic detection: it is the model's internal representation that a proposition has no single agreed truth-value, tested only after jointly controlling for truth, entropy/uncertainty, topic, and partisan ideology. Where controls are not airtight we make the more defensible claim of an internal representation correlated with contestedness labels rather than a clean conceptual flag.
Related Work: Prior interpretability work isolates a linear truth-value direction and treats propositions as binary true/false (Geometry of Truth 2023; Azaria & Mitchell 2023; Truth-value judgment: belief directions are context sensitive 2024). Belief-representation work studies self/other ToM beliefs (Language Models Represent Beliefs of Self and Others 2024; Brittle Minds 2024), representational stability of truth for fictional/synthetic content (Representational Stability of Truth 2025), and depth of implanted beliefs (Believe It or Not 2025). Political-perspective work finds a linear ideology direction usable to steer slant (Linear Representations of Political Perspective 2025). DynamicQA (2024) behaviorally distinguishes 'disputable dynamic facts' (viewpoint-dependent) and shows higher intra-memory conflict, but only at the output/persuasion level. Critically, NONE of these isolate an internal, decodable flag for whether a proposition is CONTESTED (has no single agreed truth) as an axis SEPARATE from the truth-value direction and from a partisan ideology direction. Existing truth probes force a true/false readout even on inherently contested claims; we ask instead whether the model internally represents 'this is genuinely disputed' as its own variable, and whether that variable causally controls unwarranted assertiveness vs. hedging. This is not a trivial extension: it reframes contested-topic overconfidence (and false balance) as a mechanistic, steerable epistemic signal orthogonal to truth-value. Closest prior work is DynamicQA (2024), which already separates disputable/dynamic from settled facts behaviorally and shows elevated knowledge conflict; our novelty is therefore not the distinction itself but its internal decodability, its orthogonality to both truth-value and a partisan-ideology direction, and its causal gating of assertiveness/hedging. We add explicit baselines that DynamicQA-style behavioral work does not rule out — entropy/uncertainty, topic/domain classification, subjectivity, answerability/verifiability, and lexical-controversy cues — and evaluate contestedness after controlling for all of them jointly, not one at a time.
Abstract: Not every proposition has a single truth-value: 'The capital of France is Paris' is settled, while 'Nuclear power is the best path to decarbonization' is genuinely contested. Humans robustly flag such claims as disputed and hedge accordingly, but LLMs are known to state contested claims with unwarranted confidence (or, conversely, to hedge on settled facts). Prior interpretability work isolates a linear truth-value direction and treats every claim as binary true/false; behavioral work notes that 'disputable' facts cause knowledge conflict, but no work has asked whether the model internally represents contestedness as its own variable. We hypothesize that LLMs maintain a 'contestedness' flag that distinguishes settled/consensus propositions from genuinely contested ones, and that this flag is (i) linearly decodable from residual-stream activations, (ii) largely orthogonal to both the truth-value direction and any partisan-ideology direction, and (iii) causally gates whether the model asserts a claim as settled fact vs. hedges. We construct a controlled dataset of item-state propositions labeled for contestedness (settled-true, settled-false, and genuinely-contested claims) balanced across topic domains, plus synthetic in-context 'consensus vs. dispute' framings to control priors. We train linear probes on frozen open-weight models (Llama-3, Qwen2.5, Gemma-2, Pythia) to decode contestedness vs. truth-value, measure their geometric relationship (subspace angles, projected-out decodability), and separate contestedness from the partisan-ideology direction. We localize responsible heads via activation patching and test causal control: steering along the contestedness direction should modulate assertiveness/hedging on a matched set of prompts. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, subspace angle, projected-out decodability, patching effect sizes, assertiveness/hedging-rate shifts, and perplexity. So what: contestedness-aware control should reduce harmful overstatement on genuinely disputed issues while preserving crisp answers on settled facts — a tradeoff standard scalar uncertainty does not capture, since a settled-but-model-uncertain fact and a genuinely contested claim demand different behavior. This matters for search assistants, health/policy advice, educational tools, and political-information systems. We add a decision-centric evaluation (calibration/helpfulness tradeoff and reduction in unsupported assertive claims, blinded-human-rated) and release a stratified contestedness benchmark with an adjudication protocol and inter-annotator agreement by category.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 — a contestedness flag is linearly decodable): Tests that settled vs. genuinely-contested is recoverable, separate from truth. Data: built from scratch, 6,000 propositions: SETTLED-TRUE, SETTLED-FALSE, and GENUINELY-CONTESTED (policy, unresolved science, aesthetics, moral dilemmas), contested items balanced across the political spectrum and non-political domains; plus a synthetic track stipulating consensus vs. dispute over novel entity-attributes; labels human-validated on a 500-item sample; split 70/15/15 by proposition. Model: Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Pythia-2.8B, frozen; trainable only a logistic-regression probe at the state token, per layer; 5 seeds. Systems compared: contestedness probe (settled vs. contested) vs. shuffled-label control vs. keyword baseline ('debate/opinion/best'). Decisive metric first: contestedness-probe test AUROC at best layer. Convincing: >= 0.80, control 0.50 +/- 0.05, >= 0.05 above keyword baseline, on >=3 of 4 models. Indecision band: 0.60-0.70 or within 0.05 of keyword baseline is inconclusive. Negative: < 0.60 means no decodable contestedness flag.

Experiment 2 (H2 — contestedness is orthogonal to BOTH truth-value and a partisan-ideology direction): Fit a truth direction (settled-true vs. settled-false) and an ideology direction (from political contested items). Decisive metric first: contestedness AUROC after projecting out truth, and separately after projecting out ideology (validated on non-political contested items); secondary: subspace angles. Convincing: >= 90% retention against both and angles > 60 degrees. Indecision band: 70-90% retention against either is partial. Negative: < 70% retention against truth means contestedness is just 'no truth-value'; < 70% against ideology means it is mere political slant.

Experiment 3 (H3 — the contestedness flag causally gates assertiveness vs. hedging): Build a contestedness CAA vector (contested minus settled activations). Data: a 1,000-item matched assertiveness probe. Systems compared: contestedness-direction vs. random vs. truth-direction steering, alpha 2/4/8% residual norm. Decisive metric first: change in hedging rate when steering settled items toward 'contested', and in unwarranted-assertiveness when steering contested items toward 'settled'; secondary: MMLU-subset, perplexity. Convincing: >= 15-point shift in the targeted direction, random < 5 points, perplexity rise < 10%. Indecision band: 5-15 points suggestive. Negative: < 5 beyond random or equals truth steering.

Experiment 4 (H1 — localization): Activation patching between settled and contested runs; compare heads to truth/belief heads and ideology-predictive heads. Decisive metric first: fraction of the contestedness distinction recovered by top heads. Convincing: reproducible <= 20-head set recovers >= 50%. Indecision band: diffuse = distributed. Negative: no head > 20%.

Experiment 5 (H3 — predictiveness): Decisive metric first: AUROC using the contestedness probe to predict behavioral over-assertiveness (asserting a contested claim as settled) vs. a log-prob baseline. Convincing: >= 0.70 and >= 0.05 above log-prob. Indecision band: 0.60-0.70. Negative: <= 0.60.

Experiment 6 (H1,H3 — generalization): Apply frozen probe/steering across domains (policy, science, ethics, aesthetics), synthetic-to-real, and open-ended prompts. Decisive metric first: transfer AUROC and hedging-effect retention. Convincing: >= 0.70 and half retained. Indecision band: 0.60-0.70. Negative: <= 0.60.

Experiment 7 (H1,H2,H3 — taxonomy stratification, joint confound control, and decision-centric eval): Data: the contested items re-labeled under a taxonomy (settled-factual, unresolved-empirical, normative/policy, subjective/aesthetic, morally-pluralistic) with a larger human-validated subset (>= 1,500 items), an adjudication protocol, and inter-annotator agreement reported per category; scope is narrowed to unresolved-empirical vs. settled-factual for the primary endpoint. Decisive metric first: contestedness-probe AUROC that survives JOINT partialling of truth, entropy, topic, and ideology (not one direction at a time), plus a decision-centric endpoint — change in unsupported assertive claims on contested items and over-hedging on settled facts under steering, blinded-human-rated. Convincing: AUROC >= 0.05 above the joint-confound baseline and steering improves calibration on contested items without dropping settled-fact correctness > 3 points. Indecision band: AUROC within 0.05 of the joint baseline is inconclusive. Negative: no residual signal after joint control means contestedness is a mixture of the confounds.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Contestedness may be entangled with surface cues (words like 'debate', 'opinion', 'best') rather than an abstract epistemic representation; we mitigate with diverse framings, paraphrases, matched-content controls, and by testing transfer to unseen cue types and the synthetic in-context track where contestedness is stipulated rather than lexically signaled. The label 'genuinely contested' is partly subjective and may reflect the model's training-data distribution rather than an objective epistemic category; we human-validate labels, balance across domains, and treat the model's internal notion of contestedness as itself the object of study. Contestedness may partially overlap with the truth-value direction (contested items lack a clean truth-value) or with a partisan-ideology direction; the projected-out analyses and non-political contested items quantify and disentangle this, and even a characterization of entanglement is informative. The signal may not be cleanly linearly separable or may be layer/model-specific; we report layerwise results with control tasks. Steering could degrade fluency (off-manifold) or overshoot into indiscriminate hedging/assertiveness; we use small magnitudes, random/truth-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity and general benchmarks. Results may not transfer to very large closed models. Labeling uses a taxonomy, an adjudication protocol, inter-annotator agreement by category, and expert review for science/policy items; the primary endpoint is preregistered and restricted to unresolved-empirical vs. settled-factual to avoid subjectivity. Harder negative controls (subjectivity, domain/topic, uncertainty/entropy, answerability/verifiability, style/template, lexical-controversy) are included, and cross-template/cross-surface-form generalization is required so the probe cannot rely on 'best'/'should'/'controversial' cues. E4 localization is cut or exploratory to keep focus on the central hypothesis. Assertiveness/hedging is measured with a blinded human eval or a rubric-based model grader with examples.

Name: valenced_belief_update_asymmetry
Title: Good News, Bad News: Do LLMs Update Beliefs Asymmetrically Toward Desirable Evidence, and Is the Asymmetry Causally Steerable?
Short Hypothesis: Like humans (Sharot et al.'s 'good news/bad news effect'), LLMs update their internal beliefs about an item's state MORE in response to desirable/favorable evidence than to equally-strong undesirable evidence — a valence-driven optimism asymmetry that is independent of evidence strength. We hypothesize this asymmetry is (i) present in the model's internally-decoded belief trajectory (not just its verbal output), (ii) mediated by an identifiable internal component (a valence-of-evidence direction / set of heads that gates how much an update is applied), and (iii) causally removable/reversible by intervening on that component, restoring symmetric (rational) updating.
Related Work: The human 'good news/bad news effect' (Sharot et al. 2011; Selectively altering belief formation, 2012; 198+ citations) shows humans discount undesirable evidence and over-weight desirable evidence when updating self-relevant beliefs, and that disrupting left IFG restores symmetry. In LLM interpretability, belief-state geometry and belief updating are studied (Transformers Represent Belief State Geometry 2024; The Shape of Beliefs 2026; Constrained Belief Updates 2025), and social-pressure overrides of belief are mechanistically characterized (When Truth Is Overridden: sycophancy 2025; Signal Competition / compliance subspace 2025). Behavioral work notes non-Bayesian updating (Martingale Score) but not valence-conditioned asymmetry. Crucially, (to our knowledge) no prior work asks whether LLMs exhibit a *desirability/valence-driven* asymmetry in belief updating — over-updating toward favorable outcomes and under-updating toward unfavorable ones at equal evidence strength — nor localizes and causally reverses it. This differs from sycophancy work (which is about *social* signals from a user, not the intrinsic desirability of the evidence's content) and from my prior proposals (which concern epistemic attribute tags such as provenance/currency/contestedness, not valence-driven update magnitude). We transfer a canonical human-cognition finding into LLMs and give it a mechanistic, causal treatment.
Abstract: Humans famously update their beliefs asymmetrically: we readily absorb good news but discount bad news, an optimism bias whose neural basis has been isolated and even reversed with targeted brain stimulation. As LLMs increasingly form and revise beliefs about outcomes (a treatment will work, a plan will succeed, a risk is low), we ask whether they inherit an analogous valence-driven asymmetry — updating internal beliefs more toward desirable evidence than toward equally-strong undesirable evidence — and whether, unlike in humans, we can precisely locate and switch it off. We construct a controlled belief-updating paradigm in which an item's outcome probability is revised by a stream of evidence pieces whose *strength* (how much a rational Bayesian should update) is held constant while their *desirability* is varied: for self-relevant framings (the model's own predicted success, a user's health prognosis, a plan's payoff) some evidence is favorable and some unfavorable. We train linear belief probes on frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) to read the internal belief before and after each evidence piece, computing a per-update *asymmetry score* = (internal update to favorable evidence) − (internal update to matched unfavorable evidence). We test whether the asymmetry appears internally (not just verbally), whether it grows with self-relevance, and whether it correlates with behavioral over-optimism. We then localize a candidate 'evidence-valence gating' component via activation patching and derive a contrastive steering direction, testing whether ablating/steering it restores symmetric updating without harming overall evidence-integration accuracy or fluency. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, per-update asymmetry score, self-relevance modulation, asymmetry–optimism correlation, patching effect sizes, post-intervention symmetry restoration, integration accuracy, and perplexity.
Experiments:
Setup shared by all experiments below. Models: four frozen open-weight base LLMs — Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B; model weights are never updated (frozen), the only trainable objects are lightweight linear read-out probes and difference-of-means steering vectors. Probes: L2-regularized logistic-regression classifiers (or ridge regressors for graded read-outs) fit on residual-stream activations at the named token, one probe per layer, regularization set by 5-fold cross-validation; every probe is trained and evaluated with 5 seeds {0,1,2,3,4} (mean±95% CI reported) and paired with a shuffled-label control task. A probe counts as genuinely reading the target attribute only if held-out AUROC ≥ 0.75 while its control-task AUROC ≤ 0.55; the band 0.55–0.75 (or control AUROC > 0.55) is the indecision zone — that layer/model is reported as 'representation too weak to interpret', not as evidence. Steering vectors are contrastive difference-of-means (activation-addition) directions between the two matched conditions named in each experiment; steering strength is swept over 5 magnitudes and reported as a dose-response. Collateral-damage guardrails for every causal intervention: perplexity on held-out text must rise ≤ 5% and 5-shot MMLU (1k-item subset) must drop ≤ 2 points to count as 'clean'; 5–10% perplexity or 2–4 MMLU points is the indecision band (effect real but not cleanly separable); worse than that fails the guardrail.

Data. 5,000 belief-updating scenarios built from scratch about an item's outcome (medical prognosis, project deadline, exam pass). Each scenario streams evidence pieces with stipulated likelihood ratios so a Bayesian-oracle posterior is computable, and favorable vs. unfavorable pieces are matched to identical |log-likelihood-ratio| (|LLR|). Desirability (favorable/unfavorable) is crossed with self-relevance framing (model's own success / sympathetic user / neutral third party / an outcome the model is framed to disprefer). Comprehension checks (the model must restate each piece's direction and strength) discard misread items; ~4,000 pass and are used (80/20 train/test on scenarios, no scenario shared across splits). A neutral-valence set and paraphrase perturbations are held out for controls.

Experiment 1 (H1 — a valence-driven update asymmetry exists in the internally-decoded belief, independent of evidence strength). Read the linear belief probe at the token boundary before and after each evidence piece; for each matched favorable/unfavorable pair of equal |LLR|, asymmetry = |internal update to favorable| − |internal update to unfavorable| on the 0–1 belief scale. Systems compared: the model's internal trajectory vs. the symmetric Bayesian-oracle null vs. the model's verbal posteriors. Decisive metric: mean asymmetry. Convincing: mean asymmetry ≥ 0.10 with 95% CI excluding 0 in ≥ 3 of 4 models, and the sign flips under the model-dispreferred framing (confirming it tracks valence, not a fixed drift). Indecision band: |asymmetry| < 0.05 or CI includes 0 → treat as no asymmetry, a substantive negative result meaning these LLMs update more rationally than humans on valenced evidence; 0.05–0.10 = suggestive only, not claimed.

Experiment 2 (H2 — the asymmetry is mediated by an identifiable internal component). Activation patching / causal mediation: patch favorable-evidence activations into unfavorable-evidence runs and vice versa to locate heads/layers whose state gates update magnitude by evidence valence; measure the subspace angle between this direction and a sycophancy/compliance direction (difference-of-means on user-pressure data) to show it is not the social-pressure mechanism. Decisive metric: fraction of the Experiment-1 asymmetry recovered by patching the located component. Convincing: ≤ 5% of heads recover ≥ 50% of the asymmetry and the angle to the compliance direction > 60°. Indecision band: 20–50% recovered or angle 45–60° → partially localized/entangled; < 20% recovered → the asymmetry is distributed, reported as a null for localizability.

Experiment 3 (H3 — the asymmetry is causally removable and reversible). Using the valence-gating steering direction from Experiment 2, (a) subtract/project it out to test restoration of symmetric updating and (b) amplify it to exaggerate optimism; baselines are matched random-direction and truth-direction steering. Decisive metric first: post-intervention asymmetry; secondary: oracle-agreement of the final posterior, then the perplexity/MMLU guardrails from Setup. Convincing: subtraction drives asymmetry to ≤ 0.05 (≥ 50% relative reduction) and improves oracle-agreement while staying clean on the guardrails; amplification raises asymmetry ≥ 50%; random/truth directions move asymmetry < 0.02. Indecision band: 20–50% reduction, or guardrails only in their 5–10%/2–4-point band. A negative result (no direction reduces asymmetry without breaching guardrails) means the asymmetry is not a modular, steerable component. Generalization (supports H1–H3): re-fit on medical vs. planning vs. forecasting and synthetic vs. naturalistic scenarios; transfer AUROC ≥ 0.70 and asymmetry-reduction retained ≥ 50% = generalizes, below the respective indecision bands = domain-specific.

Statistical analysis (all experiments). Effects are estimated with mixed-effects models carrying random intercepts for item and for model family, so results are pooled across the four models without pseudo-replication; every rate, slope, AUROC, and effect size is reported with a bootstrap 95% CI (10,000 item-level resamples). Multiplicity across layers, heads, and steering magnitudes is controlled with Benjamini–Hochberg FDR at q = 0.05. H1 is the pre-registered primary hypothesis; H2 is secondary and the localization/steering hypothesis is confirmatory-exploratory, reported as such unless its pre-stated causal criterion is met.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The observed asymmetry could reflect the model misjudging evidence *strength* for valenced items rather than a genuine update-magnitude bias; the synthetic explicit-likelihood-ratio design, comprehension checks, and matched |LLR| controls are built to dissociate strength-misperception from valence gating (though for naturalistic items strength is only approximate). The asymmetry might be absent (a robust negative result is still valuable, showing LLMs update more rationally than humans on valenced evidence, or only mimic optimism in wording not internally). Valence gating may not be cleanly linear or single-locus; we report layerwise results and treat 'restore symmetry' vs. 'exaggerate' as the causal test rather than pinning an exact component. Self-relevance framing may just trigger sycophancy-like compliance; step 6's comparison to compliance-subspace directions and the dis-preferred-framing sign-flip test disentangle valence-of-content from social pressure. Steering could degrade fluency or blunt all updating (making the model ignore evidence); we monitor perplexity, neutral-scenario integration accuracy, and general benchmarks, and use small magnitudes with random-direction baselines. 'Desirability' labels are partly subjective and may reflect training-data framing; we human-validate a sample and balance across domains. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

Name: belief_currency_flag
Title: Still True? Probing Whether LLMs Internally Flag Beliefs as Current or Stale
Short Hypothesis: LLMs maintain an internal 'currency' flag on beliefs about item-states that distinguishes content the model treats as still-valid-now from content it treats as once-true-but-now-superseded (stale). This currency signal is linearly decodable from residual-stream activations, largely orthogonal to the truth-value direction, and causally gates whether outdated content is asserted as a current fact. This targets an epistemic axis (belief currency) distinct from temporal fact recall and from truth-value, and connects to the concrete failure mode of stating outdated facts as if current. We reframe the decodability and geometry sub-claims as validation in a sharper item-state setting; the load-bearing novel claim is H3 — that intervening on a currency direction changes stale-as-current assertion behavior beyond what truth- or uncertainty-magnitude steering achieves — which in turn licenses a concrete decision rule: detect a stale belief, then abstain, trigger retrieval, or downgrade confidence.
