Related Work: Existing interpretability work on time in LLMs studies recall of time-specific facts and geometry of chronology: Temporal Heads (2025) localizes heads that recall year-conditioned facts; Language Models Represent Space and Time (2023) finds linear space/time coordinate representations; Time Travel Engine (2026) treats chronology as a traversable manifold; TARDIS (2025) and Time Vectors (2023) steer/interpolate for temporal misalignment; History Matters (2024) edits temporal knowledge while preserving history; Layer of Truth (2025) tracks belief flips under poisoning. All of these represent *when a fact holds* or *how to recall/update it*, but none isolate an internal, decodable flag for the CURRENCY of a belief - i.e., whether the model tags a proposition as still-valid-now vs. once-true-but-now-stale - as an axis separate from the truth-value direction studied in Azaria & Mitchell (2023) and Truth-value judgment (2024). Prior belief work asks 'does the model believe X is true?' but not 'does the model believe X is still true?'. We introduce belief-currency as an orthogonal, steerable variable and link it causally to asserting outdated facts as current, which no prior work does. We position directly against temporal-drift geometry work (e.g., 'Geometry of Forgetting'): that line shows a decodable drift/recency structure, so we do not claim to be first to find a temporal axis; our delta is (i) causal steering of the currency direction, (ii) a leakage intervention on stale-as-current assertion, and (iii) a synthetic update-history track that isolates the currency mechanism from stale parametric knowledge. We soften absolute 'none isolate' claims to 'to our knowledge, prior work does not causally test a currency axis'. If 'currency' is a renamed subcase of temporal drift we say so; we define it as the still-valid-now vs. once-true-now-superseded contrast conditional on having been true, distinct from never-true falsehood.
Abstract: A fact can be true, false, or - crucially - it can have *been* true and since been superseded (a former capital, a retired record, a previous CEO). Humans robustly flag such content as stale rather than current. Large language models are notorious for confidently stating outdated facts as if they were current, yet prior interpretability work on time studies only how models recall time-specific facts or represent chronological coordinates, not whether models internally tag a belief by its currency. We ask a sharper, mechanistic question: does an LLM maintain an internal 'currency' flag that distinguishes beliefs it treats as still-valid-now from beliefs it treats as once-true-but-now-superseded? We hypothesize this flag is (i) linearly decodable from residual-stream activations, (ii) largely orthogonal to the well-studied truth-value direction, and (iii) causally gates whether stale content is asserted as a current fact. We construct a controlled dataset of item-state propositions in matched frames that vary currency (current vs. superseded) while holding proposition content and surface form as constant as possible, including synthetic entity-attribute facts with explicit update histories to control priors, plus a critical leakage probe that asks for the *current* value after a stale fact is present. We train linear probes on frozen open-weight models (Llama-3, Qwen2.5, Gemma-2, Pythia) to decode currency vs. truth, measure their geometric relationship, localize the responsible heads via activation patching (comparing to known Temporal Heads and truth heads), and test causal control: steering along the currency direction should modulate whether outdated content contaminates 'current-value' answers. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, subspace angle, projected-out decodability, patching effect sizes, and a staleness-leakage rate. So what: a decodable, steerable currency flag enables search assistants, finance/legal/biographical QA, and enterprise copilots over fast-changing entities to abstain or retrieve when a belief is internally flagged stale, rather than confidently asserting outdated values; it is also a testbed for training- or inference-time anti-staleness controls. Its deployment value depends on robustness/generalization, which our transfer experiments probe. We release a timestamped currency benchmark (real + synthetic update-history tracks), a currency probe, and the leakage-intervention/RAG-diagnostic.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 — a belief-currency flag is linearly decodable): Tests that current-valid vs. once-true-now-superseded is recoverable, separate from truth. Data: built from scratch, 6,000 propositions in two tracks: (a) 3,000 real facts with known changes (former vs. current leaders/CEOs/records/tallest-building), each as CURRENT and SUPERSEDED variants; (b) 3,000 synthetic entity-attribute facts with explicit in-context update histories to control priors and fix ground-truth currency; currency crossed with a never-true (false) axis; comprehension checks included; split 70/15/15 by proposition. Model: Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Pythia-2.8B, frozen; trainable only a logistic-regression probe at the state token, per layer; 5 seeds. Systems compared: currency probe vs. shuffled-label control vs. keyword-only baseline (presence of 'former/used to/year'). Decisive metric first: currency-probe test AUROC (restricted to true-at-some-point items) at best layer. Convincing: >= 0.80, control 0.50 +/- 0.05, >= 0.05 above keyword baseline, on >=3 of 4 models. Indecision band: 0.60-0.70 or within 0.05 of keyword baseline means possibly lexical — H1 not asserted. Negative: < 0.60 means no decodable currency flag.

Experiment 2 (H2 — currency is largely orthogonal to truth-value): Fit a truth direction (true vs. never-true). Decisive metric first: currency AUROC after projecting out truth (and symmetrically); secondary: subspace angle. Convincing: >= 90% retention and angle > 60 degrees. Indecision band: 70-90% or 40-60 degrees partial. Negative: < 70% or < 40 degrees means currency coincides with truth.

Experiment 3 (H3 — the currency flag causally gates asserting stale content as current): Build a currency CAA vector (current minus superseded activations). Data: a 1,000-item leakage subset asking for the CURRENT value after a superseded fact is present (synthetic track, so parametric staleness is excluded). Systems compared: currency-direction vs. random vs. truth-direction steering, alpha 2/4/8% residual norm. Decisive metric first: change in staleness-leakage rate (stale value asserted as current) when steering toward 'current' vs. 'stale'; secondary: hedging rate on genuinely current facts when steered toward 'stale', MMLU-subset, perplexity. Convincing: >= 15-point leakage shift, random < 5 points, perplexity rise < 10%. Indecision band: 5-15 points suggestive. Negative: < 5 beyond random or equals truth steering means no distinct currency gate.

Experiment 4 (H1 — localization): Activation patching between current and superseded runs; compare heads to Temporal Heads and truth heads from prior work. Decisive metric first: fraction of currency distinction recovered by top heads. Convincing: reproducible <= 20-head set recovers >= 50%. Indecision band: diffuse = distributed. Negative: no head > 20%.

Experiment 5 (H3 — predictiveness): Decisive metric first: AUROC using the currency probe readout to predict behavioral staleness-leakage errors vs. a log-prob baseline. Convincing: >= 0.70 and >= 0.05 above log-prob. Indecision band: 0.60-0.70. Negative: <= 0.60.

Experiment 6 (H1,H3 — generalization): Apply frozen probe/steering across domains (leaders, records, corporate, geographic) and synthetic-to-real. Decisive metric first: transfer AUROC and leakage-effect retention. Convincing: >= 0.70 and half retained. Indecision band: 0.60-0.70. Negative: <= 0.60.

Experiment 7 (H1,H3 — confound-hardened decoding and expanded baselines): Strengthens the decoding and predictiveness claims against lexical/template confounds and richer baselines. Data: the Experiment-1 pool re-split with entity-disjoint, relation-disjoint, and template-disjoint folds, plus cue-free templates that remove explicit temporal markers ('former', 'used to', years). Decisive metric first: currency-probe AUROC on template-disjoint, cue-free items compared against entropy, verbalized-confidence, an uncertainty probe, and a temporal-keyword heuristic; and E3 dose-response with unrelated-direction and nearby-layer steering controls. Convincing: cue-free AUROC >= 0.75 and >= 0.05 above every baseline, with a monotone dose-response selective to stale-current assertions. Indecision band: cue-free AUROC 0.65-0.75 or within 0.05 of the best baseline is limited. Negative: <= 0.65 cue-free, or no gain over uncertainty baselines, means currency is largely lexical or a re-description of uncertainty.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Currency may be entangled with surface temporal cues (words like 'former', 'used to', explicit years) rather than an abstract currency representation; we mitigate with diverse framings, paraphrases, matched-content controls, and by testing transfer to unseen cue types and to the synthetic track where currency is inferred from an update history rather than a keyword. The distinction may not be cleanly linearly separable or may be layer/model-specific; we report layerwise results with control tasks. Currency and truth directions may be less orthogonal than hypothesized, in which case the finding characterizes their entanglement (still informative). Leakage errors could stem from stale pretraining knowledge (the model never learned the update) rather than a currency-flag failure; the synthetic track with fully in-context update histories isolates the currency mechanism from stale parametric knowledge. For real facts, some 'current' values may drift after data collection; we timestamp the dataset and restrict claims accordingly. Steering could degrade fluency (off-manifold) or overshoot into indiscriminate hedging; we use small magnitudes, random/truth-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity and general benchmarks. Results may not transfer to very large closed models. 'Currency' is defined formally (still-valid-now vs. once-true-now-superseded, conditional on prior truth) and labeled consistently across real and synthetic data, with 'current' fixed relative to a stated dataset timestamp. Splits are entity-, relation-, and template-disjoint. E4 localization is treated as exploratory unless a sharper head-level currency hypothesis is supported. Staleness-leakage rate is defined precisely with answer-format and calibration/entropy controls to exclude generic hedging.

Name: defeasibility_flag_belief
Title: Rule or Rule-of-Thumb? An Internal Defeasibility Flag That Gates How a Single Counterexample Revises an LLM's Belief
Short Hypothesis: LLMs internally tag a general belief about a category as either DEFEASIBLE (a default/generic that tolerates exceptions, e.g. 'birds fly') or STRICT (an exception-intolerant universal, e.g. 'all bachelors are unmarried'). This defeasibility flag is (i) linearly decodable from residual-stream activations, (ii) largely orthogonal to the truth-value direction, and (iii) causally gates counterexample-driven revision: presenting a single exception should collapse belief in a strict universal but only mildly dent belief in a defeasible generic; steering the flag reverses this asymmetry, and mis-flagging predicts the two canonical human/LLM errors (misreading generics as universals -> overgeneralization; and unstable beliefs that overreact to one exception). (Throughout, "belief" denotes an internal, probe-decoded belief-state proxy, validated against behavior, not a claim of phenomenal belief.)
Related Work: Behavioral work robustly shows LLMs mishandle generics and defeasible reasoning: they conflate generics with universals and overgeneralize (Penguins Don't Fly 2022; Exceptions, Instantiations, and Overgeneralization 2024), fail to maintain stable beliefs when exceptions or irrelevant facts are added (Are LLMs classical or nonmonotonic reasoners? 2024), and vary widely on 20 defeasible patterns with CoT often hurting (Generics and Default Reasoning in LLMs 2025); MLMs are insensitive to quantification yet encode a generic-form meaning (Interpretation of Generalization in MLMs 2023). Classic interpretability isolates a linear truth-value direction (Geometry of Truth 2023; Truth-value judgment 2024). CRITICALLY, all defeasibility/generics work is behavioral or about quantifier probabilities; none isolate an internal DEFEASIBILITY flag (defeasible-default vs. strict-universal) as a decodable variable distinct from truth-value, nor test whether it causally gates how a single counterexample revises the belief. This differs from my prior essentialist_belief_mutability proposal, which tags a specific instance's property as essential vs. accidental; here the axis is the LOGICAL FORM of a general belief (exception-tolerant generic vs. exception-intolerant universal) and its role in counterexample-driven, non-monotonic revision. We transfer a canonical non-monotonic-reasoning phenomenon into LLM belief internals with a mechanistic, causal treatment. The nearest missing prior experiment, stated plainly: no prior work tests whether an internal LOGICAL-FORM variable (defeasible generic vs strict universal) CAUSALLY modulates one-counterexample revision while being distinct from the truth direction. Three candidate explanations are separated up front and each mapped to a control: lexical-cue detection ('all'/'typically') -> surface-matched paraphrases + cue-balanced synthetic track; prior-confidence/certainty -> a calibrated-confidence baseline and confidence-conditioned error prediction; abstract defeasibility -> the residual signal after both. 'Strict' is defined to include BOTH analytic/definitional universals AND empirically-universal and explicitly-stipulated strict rules, so definitional certainty is not conflated with logical form. An outcome that merely rediscovers quantifier/lexical cues (probe fails on the cue-balanced set) would NOT count as a new internal variable.
Abstract: 'Birds fly' and 'all squares have four sides' look grammatically similar but behave differently under a counterexample: a penguin leaves the first belief essentially intact, while a single three-sided 'square' would destroy the second. Humans track this difference (defeasible generics vs. strict universals), and LLMs are notorious for confusing them - overgeneralizing generics into universals, or letting one exception (or even an irrelevant fact) destabilize a belief. We ask a mechanistic question: does an LLM internally represent whether a general belief is defeasible or strict, and does that representation govern how a counterexample revises it? We hypothesize that a 'defeasibility' flag is (i) linearly decodable from residual-stream activations, (ii) largely orthogonal to the truth-value direction, and (iii) causally gates counterexample-driven revision - so that beliefs internally tagged strict collapse under one exception while those tagged defeasible barely move, and steering the flag reverses this asymmetry. We build a controlled dataset of general claims labeled defeasible (generics) vs. strict (analytic/definitional universals), matched in surface form, plus a synthetic-category track that stipulates a rule's logical form in-context to control priors, each paired with a single counterexample. On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3, Qwen2.5, Gemma-2, Mistral) we train linear probes to decode defeasibility vs. truth, measure their geometry, quantify a per-item revision-plasticity gap under a counterexample, test whether internal mis-flagging predicts overgeneralization and instability errors, localize the responsible heads via activation patching, and test causal steering. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, subspace angle, projected-out decodability, counterexample-revision gap, error-prediction AUROC, patching effect sizes, post-steering plasticity reversal, and perplexity. Calibrated exception handling matters for knowledge editing, legal/medical QA, and safety policies with exceptions; the promised improvement is less overreaction to rare anecdotes and less refusal collapse, i.e. better update specificity. We separate the scientific case (an internal logical-form variable gating non-monotonic revision) from the engineering case (a steer for calibrated exception handling), and add a transfer test to an external default-reasoning benchmark. If the behavioural generic/universal confusion is NOT backed by such an internal representation (a negative), default-reasoning behaviour is reducible to truth/confidence/lexical form — itself a useful constraint on the generics-in-LLMs literature.
Experiments:
The hypothesis has three testable parts: H1 — an LLM internally tags a general belief as DEFEASIBLE (a generic that tolerates exceptions) vs STRICT (an exception-intolerant universal), and this flag is linearly decodable from residual-stream activations; H2 — the flag is largely orthogonal to the truth-value direction; H3 — the flag causally gates counterexample-driven revision (one exception should collapse a strict universal but barely dent a defeasible generic), steering the flag reverses this asymmetry, and internal mis-flagging predicts the two canonical errors — overgeneralization (reading a generic as universal) and instability (revising a generic on irrelevant/supporting info).

Data (built from scratch). ~6,000 general claims labeled by logical form: DEFEASIBLE generics ("Birds fly", "Metals conduct electricity") and STRICT universals ("All squares have four sides", "Every prime > 2 is odd"), balanced across biology/artifacts/math-definitions/social, surface-matched where possible (bare-plural vs explicitly-quantified) with paraphrases swapping "birds fly"↔"all birds fly" to separate form from cue. Two tracks: REAL (~4,000) and a SYNTHETIC novel-category track (~2,000) that stipulates form in-context ("Every zorb is by definition three-eyed [strict]" vs "Zorbs typically have three eyes [defeasible]") to control priors and decouple form from lexical triggers. We use ~6,000 of ~6,000 (fewer only if the human-validated label filter drops borderline items). Each claim has a matched SINGLE-COUNTEREXAMPLE, an IRRELEVANT-FACT control, and a SUPPORTING-INSTANCE control, plus a behavioral REVISION probe, comprehension checks, and 3 paraphrases; defeasible/strict labels human-validated on 300 items.

Models. Frozen open-weight Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B. No transformer weights trained; only linear probes on frozen activations (L2 logistic regression per layer, item-disjoint 80/20, 5-fold CV, seeds {0,1,2}, mean±sd). Steering via contrastive activation addition, α ∈ {±2,±4,±8} × per-layer std.

Experiment 1 (H1 — defeasibility flag is decodable). At the claim tokens, train probes for (i) TRUTH-VALUE and (ii) DEFEASIBILITY, with shuffled-label control tasks, testing generalization to the synthetic track and across surface-matched paraphrases (so the probe cannot rely on "all"/"typically" cues). Decisive metric first: defeasibility probe AUROC on the synthetic, cue-balanced held-out set. Convincing: AUROC ≥ 0.80 on the cue-balanced set in ≥3 of 4 models with control-task at chance. Indecision band: 0.65–0.80 — decodable but possibly cue-assisted. Negative (≤0.65 on cue-balanced items): no abstract defeasibility representation, only lexical cues — H1 rejected.

Experiment 2 (H2 — orthogonality to truth). Compute cosine/subspace angle between defeasibility and truth directions; test residual decodability after projecting out truth; test cross-track generalization. Decisive metric: subspace angle and fraction of defeasibility decodability retained after projecting out truth. Convincing: angle ≥ 45° and ≥70% retained in ≥3 models. Indecision band: angle 20–45° or 40–70% retained — partial entanglement, characterized. Negative (angle <20°): not separable from truth — H2 rejected.

Experiment 3 (H3 — causal gating of counterexample revision). Present each true general claim, then its single counterexample; measure internal belief change (truth probe) and behavioral retraction, defining a per-item plasticity. Confirm the IRRELEVANT-FACT and SUPPORTING-INSTANCE controls do not revise a well-behaved generic. Localize via activation patching (patch defeasible↔strict activations at the counterexample point). Derive a defeasibility steering direction (controlling for truth) and test: (a) steering strict→defeasible makes universals resist a counterexample; (b) steering generic→strict makes one counterexample collapse them; (c) steering toward the CORRECT form improves calibrated revision; (d) specificity — random/truth directions do not selectively move revision, factual belief preserved; (e) collateral — MMLU (1k subset), non-manipulated accuracy, WikiText perplexity (2k lines). Also test whether the pre-counterexample defeasibility readout predicts overgeneralization and instability errors (AUROC) beyond log-prob and lexical baselines. Retraction/overgeneralization on open output is LLM-judge scored (300 items human-validated, κ ≥ 0.7). Decisive metric first: the strict-vs-defeasible counterexample-revision plasticity gap, and its reversal under steering. Convincing: baseline plasticity gap ≥ 0.3 (normalized belief-change units), reduced/reversed by ≥50% under form-flipping steering, controls <15% change, error-prediction AUROC ≥ 0.05 over baselines, <2 pt MMLU drop. Indecision band: baseline gap 0.1–0.3 or steering effect 20–50% — weak/partial. Negative (gap <0.1 or steering matched by controls): no internal flag gates revision — H3 rejected (a valuable constraint on the generics-in-LLMs literature). All results are planned, not measured.


Abstraction, controls, and baselines. The SYNTHETIC stipulated-form track is the PRIMARY evidence for H1/H3, with natural claims as external validation; we run cross-track transfer (train probe on synthetic stipulations, test on natural claims and vice versa) and train on one surface-form family testing on unseen paraphrase families, including cue-stripped phrasings and items where quantifier words are absent/present in BOTH classes. The truth probe's training data is balanced across logical forms with leakage prevention between truth and defeasibility. A confidence baseline stronger than log-prob (calibrated elicited probability, entropy, and a latent-certainty probe) tests whether plasticity is merely confidence-driven. H3 steering specificity uses random, neighbouring-probe, truth-direction, and decoder-accuracy-matched same-norm control directions; 'collapse' and 'barely dents' are given operational belief-change definitions so results do not rest on the LLM-judge alone.

Statistical analysis plan. Unit of analysis is the claim; we report bootstrap 95% CIs, fit mixed-effects models with random intercepts for claim/domain and fixed effects for logical form and model family, and apply Benjamini-Hochberg correction; a power analysis fixes items-per-cell to a minimum detectable plasticity gap of 0.1. The PRIMARY endpoint is the Experiment 3 (H3) strict-vs-defeasible counterexample-revision plasticity gap and its reversal under form-flipping steering; the thresholds (AUROC 0.80, angle 45deg, gap 0.3, 2pt MMLU) are heuristic desiderata. Validation is expanded to stratified audits by domain/label type rather than a fixed 300 items; head localisation is de-emphasised in a first submission unless it materially strengthens causality.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Revision behavior could be driven by the claim's pretraining confidence rather than a distinct defeasibility flag; the synthetic novel-category track (form stipulated in-context, decoupled from prior strength), surface-matched paraphrases, and conditioning error-prediction on a confidence baseline are designed to dissociate defeasibility from raw confidence. The flag may be entangled with surface cues (bare plural vs. 'all'/'every', 'by definition' vs. 'typically'); we mitigate with paraphrase perturbations, comprehension checks, and the synthetic track where cues are balanced. Defeasibility and truth directions may be less orthogonal than hypothesized, in which case the finding characterizes their entanglement (still informative). The defeasible/strict label is partly graded/subjective (some generics are near-universal); we human-validate and treat borderline items separately. The effect may be absent internally - a robust negative result (LLMs' behavioral generic/universal confusion is NOT backed by an internal defeasibility representation gating revision) is itself a valuable, publishable finding constraining the generics-in-LLMs literature. Probes may not be cleanly linear at every layer; we report layerwise results with control tasks. The gating component may be distributed; we treat 'steer to reverse/calibrate plasticity' as the causal test rather than pinning an exact head. Behavioral retraction/overgeneralization scoring on open-ended output needs an LLM-judge plus human validation. Steering could degrade fluency or make the model indiscriminately rigid or labile; we use small magnitudes, random/truth-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity, non-manipulated accuracy, and general benchmarks. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

Name: belief_contingent_emotion_leak
Title: How Would They Feel? Probing Whether LLMs Predict Emotions From an Agent's (False) Belief or From Reality
Short Hypothesis: When predicting how an agent will feel about an outcome, an LLM internally computes TWO linearly separable subspaces -- affect grounded in the agent's (possibly false) BELIEF and affect grounded in REALITY -- rather than a single valence/appraisal code; and, mirroring the human curse-of-knowledge in affective theory of mind, the reality-grounded affect leaks into and biases the belief-grounded prediction. The two subspaces are decodable and largely dissociable, and the leak is causally reducible by steering, yielding correct false-belief emotion attributions.
Related Work: ToM interpretability decodes an agent's COGNITIVE belief STATUS (true/false) from attention heads and describes a 'lookback' binding mechanism (Language Models Represent Beliefs of Self and Others 2024; Language Models use Lookbacks to Track Beliefs 2025; Brittle Minds 2024; GridToM 2025). A 2025 paper (Decomposing Theory of Mind) shows ToM steering is mediated by increased emotional processing, and Mechanistic Interpretability of Emotion Inference (2025) localizes emotion representations to mid-layers via appraisal concepts. In human neuroscience, AFFECTIVE ToM — inferring how someone will FEEL given their belief state, dissociable from cognitive belief tracking — is robustly established (Skerry & Saxe 2014 'A Common Neural Code for Perceived and Inferred Emotion'; Hooker 2008 'Mentalizing about emotion'; Sebastian 2013; Skerry 2015 three-dimensional mental-state code), and the curse of knowledge biases such affective attributions toward what the observer knows. CRITICALLY, no LLM interpretability work isolates a BELIEF-CONTINGENT emotion prediction (how a false-believing agent will feel) as an internal channel SEPARATE from a REALITY-CONTINGENT emotion prediction, nor tests whether the reality channel contaminates the belief channel (an affective curse-of-knowledge), nor localizes/steers this. This differs from cognitive-belief-status decoding (about what the agent believes, not how they will feel about it) and from my prior curse_of_knowledge_leakage proposal (which concerns leakage into a factual ignorant-BELIEF channel, not an EMOTION-prediction channel). We transfer canonical affective-ToM neuroscience into LLM belief internals with a mechanistic, causal treatment. Sharper falsifiable claim and its alternative: genuine dual-channel evidence requires two linearly separable subspaces (belief-grounded vs reality-grounded affect) that dissociate under matched valence, NOT a single integrated emotion code that a task-conditioned decoder merely reads out two ways; we pre-specify that a single-code account predicts no dissociation after valence matching and no selective steering. Contrast with prior emotion-processing/mediation papers: they localize or mediate an emotion signal but do not decompose it into belief- vs reality-grounded channels or show contamination between them. Adopters: model auditors, social-AI designers, and the cognitive-science/interpretability communities, not only benchmark builders.
Abstract: A child who believes a box holds chocolate will feel delighted opening it — even if we know it now holds broccoli. Predicting how someone will feel requires reasoning from THEIR belief, not from reality, a capacity human neuroscience identifies as affective theory of mind and shows to be systematically biased by the observer's own knowledge (the curse of knowledge). As LLMs increasingly reason about how people will feel (in assistance, tutoring, mental-health, and social settings), we ask a mechanistic question: when an LLM predicts an agent's emotional reaction, does it compute a belief-contingent emotion (grounded in the agent's possibly-false belief) as a channel distinct from a reality-contingent emotion, and does reality leak into the belief channel? We hypothesize that (i) belief-contingent and reality-contingent emotion predictions are two linearly-decodable, largely dissociable channels in the residual stream, (ii) the reality-contingent emotion contaminates the belief-contingent emotion — an internal signature of affective curse-of-knowledge — (iii) the leak is graded with outcome valence intensity and predicts false-belief emotion-attribution errors, and (iv) the leak is carried by an identifiable component such that steering it restores correct belief-grounded emotion prediction. We build controlled false-belief emotion-attribution scenarios where an agent's belief and reality imply different emotions, with matched conditions where reality is or is not revealed and a synthetic track to control priors. On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) we train linear probes to decode the two emotion channels, measure their geometry, quantify a per-item affective-leak score, test predictiveness, localize responsible heads via activation patching (comparing to cognitive-belief and emotion-inference heads), and test causal control. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, subspace angle, projected-out decodability, affective-leak magnitude, valence modulation, leak–error AUROC, patching effect sizes, post-steering error reduction, and perplexity. User-visible failure mode: mispredicting how a user feels when the system knows facts the user does not -- directly relevant to tutoring empathy, support-bot and counseling responses, and interpersonal planning. If the dual-channel structure is absent (a single integrated code), that is an informative negative for affective-ToM interpretability.
Experiments: Common setup (stated once): Models — Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B-v0.3; frozen weights, only linear probes trained (L2 logistic, C by CV). Activations: residual stream at emotion-relevant tokens read WITHOUT the emotion query, all layers, per-head for localization; seeds {0,1,2}; item-level splits. Dataset built from scratch (adapted from BigToM/Skerry-Saxe-style stimuli): ~6k affective false-belief scenarios where an AGENT's belief-implied emotion differs from the REALITY-implied emotion, REAL and SYNTHETIC novel-entity tracks, with a key manipulation (model IS vs IS NOT told reality, agent's belief fixed), graded outcome-valence intensity, TRUE-BELIEF control items (both channels agree — no leak expected), and probe time-locked to the pre-discovery moment. We generate 6k and use all (~1k true-belief controls). Belief/reality/emotion labels human-validated on 300 items (kappa ≥ 0.7 gate). Experiment 1 (H1 — belief-contingent and reality-contingent emotion are two linearly-decodable, largely dissociable channels): train probe A = BELIEF-CONTINGENT emotion and probe B = REALITY-CONTINGENT emotion, anchored on agreeing/single-source control items; compute the principal angle between them and projected-out decodability. Decisive metric first: held-out AUROC of A and B (vs shuffled control 0.50±0.05) AND the angle theta. Convincing H1: both AUROC ≥ 0.70 (emotion is graded, so a lower bar than binary facts) AND theta ≥ 45 degrees with projected-out drop < 0.05. Indecision: AUROC 0.55–0.70 or theta 25–45 degrees → channels weakly separable; AUROC ≤ 0.55 or theta < 25 degrees refutes clean two-channel structure. Experiment 2 (H2 — reality leaks into the belief channel): define per-item AFFECTIVE LEAK = shift of probe A toward the reality-emotion in reality-revealed minus reality-withheld conditions. Decisive metric first: mean signed leak, with true-belief controls confirmed at ~0. Convincing: leak > 0 with Cohen's d ≥ 0.3 in the majority of models on both tracks, controls near 0. Indecision |leak| within ±1 s.e. of 0 or d 0.1–0.3; leak ≤ 0 refutes H2 (clean belief-grounding — informative negative). Experiment 3 (H3 — the leak is graded with outcome-valence intensity and predicts false-belief emotion-attribution errors): decisive metric first: (a) slope of leak vs valence intensity (convincing if positive, CI excludes 0) and (b) AUROC of the pre-query leak predicting behavioral emotion-attribution errors (convincing ≥ 0.70, beating log-prob and lexical baselines by ≥ 0.05). Indecision: slope CI straddles 0 and AUROC 0.55–0.70; negative slope / AUROC ≤ 0.55 refutes H3. Experiment 4 (H4 — an identifiable component carries the leak; steering restores correct belief-grounded emotion prediction): activation patching reality-revealed<->withheld to locate the minimal transporting component (logit-difference effect sizes), compared to cognitive-belief/lookback heads and mid-layer emotion-inference units; derive a contrastive affective-leak direction and ablate/subtract. Decisive metric first: reduction of leak and of false-belief emotion errors. Convincing H4: leak reduced ≥ 50% and errors reduced ≥ 15 pp, with random/cognitive-belief-direction baselines not selectively acting, the model's own knowledge of reality preserved, perplexity increase < 10%, MMLU-subset drop < 3 pp. Indecision 20–50% / 5–15 pp; < 20% / < 5 pp means not localized. Experiment 5 (generalization): transfer across scenario types (positive/negative surprises, second-order beliefs), real vs synthetic, valence levels (retention ≥ 0.65). Thresholds fixed pre-data. Scope is reduced to 1-2 PRIMARY claims (dual-channel decodability + reality->belief leak); dissociation geometry and localization are secondary. Label definition: because emotions are multi-dimensional, 'belief-emotion' and 'reality-emotion' targets are defined on a fixed valence/arousal + discrete-category scheme, with items constructed so the two targets differ only because belief and reality differ. Controls: same-valence pairs, lexical controls, belief-only and reality-only prompts, random-label probes, matched task-format controls, and a NON-SOCIAL false-belief / factual-uncertainty negative control to establish affective-ToM specificity. Ablations for prompt wording, answer format, and time-locking rule out output-token bias and recency. Steering is reported only if selective (unrelated emotional and factual competence preserved within stated bounds).
Risk Factors and Limitations: The belief-contingent and reality-contingent emotion channels may be hard to separate cleanly because emotion is a graded, multi-dimensional readout; we mitigate by using scenarios with categorically distinct belief- vs. reality-emotions, anchoring each channel on agreeing/single-source control items, reporting layerwise results with control tasks, and focusing on the relative shift (leak) rather than absolute emotion decoding. The observed leak could reflect legitimate inference (once the agent tastes/opens, reality genuinely changes their emotion) rather than an anticipatory curse-of-knowledge; we time-lock the probe to the pre-discovery moment (agent still holding the false belief), use the reality-withheld-vs-revealed contrast, and the synthetic track to isolate contamination from valid update. The effect may be absent internally — a robust negative result (LLMs cleanly ground emotion predictions in the agent's belief, firewalling reality) would itself be a valuable, publishable finding refining the affective-ToM-in-LLMs picture. Emotion/belief-emotion directions may overlap with a generic valence direction; we include matched-valence controls and compare to an emotion-inference direction. The leak may be a distributed component rather than a discrete head; we treat 'steer to restore belief-grounded emotion' as the causal test rather than pinning an exact head. Emotion labels are partly subjective; we human-validate and treat borderline items separately. Comprehension checks separate genuine affective-ToM failure from parsing failure. Steering could degrade fluency or flatten all emotion prediction; we use small magnitudes, random/cognitive-belief-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity, non-manipulated accuracy, and general benchmarks. Results may not transfer to very large closed models. The steering claim is stated conservatively: it counts only if belief-grounded affect is corrected while unrelated emotional and factual competence are preserved; otherwise we report the dissociation as correlational.

Name: sleeper_effect_belief_decay
Title: The Sleeper Effect Inside: Does Source-Discounting Decay Faster Than Content-Belief Over an LLM's Context?
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the human sleeper effect, when an LLM reads a claim explicitly discounted by its source (attributed to an unreliable source or accompanied by a disclaimer), the model separates the claim into two decodable channels -- CONTENT-belief and SOURCE-discount -- whose signals decay at DIFFERENT rates over conversational/token distance: the source-discount decays faster, so internal belief in the discounted claim's content RISES with distance. The single falsifiable signature is: source-discount decay slope < content-belief decay slope AND behavioral endorsement rises with distance only for source-discounted claims (not for undiscounted or content-refuted controls).
Related Work: The sleeper effect — a delayed increase in persuasion from a discounted message, driven by faster decay of source memory than message memory — is a canonical, heavily-cited human finding (Kumkale & Albarracin 2004 meta-analysis, 333 citations; Hovland; the dissociation account limiting it to discounted highly-credible messages; misinformation grows stronger over time, 2023). In LLM interpretability, 'Trust Me, I'm an Expert' (2026) shows authority/credibility bias is encoded and steerable, 'CrAM' (2025) modifies credibility-weighting attention heads for RAG, 'Linear representations change over a conversation' (2026) shows factuality directions can flip across a dialogue, and 'Contextual Feature Drift' (2024) shows context retention decays over sequential inputs. My prior 'belief_source_tags' proposal tags provenance statically, and 'continued_influence_belief' concerns explicit retraction. CRITICALLY, none isolate the sleeper-effect signature: two internal channels — content-belief and source-discount — that DECAY AT DIFFERENT RATES over conversational distance, producing a delayed RISE in the internally-decoded belief in a discounted claim. We transfer this canonical human phenomenon into LLM belief internals with a mechanistic, causal treatment, distinct from static credibility-bias work and from retraction/CIE work. Prior-art gap, stated precisely: no prior work shows SOURCE-SPECIFIC DIFFERENTIAL decay (source-discount fading faster than content-belief) producing a delayed rise in endorsement; existing results show only broad context drift, recency effects, or authority encoding. Negative competitors we must rule out: (a) uniform context forgetting (both channels decay together), (b) generic recency bias (any early content fades), and (c) authority-bias drift (all sourced claims shift equally); the two-channel differential-decay signature is distinguished from all three by the controls below. Closest LLM papers and what each lacks: authority/source-encoding probes (encode the source but do not track differential decay), representation-drift-over-context work (shows drift, not source-specific channels), contextual-belief work (updates belief, no two-channel decay).
Abstract: People discount a claim from an untrustworthy source at first, but weeks later often believe it anyway — the sleeper effect, one of the most reproduced findings in persuasion research, explained by source memory decaying faster than message memory. As LLMs process ever-longer contexts where discounted claims sit far upstream of the point of use (long RAG passages, multi-turn dialogues, extended documents), a consequential question arises: does an LLM inherit the sleeper effect at the level of its internal beliefs — does its belief in a source-discounted claim silently rise as conversational distance grows? We hypothesize that (i) the model represents two separable channels, a content-belief signal and a source-discount signal, both linearly decodable; (ii) the source-discount signal decays faster than the content-belief signal as token/turn distance from the claim increases, so the net internally-decoded belief in a discounted claim RISES with distance (the internal sleeper signature); (iii) this rise predicts delayed behavioral endorsement of the discounted claim; and (iv) the differential decay is carried by an identifiable component such that boosting/preserving the source-discount signal abolishes the sleeper rise. We build a controlled dataset of claims paired with source-discount cues (unreliable-source attribution, disclaimers), read out at varying downstream distances, with a synthetic-entity track to control priors. On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) we train linear probes for content-belief and source-discount, trace their decay curves across distance, quantify the belief-rise, test predictiveness, localize the responsible heads via activation patching, and test causal control. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, per-distance content-belief and source-discount decay slopes, net belief-rise magnitude, delayed-endorsement AUROC, patching effect sizes, post-intervention sleeper-rise change, and perplexity. Real-world failure mode: in long RAG/chat sessions, stale claims that were explicitly discounted earlier can resurface as endorsed later; those affected include RAG builders, safety teams, enterprise assistants, and misinformation defenses. We quantify magnitude in a deployment metric (unsafe/erroneous endorsement rate and calibration shift across distance), not only probe units, and point to source-memory tagging or retrieval-refresh policies as mitigations.
Experiments: Common setup (stated once): Models — Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B-v0.3 (base + instruct); frozen weights, only linear probes trained (L2 logistic, C by CV). Activations: residual stream at the claim's key tokens re-instantiated at the read-out point, all layers, per-head for localization; seeds {0,1,2}; item-level splits. Dataset built from scratch: ~6k claims each paired with a SOURCE-DISCOUNT cue (low-credibility attribution or explicit disclaimer), REAL and SYNTHETIC stipulated-truth tracks; each placed at graded DISTANCE D in {0, 200, 800, 2000} tokens (and 0/2/5 turns) from the read-out, with neutral filler. Controls per item: CREDIBLE-SOURCE variant (should show no rise), NO-SOURCE variant, LENGTH-MATCHED filler at D=0, and a SOURCE-REMINDER-at-readout variant. We generate 6k and use all (balanced across distances). Source-recall comprehension checks included. Experiment 1 (H1 — content-belief and source-discount are two decodable channels): read activations WITHOUT the endorsement query; train probe X = CONTENT-BELIEF P(content true) and probe Y = SOURCE-DISCOUNT (currently flagged unreliable/disclaimed). Decisive metric first: held-out AUROC of X and Y vs shuffled-label controls (0.50±0.05). Convincing H1: both ≥ 0.75 at D=0. Indecision 0.55–0.65 → weak; ≤ 0.55 for either refutes that channel. Experiment 2 (H2 — source-discount decays faster than content-belief over distance, so net decoded belief in a discounted claim RISES with D): fit decay curves of X and Y vs D. Decisive metric first: the difference in decay slopes (Y steeper than X) and the resulting net-belief-rise slope for discounted claims. Convincing: Y decays significantly faster than X (slope difference CI excludes 0) AND net decoded belief rises with D by ≥ 0.1 (probe units) from D=0 to D=2000, while the CREDIBLE-SOURCE control shows no rise (slope CI includes 0) and the LENGTH-MATCHED control rules out length artifacts. Indecision: slopes differ but net rise < 0.1 / CI straddles 0 → sleeper signature weak; Y not faster than X → no internal sleeper effect (H2 refuted; reassuring for long-context reliability). Experiment 3 (H3 — the internal rise predicts delayed behavioral endorsement): collect behavioral endorsement at each D. Decisive metric first: AUROC of the internal net-rise predicting increased endorsement at distance, plus the human-derived prediction that the SOURCE-REMINDER condition abolishes both. Convincing: AUROC ≥ 0.70 (beating log-prob and D=0 stated-belief baselines by ≥ 0.05) AND source-reminder cuts the endorsement rise by ≥ 50%. Indecision 0.55–0.70; ≤ 0.55 refutes H3. Experiment 4 (H4 — the differential decay is carried by an identifiable component; preserving source-discount abolishes the rise): activation patching D=0 source-discount activations into far-distance runs to find the minimal component whose weakening produces the rise (logit-difference effect sizes), compared to credibility-weighting heads and authority-bias directions; then inject/preserve a contrastive source-discount direction at read-out. Decisive metric first: reduction of the net belief-rise and of delayed endorsement. Convincing H4: rise reduced ≥ 50% and delayed endorsement reduced ≥ 15 pp, with random/truth-direction baselines not selectively acting, perplexity increase < 10%, MMLU-subset drop < 3 pp, credible-claim accuracy preserved. Indecision 20–50% / 5–15 pp; < 20% / < 5 pp means not localized. Experiment 5 (generalization): transfer across discount types, real vs synthetic, distance units, and domains (retention ≥ 0.65). Thresholds fixed pre-data. This proposal is reduced to ONE primary hypothesis (differential decay -> delayed endorsement), ONE primary metric (the source-discount-minus-content-belief decay-slope difference, with the paired behavioral endorsement-rise slope for discounted vs control claims), and ONE primary causal test (refreshing/re-injecting the source-discount cue at distance should abolish the endorsement rise). Controls separating source decay from generic forgetting: a no-discount cue condition, neutral-filler distance matched to discounted distance, same-distance/different-structure contexts, and an explicit source-memory probe (can the model still report the source/disclaimer at each distance). Localization/patching is EXPLORATORY unless a specific circuit family is identified. Thresholds are accompanied by pilot-calibrated effect sizes with 95% CIs rather than hard cutoffs alone; probe labels are pre-registered with paraphrase and tokenization robustness checks.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The belief-rise could reflect generic context-retention decay (Contextual Feature Drift) rather than a specific source-vs-content differential decay; the credible-source baseline (control A, which should show no rise), length-matched control (C), and the requirement that the SOURCE-DISCOUNT channel decay FASTER than the content channel (not both equally) are designed to distinguish a genuine sleeper signature from uniform drift. The effect may be absent internally — a robust negative result (LLMs retain source-discounting as strongly as content over distance, showing no sleeper effect) would itself be a valuable, publishable finding contrasting with humans and reassuring for long-context reliability. Re-instantiating the claim at the read-out point to probe content-belief is imperfect since surrounding context differs; we anchor probes at matched claim tokens, use paraphrase perturbations, and report layerwise results. The two channels may be entangled such that a clean differential decay is not observable — still an informative characterization. Distance in tokens/turns is only a proxy for the human temporal delay; we test both units and note the analogy is structural, not literal time. Comprehension/source-recall checks separate genuine forgetting-of-source from parsing failure. The decay/localization component may be distributed rather than a discrete head; we treat 'preserve source-discount to abolish the rise' as the causal test rather than pinning an exact component. Behavioral endorsement scoring on open-ended items needs care; we use forced truth-judgments where possible plus human validation. Steering could degrade fluency or make the model indiscriminately distrust all upstream content; we use small magnitudes, random/truth-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity, credible-claim accuracy, and general benchmarks. Results may not transfer to very large closed models. We present any circuit-localization result as exploratory rather than confirmatory, and report effect sizes with CIs alongside the pre-registered slope thresholds so a null (no differential decay) is cleanly interpretable as uniform forgetting.

Name: false_consensus_belief_leak
Title: Everyone Agrees With Me: Does an LLM's Own Belief Leak Into Its Estimate of How Many People Believe It?
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the human False Consensus Effect, an LLM's internally-decoded estimate of the SOCIAL PREVALENCE of a claim (how many people believe X) is contaminated by the model's OWN belief in X: the prevalence-estimate readout is pulled toward high when the model endorses X and toward low when it rejects X, holding the actual real-world prevalence constant. We hypothesize that (i) social-prevalence estimate and own-belief are two linearly-decodable channels, (ii) they are partially entangled such that own-belief leaks into the prevalence channel (a decodable false-consensus leak), (iii) the leak is graded with own-belief confidence and largest for contested claims, and (iv) an identifiable component carries the leak so that ablating it restores an unbiased prevalence estimate.
Related Work: Human cognitive/social science robustly establishes: the False Consensus Effect (people overestimate how many others share their own belief), that perceived social prevalence rationally feeds belief updating (Social Prevalence Is Rationally Integrated in Belief Updating 2021/2022; Beliefs are most swayed by social prevalence under uncertainty 2021), an illusory consensus effect from repetition (2024), and 'false social reality' pluralistic ignorance where estimates of others' views are systematically biased (climate-support 2022; scientific/social consensus 2018). In LLMs, 'People will agree what I think: Investigating LLM's False Consensus Effect' (2024) shows LLMs BEHAVIORALLY exhibit FCE, and 'Personas as a Way to Model Truthfulness' (2023) / 'Linear Representations of Political Perspective' (2025) show truth/ideology are linearly represented and steerable. Interpretability isolates a linear truth/belief direction (Geometry of Truth 2023; Truth-value judgment 2024) and belief-state geometry (Transformers Represent Belief State Geometry 2024; Shape of Beliefs 2026). CRITICALLY, no work isolates the LLM's INTERNAL representation of the SOCIAL PREVALENCE of a claim (estimated fraction of people who believe X) as a channel SEPARATE from the model's own truth-belief, nor tests whether own-belief CAUSALLY CONTAMINATES the prevalence estimate (the internal signature of false consensus), nor localizes/removes that leak. This differs from my prior 'illusory_truth_internal' (repetition->own belief), 'source_independence_discounting' (source counting), and 'contestedness' (is it disputed) proposals: here the target variable is the model's estimate of OTHERS' belief prevalence and its egocentric contamination by the model's own stance. We transfer the canonical False Consensus Effect into LLM belief internals with a mechanistic, causal treatment. Novelty claims: N1 social-prevalence estimate and own-belief are two decodable channels; N2 own-belief leaks into the prevalence channel (a decodable false-consensus signature); N3 the leak is graded with own-belief confidence and largest for contested claims; N4 an identifiable component carries it and can be ablated. Discriminators (must be ruled out): we compare the prevalence channel against probes for factuality, familiarity, token frequency, answer-prior popularity, and an ideology/political direction, and require the leak to survive after all are regressed out; the contribution is not detecting output false-consensus (already shown behaviorally in 2024) but isolating an internal prevalence variable and showing causal contamination plus selective ablation.
Abstract: People overestimate how many others share their own opinions and beliefs — the False Consensus Effect, one of the most reproduced findings in social psychology. As LLMs are increasingly asked to estimate public opinion, gauge consensus, or predict how many people would endorse a claim, a consequential question arises: does the model form an estimate of a belief's social prevalence that is independent of its own stance, or does its own belief egocentrically contaminate that estimate? We hypothesize that (i) an LLM's estimate of how many people believe a claim (social prevalence) and its own belief in the claim's truth are two distinct, linearly-decodable channels, (ii) these channels are partially entangled such that the model's own belief leaks into the prevalence channel — an internal signature of false consensus — (iii) the leak is graded with own-belief confidence and largest for genuinely contested claims where a real prevalence is uncertain, and (iv) the leak is carried by an identifiable internal component that can be ablated to restore an unbiased prevalence estimate. We build a controlled dataset of claims for which an external ground-truth social prevalence exists (from public-opinion polls and consensus surveys), spanning claims the model endorses, rejects, and is uncertain about, plus a synthetic-entity track that decouples own-belief from stipulated prevalence. On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) we train linear probes to decode own-belief and estimated prevalence, quantify a per-claim false-consensus leak (prevalence-estimate deviation from ground truth in the direction of own-belief), test its graded structure, localize the responsible heads via activation patching, and test causal control by steering/ablating a leak direction. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, subspace angle, false-consensus leak magnitude and sign, confidence/contestedness modulation, leak–error AUROC, patching effect sizes, post-ablation debiasing, and perplexity. Stakeholders: computational social scientists, opinion-simulation and synthetic-population benchmark builders, alignment teams, and product teams doing moderation/policy forecasting. Practical payoff: predicting survey marginals / endorsement distributions before vs after debiasing. A robust null (LLMs estimate others' beliefs independently of their own stance) contrasts with the human FCE and is itself valuable.
Experiments: Common setup (stated once): Models — Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B-v0.3 (base + instruct); frozen weights, only linear probes trained (own-belief: logistic; prevalence: ridge regression to a graded target, C/alpha by CV). Activations: residual stream at claim tokens, all layers, per-head for localization; seeds {0,1,2}; item-level splits. Dataset built from scratch/assembled: ~6k claims each paired with an external GROUND-TRUTH social prevalence (fraction endorsing), drawn from public-opinion polls and consensus surveys plus settled factual claims (prevalence ~100%); REAL track spans claims the target models ENDORSE, REJECT, and are UNCERTAIN about (verified via own-belief probe/behavior), and a SYNTHETIC novel-entity track stipulates prevalence decoupled from any own-belief cue. We generate/assemble 6k and use all; prevalence labels human-validated on 300 items (kappa/agreement gate ≥ 0.7) and timestamped/scoped. Experiment 1 (H1 — social-prevalence estimate and own-belief are two linearly-decodable channels): read activations WITHOUT posing either question; train probe A = OWN-BELIEF P(claim true) and probe B = estimated PREVALENCE calibrated against ground truth on held-out claims. Decisive metric first: probe A held-out AUROC and probe B held-out calibration (R^2 / mean absolute error vs ground-truth prevalence), against shuffled-label controls (AUROC 0.50±0.05; R^2 ~0). Convincing H1: A AUROC ≥ 0.75 AND B R^2 ≥ 0.3 (MAE ≤ 15 prevalence points). Indecision: B R^2 0.1–0.3 → prevalence only weakly decodable, H1 partial; R^2 < 0.1 refutes a usable prevalence channel. Experiment 2 (H2 — own-belief leaks into the prevalence channel): define per-claim FALSE-CONSENSUS LEAK = signed deviation of the internal prevalence readout from ground truth in the direction of own-belief (over-estimate for endorsed, under-estimate for rejected). Decisive metric first: mean signed leak. Convincing: leak > 0 with Cohen's d ≥ 0.3 in the majority of models, present in the SYNTHETIC track (isolating from valid truth->prevalence inference) and on contested claims where truth and prevalence diverge. Also report subspace angle between channels as corroboration. Indecision: |leak| within ±1 s.e. of 0 or d 0.1–0.3 → not established; leak ≤ 0 refutes H2 (clean channel separation — an informative negative). Experiment 3 (H3 — the leak is graded with own-belief confidence and largest for contested claims): decisive metric first: slope of leak vs own-belief confidence, and leak(contested) minus leak(settled). Convincing: positive confidence slope (bootstrap CI excludes 0) AND contested > settled by a positive margin (CI excludes 0). Indecision: CIs straddle 0 → grading not established; negative refutes H3. Experiment 4 (H4 — an identifiable component carries the leak; ablating restores an unbiased prevalence estimate): activation patching high/low own-belief into matched prevalence runs to find the minimal transporting component (logit-difference effect sizes), compared to truth heads and any ideology direction; derive a contrastive leak direction and ablate. Decisive metric first: reduction of leak toward 0 and improvement of prevalence accuracy toward ground truth. Convincing H4: leak reduced ≥ 50% and prevalence MAE improved ≥ 5 points, with random/truth-direction ablations not selectively debiasing, own-belief preserved (AUROC within 0.03), perplexity increase < 10%, MMLU-subset drop < 3 pp. Indecision 20–50% / 2–5 points; < 20% / < 2 points means not localized. Experiment 5 (predictiveness): internal leak predicts behavioral verbal-prevalence error (AUROC ≥ 0.70, beating log-prob and lexical baselines by ≥ 0.05). Experiment 6 (generalization): transfer across domains (policy/science/moral/factual), real vs synthetic, and own-belief levels (retention ≥ 0.65). Thresholds fixed pre-data. Representation-level check (to show the channel is not a linear-probe artifact): report CCA/subspace overlap and a nonlinear-probe sanity check alongside the linear probes; whether 'localized component' is a head, MLP feature, direction, or distributed subspace is reported explicitly rather than assumed. Confound suite: regress out truth, familiarity, frequency, controversy, and ideology before claiming a unique leak. Experiment 7 (end-to-end application): predict real endorsement distributions (poll marginals) and measure whether leak-direction ablation reduces marginal-prediction error on held-out claims where own-belief and true prevalence diverge (convincing if MAE improves >= 5 points with own-belief preserved). Steering baselines are equal-norm random, truth-direction, ideology-direction, and matched-degradation. Power reported for d>=0.3 at the stated item counts.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The prevalence-estimate probe requires a calibrated graded readout, which is harder than a binary belief probe; miscalibration could inflate or deflate the measured leak. We mitigate by calibrating against external ground-truth prevalence on held-out claims, reporting layerwise results with control tasks, and using the SYNTHETIC track where stipulated prevalence gives an exact target. The observed leak could reflect legitimate inference (in the real world, claims the model endorses because they are true genuinely tend to be widely believed) rather than an egocentric bias; the synthetic-entity track (own-belief decoupled from stipulated prevalence) and the contested-claim subset (where truth and prevalence diverge, e.g. false-but-popular or true-but-unpopular claims like the climate-support 'false social reality') are designed to dissociate genuine false-consensus contamination from valid truth->prevalence inference. The effect may be absent internally — a robust negative result (LLMs estimate others' beliefs independently of their own stance) would itself be a valuable, publishable finding contrasting with the human FCE and with the behavioral LLM-FCE report. The two channels may be strongly entangled such that the 'leak' is really imperfect channel separation — still an informative characterization. Own-belief and prevalence directions may overlap with an ideology/political direction; we include non-political claims and compare against an ideology probe. Probes may not be cleanly linear at every layer; we report layerwise results with control tasks. The leak component may be distributed rather than a discrete head; we treat 'ablate to debias prevalence' as the causal test rather than pinning an exact head. Ground-truth prevalence labels are time- and population-dependent; we timestamp/scope claims and human-validate a sample. Steering could degrade fluency or make prevalence estimates indiscriminately regress to a prior; we use small magnitudes, random/truth-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity, non-manipulated prevalence accuracy, and general benchmarks. Results may not transfer to very large closed models. We temper localization language: unless sparse/selective effects are demonstrated, the leak is reported as a possibly-distributed subspace rather than a discrete component, and sample sizes/power are stated for the pre-registered effects.

Name: counterfactual_dual_meaning_belief
Title: Two Worlds at Once: Do LLMs Internally Hold Both the Supposed and the Backgrounded-Factual Meaning of a Counterfactual?
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the canonical psycholinguistic 'dual meaning' of counterfactual conditionals (a subjunctive like 'If Tom had studied, he would have passed' conveys BOTH a supposed dependency AND the backgrounded fact that Tom did NOT study and failed), an LLM processing a counterfactual simultaneously maintains two internally-decodable belief layers about the same proposition: the SUPPOSED belief (P holds in the counterfactual world) and the BACKGROUNDED-FACTUAL belief (P is actually false). These two layers are separately linearly decodable, largely orthogonal, and causally dissociable: which layer dominates the model's downstream answer can be steered, and failures to maintain the factual layer produce a characteristic error (treating the counterfactual antecedent as actually true). (Throughout, "belief" denotes an internal, probe-decoded belief-state proxy, validated against behavior, not a claim of phenomenal belief.)
Related Work: Cognitive/psycholinguistic work robustly establishes counterfactual DUAL MEANING: subjunctive-counterfactuals express a supposition while implying the opposite factual state of affairs (Understanding Counterfactuality: A Review, Kulakova & Nieuwland 2016, 119 citations; Marking the counterfactual: ERP evidence for pragmatic processing of German subjunctives 2014, 48 citations). In LLM interpretability, 'Counterfactual reasoning: in-context emergence' (2025) finds a latent concept is linearly encoded with noise-abduction heads, and the 'Competition of Mechanisms' line (Ortu et al. 2024; reproductions 2025) traces how factual-recall vs. in-context counterfactual tokens compete, localizing factual/counterfactual info to subject/attribute positions and attention heads. Truth-probe work isolates a single linear truth direction (Geometry of Truth 2023; Truth-value judgment 2024). CRITICALLY, the competition-of-mechanisms work treats fact vs. counterfactual as a WINNER-TAKE-ALL competition for the output token and does NOT ask whether the model concurrently maintains TWO belief layers (supposed AND backgrounded-factual) about the SAME proposition, as human dual-meaning theory predicts; nor does it isolate these as separately decodable, orthogonal, steerable channels, nor connect the loss of the factual layer to the specific error of endorsing a false antecedent. My prior suppositional_belief_gating proposal concerns a binary endorsed-vs-entertained framing flag; this proposal is specifically about the two CO-PRESENT belief layers that are the signature of counterfactual conditionals. We transfer a canonical cognitive-science phenomenon (counterfactual dual meaning) into LLM belief internals with a mechanistic, causal treatment. Novelty stated as claims, conceptual vs empirical: CONCEPTUAL — the hypothesis of TWO CO-PRESENT belief layers for the SAME proposition (supposed-P-holds and backgrounded-P-is-actually-false), the signature of counterfactual conditionals, as opposed to a winner-take-all competition for the output token; EMPIRICAL — (1) both layers are separately decodable and (2) causally dissociable by steering, with (3) incomplete factual-layer maintenance producing false-antecedent endorsement. The 'backgrounded-factual' layer is specified as a representation of not-P for THIS proposition (anchored on frames where it diverges from the supposed layer), not merely the generic truth-direction. Observation impossible under winner-take-all but expected under co-presence: high supposed-P AND low factual-P read simultaneously at the antecedent tokens before any answer. Predicted patching signatures are pre-committed: dual-layer predicts two separable patch sites restoring different layers, whereas competition predicts a single site flipping the output token.
Abstract: When we say 'If the dice had been rigged, the game would have been unfair,' we simultaneously entertain a hypothetical world (rigged dice, unfair game) AND signal a fact about the real world (the dice were NOT rigged, the game WAS fair). Decades of psycholinguistics establish this counterfactual 'dual meaning' as a hallmark of human comprehension. LLMs increasingly reason under counterfactual premises (planning, causal reasoning, hypotheticals, safety scenarios), yet it is unknown whether they preserve both layers or collapse into one. We ask a sharp mechanistic question: when an LLM reads a counterfactual conditional, does it internally maintain TWO separable belief layers about the antecedent proposition P — a SUPPOSED belief (P holds, in the counterfactual world) and a BACKGROUNDED-FACTUAL belief (P is actually false)? We hypothesize both layers are (i) separately linearly decodable from residual-stream activations, (ii) largely orthogonal, and (iii) causally dissociable, such that steering can shift which layer governs downstream answers, and that incomplete maintenance of the factual layer produces a characteristic error — treating the false antecedent as actually true. We build a controlled dataset of counterfactual conditionals, matched indicative/factual and simple-suppositional frames, and synthetic-entity items to control priors, plus factual-inference probes ('In reality, is P true?') and consequent-inference probes. On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) we train linear probes for the supposed and factual layers, measure their geometry, localize the responsible heads via activation patching (comparing to competition-of-mechanisms heads), and test causal steering. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, subspace angle, projected-out decodability, layer-dominance shift under steering, patching effect sizes, factual-endorsement error rate, and perplexity. This matters wherever agents reason under premises known to be false — planning over hypotheticals, counterfactual causal explanation, and safety-scenario simulation — since collapsing the factual layer makes a model act as if the counterfactual premise were real. If confirmed, it yields new benchmarks, targeted steering to preserve reality while reasoning in-scenario, and a model-selection criterion; a negative (no separable factual layer) is itself valuable, sharpening the competition-of-mechanisms picture and contrasting with human dual-meaning comprehension.
Experiments:
The hypothesis has three testable parts: H1 — when an LLM reads a counterfactual conditional, both the SUPPOSED belief (antecedent P holds in the counterfactual world) and the BACKGROUNDED-FACTUAL belief (P is actually false) about the same proposition are separately linearly decodable from residual-stream activations; H2 — the two layers are largely orthogonal directions; H3 — they are causally dissociable, so steering can shift which layer governs the model's downstream answer, and incomplete maintenance of the factual layer produces a characteristic error: treating the false antecedent as actually true.

Data (built from scratch). ~6,000 items, each anchored on a proposition P and rendered in three matched frames: (a) COUNTERFACTUAL subjunctive ("If P had been the case, Q would have happened" — implies NOT-P in reality); (b) INDICATIVE/FACTUAL control ("P is the case, so Q"); (c) SIMPLE-SUPPOSITION control ("Suppose P; then Q" — no factual implication). Two tracks: REAL propositions (~4,000) and a SYNTHETIC novel-entity track (~2,000, e.g. "If Zorblax had orbited Kelvath...") with stipulated truth to control priors. We use ~6,000 of ~6,000 (fewer only where a comprehension filter drops items). Probes attached: FACTUAL-INFERENCE ("In reality, is P true?" — correct answer NO for counterfactuals), SUPPOSED/CONSEQUENT-INFERENCE ("Within the scenario, does Q hold?"), comprehension checks, and 3 mood-cue paraphrases (to prevent decoding from "had"/"would" surface cues); 200 items human-validated.

Models. Frozen open-weight Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B. No transformer weights trained; only linear probes on frozen residual-stream/per-head activations (L2 logistic regression per layer, item-disjoint 80/20, 5-fold CV, seeds {0,1,2}, mean±sd). Steering via contrastive activation addition, α ∈ {±2,±4,±8} × per-layer std.

Experiment 1 (H1 — both layers decodable and co-present). At the antecedent P tokens, without asking a question, train probes for (A) SUPPOSED belief in P and (B) BACKGROUNDED-FACTUAL belief in P, anchored using the indicative-factual and simple-supposition frames plus reality-only items, with shuffled-label control tasks. Decisive metric first: in the COUNTERFACTUAL condition, the co-presence rate = fraction of items where supposed-P reads high AND factual-P reads low simultaneously. Convincing: co-presence rate ≥ 0.70 with both probes ≥ 0.80 AUROC in their anchor conditions, in ≥3 of 4 models. Indecision band: co-presence 0.5–0.70 or a probe at 0.65–0.80 AUROC — partial evidence for two layers. Negative (co-presence < 0.5 or no separable factual layer): the model collapses to one belief (winner-take-all) — H1 rejected, reported as a contrast with human dual-meaning comprehension.

Experiment 2 (H2 — orthogonality). Compute cosine/subspace angle between the supposed and factual directions; test residual decodability after projecting out one from the other; also chart per-layer emergence (does the factual/backgrounded layer arise later?). Decisive metric: subspace angle and fraction of factual-layer decodability retained after projecting out the supposed layer. Convincing: angle ≥ 45° and ≥70% retained in ≥3 models. Indecision band: angle 20–45° or 40–70% retained — partial entanglement, characterized. Negative (angle <20°): layers not separable — H2 rejected.

Experiment 3 (H3 — causal dissociation and false-antecedent error). Localize each layer via activation patching (patch counterfactual↔indicative activations; compare to factual/counterfactual competition heads, subject/attribute positions, and noise-abduction heads from prior work). Derive per-layer steering directions and test: (a) amplifying supposed / suppressing factual raises false-antecedent endorsement (model treats the premise as real); (b) amplifying factual restores correct factual inference while preserving in-scenario consequent reasoning; (c) specificity — random and truth directions do not selectively move layer dominance; (d) collateral — MMLU (1k subset), indicative-frame accuracy, WikiText perplexity (2k lines). Also test whether the pre-query factual-layer strength predicts correct factual inference (AUROC) beyond log-prob/surface baselines. Decisive metric first: change in false-antecedent-endorsement rate between +supposed and +factual steering, with controls. Convincing: ≥15-percentage-point swing, controls <5 pt, consequent-inference accuracy preserved (<3 pt drop when amplifying factual), <2 pt MMLU drop. Indecision band: 5–15 pt swing — weak dissociation. Negative (<5 pt or matched by controls): layers are not causally separable — H3 rejected. All results are planned, not measured.


Surface-cue and conflict controls. To show the dual-layer result is not recoverable from subjunctive mood cues ('had'/'would') we add cue-only baselines, tense/mood-matched non-counterfactuals, shuffled-content controls, and require probe transfer across paraphrase families; false-premise NON-subjunctive controls and negation controls separate dual meaning from generic conflict/falsity. Steering baselines beyond random/truth are matched-norm and unrelated-semantic directions plus probe directions taken from the indicative and simple-supposition controls. We report probe selectivity/calibration (not only AUROC) and run a causal-mediation analysis testing whether pre-query factual-layer strength mediates factual-inference correctness beyond surface features and LM confidence.

Statistical analysis plan. Unit of analysis is the item; we report bootstrap 95% CIs over items and seeds, fit mixed-effects models with random intercepts for item and fixed effects for frame and model family, and apply Benjamini-Hochberg correction across layers/heads/models; we require cross-model AND cross-template probe generalisation, treating template-specific success as a weakness. The PRIMARY endpoint is the Experiment 1 (H1) co-presence rate in the counterfactual condition; thresholds are heuristic desiderata. Minimum viable scope: H1 co-presence with the cue-only and mood-matched controls plus the H3 dissociation demo; full head localisation is a contingent refinement.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The 'supposed' and 'backgrounded-factual' layers may be hard to separate cleanly because both concern the same proposition P; the matched indicative/simple-supposition frames, synthetic-entity track, and probes anchored on frames where the two layers agree vs. diverge are designed to dissociate them, and projected-out analyses quantify any residual entanglement (which is itself informative). The dual layers might not be genuinely co-present internally — the model may simply implement a winner-take-all competition (as the competition-of-mechanisms work suggests) collapsing to one belief; a robust negative result (no separable factual layer during counterfactual processing) would itself be a valuable, publishable finding contrasting LLM processing with human dual-meaning comprehension and sharpening the competition-of-mechanisms picture. The layers could be decoded via surface mood cues ('had'/'would') rather than abstract belief representations; paraphrase/mood perturbations, comprehension checks, and the synthetic track mitigate this. Belief may not be cleanly linearly decodable at every layer; we report layerwise results with control tasks. The responsible components may be distributed rather than discrete heads; we treat 'steer to shift layer dominance / restore factual inference' as the causal test rather than pinning exact heads. Steering could degrade fluency or destroy the model's ability to reason within the counterfactual scenario (over-suppressing the supposed layer); we use small magnitudes, random/truth-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity, consequent-inference accuracy, indicative-frame accuracy, and general benchmarks. Human dual-meaning comparison is structural, not a claim of identical mechanism. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

Name: recursive_belief_depth_collapse
Title: Losing the Thread: Do LLMs' Nested Belief Representations Collapse Toward Reality as Recursion Deepens?
Short Hypothesis: As belief-attribution recursion deepens ('A thinks B thinks C believes X'), an LLM's internally-decoded representation of the deepest embedded agent's belief progressively DEGRADES and collapses toward the model's own ground-truth (reality) belief — an internal 'egocentric compression' that grows with nesting order, is linearly measurable as a depth-dependent loss of distinctness between the nested-agent belief channel and the reality channel, predicts higher-order ToM errors, and is causally recoverable by steering to restore nested-belief distinctness. (Throughout, "belief" denotes an internal, probe-decoded belief-state proxy, validated against behavior, not a claim of phenomenal belief.)
Related Work: Interpretability work decodes first/second-order belief STATUS (true/false) of a protagonist and an oracle from attention heads and shows steering improves ToM (Language Models Represent Beliefs of Self and Others 2024; Brittle Minds 2024; GridToM 2025), and identifies a 'lookback' mechanism binding character-object-state triples and updating beliefs via visibility (Lookbacks 2025). Behavioral work shows higher-order ToM accuracy DECLINES with recursion order (HI-TOM 2023; Multi-Order ToM 2024; Spontaneous High-Order Generalization 2025) but treats models as black boxes. CRITICALLY, no work asks whether this behavioral decline reflects an INTERNAL representational phenomenon: that with increasing nesting depth the model fails to maintain a distinct representation of the deepest embedded agent's belief and instead reuses its own reality/ground-truth belief (a depth-dependent egocentric collapse). Prior belief-decoding is at fixed order (1st/2nd); my prior curse_of_knowledge proposal concerns a single-level ignorant-belief leak, not a depth-scaling collapse across recursion orders. We reframe higher-order ToM failure as a measurable, mechanistic loss of nested-belief distinctness and give it a causal treatment.
