Novelty as a falsifiable delta: no prior work quantifies an ORDER-DEPENDENT reduction in the representational separation between the deepest-nested-agent belief and the model's own reality channel and links that reduction to behavioural higher-order-ToM errors. Prior belief decoding is at fixed order (1st/2nd); binding/lookback work explains role tracking, not depth-scaling collapse toward reality; causal-ToM-steering improves accuracy without a depth-collapse account. The subspace-angle/distinctness geometry is borrowed; its application to recursion depth and to belief-vs-reality separation is the new use. We pre-commit to a distinction between 'egocentric collapse toward reality' (deepest readout moves specifically toward the reality direction), 'generic signal loss' (lower norm/decodability without a reality shift), and 'role-binding failure' (reports a wrong non-reality agent), and treat these as competing, separately testable explanations.
Abstract: Humans can recurse: 'Ann thinks Bob believes Cara knows the ball is in the box.' LLMs reproduce this up to a point, but their accuracy falls as the nesting deepens — a robust behavioral finding whose internal cause is unknown. We ask a sharper, mechanistic question: does the model actually maintain a distinct internal representation of each nested agent's belief, or does the deepest embedded belief progressively collapse toward the model's own view of reality as recursion depth grows? We hypothesize that (i) the belief attributed to the deepest embedded agent is linearly decodable from residual-stream activations, (ii) as nesting order increases the deepest-agent belief channel loses distinctness from the reality/ground-truth channel — a depth-dependent egocentric compression — (iii) the degree of this internal collapse predicts higher-order ToM errors, and (iv) the collapse is causally recoverable by steering to restore nested-belief distinctness, improving higher-order ToM. We build a controlled dataset of stories with nested belief attributions from order 1 to 5, where at each depth the deepest agent holds a belief that diverges from reality (so the two channels are dissociable), plus a synthetic-entity track to control priors. On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) we train linear probes to read the deepest-agent belief and the reality belief at each order, quantify a per-order collapse score (loss of distinctness), test its predictiveness for behavioral errors, localize the responsible heads via activation patching (comparing to belief/lookback heads), and test causal steering. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, per-order collapse score, subspace angle by depth, collapse–error AUROC, patching effect sizes, post-steering distinctness and accuracy gains, and perplexity. This matters for negotiation and multi-party assistants, social simulation, and safety-critical human-model coordination, where losing the deepest agent's perspective produces confident but egocentric answers; it also bears on role-conditioned reasoning and world-model separation in agents generally. If confirmed, the fix targets representational separation (or binding, or prompting recursion) depending on which competing explanation wins; if nested beliefs stay distinct (a negative), higher-order errors are relocated to readout/parsing. We also deliver a lightweight per-order distinctness diagnostic applicable to new models.
Experiments:
The hypothesis has four testable parts: H1 — the belief attributed to the deepest embedded agent in a nested attribution is linearly decodable from residual-stream activations; H2 — as nesting order grows, the deepest-agent belief channel loses distinctness from the model's own reality/ground-truth channel (a depth-dependent egocentric collapse); H3 — the degree of internal collapse predicts higher-order Theory-of-Mind (ToM) errors; H4 — the collapse is causally recoverable by steering to restore nested-belief distinctness, improving higher-order ToM accuracy.

Data (built from scratch, adapting existing generators). ~5,000 stories with nested belief attributions of order O ∈ {1,2,3,4,5}, generated with the HI-TOM and Multi-Order-ToM templates (public) but constrained so the DEEPEST embedded agent holds a belief that DIVERGES from reality at every order (false-belief chains), making the deepest-agent belief and the reality state dissociable. Matched TRUE-BELIEF chains (deepest belief = reality) are included as controls, and story length is matched across orders to control context length. Two tracks: REAL entities (~3,000) and a SYNTHETIC novel-agent/object/location track (~2,000) to control pretraining priors. We use all ~5,000 (fewer for a given model only if a comprehension-check filter drops items). Each story carries a behavioral higher-order QUESTION probe (what does the deepest agent believe?), comprehension checks ("who observed what at each level"), balanced reality-location assignment, and 3 paraphrase/order perturbations; 200 items human-validated.

Models. Frozen open-weight Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B. No transformer weights trained; only linear probes on frozen residual-stream/per-head activations (L2 logistic regression, per layer, item-disjoint 80/20 split, 5-fold CV, seeds {0,1,2}, report mean±sd). Steering via contrastive activation addition, α ∈ {±2,±4,±8} × per-layer std.

Experiment 1 (H1 — deepest-agent belief is decodable). At the state/object tokens, without asking the question, train linear probes to read (A) the deepest-agent belief and (B) the reality state, anchored on true-belief-agreeing and reality-only items, with shuffled-label control tasks. Decisive metric: order-1 and order-2 deepest-agent probe AUROC vs shuffled-label chance. Convincing: AUROC ≥ 0.80 at O≤2 in ≥3 of 4 models with the control task at chance. Indecision band: AUROC 0.65–0.80 — decodable but weak, reported as such. Negative (AUROC ≤ 0.65 even at O=1): the deepest-agent belief is not linearly represented — H1 rejected and later experiments reinterpreted as readout failure.

Experiment 2 (H2 — depth-dependent collapse). On false-belief chains, measure across O ∈ {1..5}: (i) deepest-agent probe accuracy, (ii) subspace angle between the deepest-agent and reality directions, (iii) the rate at which the deepest-agent readout reports the reality value. Decisive metric first: slope of the reality-value error rate vs O (positive slope = collapse). Convincing: monotonic increase with a fitted slope whose CI excludes 0 in ≥3 models, and larger collapse on false- than true-belief chains. Indecision band: slope CI touching 0 or non-monotonic — collapse not established; report trajectory. Negative (flat/declining error rate with O): nested beliefs stay distinct — H2 rejected (a valuable finding that higher-order errors are purely readout/parsing).

Experiment 3 (H3 — collapse predicts ToM errors). Collect behavioral higher-order errors per item. Decisive metric: AUROC of the per-item collapse score (read before the question) predicting the behavioral error, vs a log-prob baseline and a surface-feature (length/order) baseline. Convincing: collapse AUROC ≥ 0.70 and ≥ 0.05 over both baselines in ≥3 models; additionally the per-model collapse-onset order predicts the accuracy cliff order (±1). Indecision band: AUROC 0.60–0.70 or <0.05 over baselines — suggestive only. Negative (≤0.60): internal collapse does not explain behavior — H3 rejected.

Experiment 4 (H4 — causal restoration). Localize via activation patching the heads carrying distinct deepest-agent belief (patch low-order distinct-belief activations into high-order runs); compare to belief heads and lookback/binding heads. Derive a "nested-belief distinctness" steering direction and test: (a) steering restores deepest-agent distinctness and raises higher-order ToM accuracy; (b) negation exaggerates collapse; (c) specificity — random and reality-direction steering do not selectively restore distinctness and the model's own reality belief is preserved; (d) collateral — MMLU (1k subset), low-order accuracy, WikiText perplexity (2k lines). Decisive metric: higher-order (O≥3) accuracy gain under steering. Convincing: ≥10 percentage-point accuracy gain at O≥3, <2 pt drop at O≤2, <5% perplexity rise, controls <3 pt. Indecision band: 4–10 pt gain or collateral drop 2–5 pt — partial/contaminated. Negative (<4 pt or matched by controls): no steerable component — H4 rejected. All results are planned, not measured.


Discriminative controls and baselines. To separate depth-collapse from generic depth degradation we add non-social recursive tasks and arbitrary nested-attribute chains, and we predict INTERMEDIATE-agent beliefs to show specificity to the deepest belief vs reality. We test whether the deepest readout moves specifically toward the reality direction (cosine to the reality axis) vs merely losing norm/decodability. H3 baselines: item difficulty, logit-margin/entropy, hidden-state norm, generic probe confidence, and an order/length/entity-count-only model. We also ablate per-order probes vs a low-order probe transferred upward, to test whether the GEOMETRY (not probe fit) changes with depth, and report token-position sensitivity (answer token vs final token vs throughout).

Statistical analysis plan. Unit of analysis is the item; we report bootstrap 95% CIs over items and seeds, fit mixed-effects models with random intercepts for item and fixed effects for order and model family, and apply Benjamini-Hochberg correction across layers/heads/orders/models; a power analysis fixes items-per-order to a minimum detectable error-rate slope. One primary causal graph is pre-registered: depth -> reduced belief/reality separation -> deepest-agent error, with each experiment mapped to one edge; the PRIMARY endpoint is the Experiment 2 (H2) reality-value-error slope vs order. Thresholds are heuristic desiderata. Minimum viable scope: H1-H2 with the signal-loss-vs-reality-shift control and H3 prediction; H4 steering is a contingent refinement framed as candidate circuitry unless lesion+rescue+specificity hold. Validation is expanded via grammar-generated stories with per-order correctness guarantees rather than a fixed 200-item audit.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The behavioral decline at higher orders could stem from parsing/binding failures (the model loses track of who is who) rather than a belief-toward-reality collapse; comprehension checks, the binding-lookback comparison, and separating 'reports reality' from 'reports a random other agent' errors help distinguish egocentric collapse from generic confusion. The deepest-agent and reality channels may be hard to separate cleanly at high orders precisely because they collapse — which is the phenomenon, but it complicates probe anchoring; we anchor probes on low-order and true-belief-agreeing items and report layerwise results with control tasks. The effect may be absent internally (a robust negative result — nested beliefs stay distinct and errors are purely a readout/parsing issue — would itself be a valuable finding). Collapse could be confounded with context length at higher orders; length-matched controls and the true-belief control chains address this. Belief may not be cleanly linearly decodable at every layer/order; we report layerwise results. The distinctness-maintaining component may be distributed rather than a discrete head; we treat 'steer to restore distinctness/accuracy' as the causal test rather than pinning an exact head. Steering could degrade fluency or corrupt the model's own reality belief; we use small magnitudes, random/reality-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity, low-order accuracy, and general benchmarks. Human ToM comparison is structural, not a claim of identical mechanism. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

Name: moral_possibility_contamination
Title: That Could Never Happen: Does an Event's Immorality Make an LLM Internally Represent It as Impossible?
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the canonical human finding that people's DEFAULT representation of what is possible is constrained by morality and rationality (immoral/irrational events are implicitly treated as impossible), an LLM's internally-decoded possibility representation of a physically-possible event is pulled toward IMPOSSIBLE when the event is immoral/norm-violating, holding physical possibility constant. This moral contamination of the possibility flag is linearly decodable, largely dissociable from a separate morality/valence direction, is stronger under fast/implicit read-out than under explicit deliberation, predicts errors in possibility judgments, and is causally removable by steering.
Related Work: Phillips & Cushman (2017, 146 citations) show humans DEFAULT to treating immoral and irrational events as impossible, a default implicit representation dissociable from explicit modal deliberation; 'How people think about possibilities' (2023) and modal-displacement neuroscience (2020) develop the possibility-representation account. In LLM interpretability, 'Is This Just Fantasy?' (2025) isolates linear modal-category vectors (probable/improbable/impossible/inconceivable) reflecting event likelihood and imageability, and 'How LLMs Conflate Logical Validity with Plausibility' (2025) shows validity and plausibility are aligned linear directions producing content effects that steering can disentangle. CRITICALLY, no work asks whether an event's MORAL status contaminates the model's internal POSSIBILITY representation - whether immoral-but-physically-possible events are internally tagged as impossible - nor whether this is a fast/default effect distinct from explicit modal reasoning, nor localizes/removes it. This differs from the modal-vector work (which represents graded physical/statistical likelihood, not moral contamination of possibility), from the validity-plausibility conflation work (logical validity vs. semantic plausibility, not morality vs. metaphysical possibility), and from my prior epistemic-tag proposals (truth/currency/contestedness/sacredness of factual beliefs). We transfer a canonical cognitive-science phenomenon into LLM belief internals with a mechanistic, causal treatment. Exact delta from human work: this is not a behavioral replication in LLMs but an INTERNAL CAUSAL claim -- that a decodable possibility coordinate is displaced toward IMPOSSIBLE by an event's immorality while physical possibility is held constant. Existing modal-category-vector papers characterize modal STRUCTURE (possible/necessary categories) but not moral contamination OF the possibility coordinate. We preempt the 'it's just rarity/improbability' explanation in the claim itself: matched base-rate, synthetic-norm, and neutral/prosocial controls (below) are essential, not optional.
Abstract: People implicitly treat things they consider wrong as things that simply cannot be - immoral and irrational events are, by default, represented as impossible, a bias dissociable from explicit reasoning about what is metaphysically or physically possible (Phillips & Cushman, 2017). As LLMs increasingly reason about what is possible (planning, safety, hypotheticals, risk assessment), a consequential question arises: does an LLM's internal representation of possibility get contaminated by an event's morality, so that immoral-but-physically-possible events are internally treated as impossible? We hypothesize that (i) a possibility representation and a morality/valence representation are two linearly-decodable channels, (ii) morality leaks into the possibility channel - the internal possibility readout for a physically-possible event is pulled toward 'impossible' when the event is immoral, holding physical possibility constant, (iii) the leak is larger under fast/implicit read-out (early layers / no chain-of-thought) than under explicit deliberation, mirroring the human default-vs-deliberative dissociation, (iv) the leak predicts behavioral possibility-judgment errors, and (v) it is carried by an identifiable component removable by steering. We build a controlled dataset crossing physical possibility (possible/impossible) with morality (immoral/neutral/prosocial), with matched wording and a synthetic-norm track to control priors. On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) we train linear probes to decode possibility vs. morality, measure their geometry, quantify a per-item moral-possibility leak, test the fast-vs-deliberative and predictiveness hypotheses, localize the responsible heads via activation patching, and test causal control. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, subspace angle, projected-out decodability, moral-possibility leak magnitude, fast-vs-deliberative modulation, leak-error AUROC, patching effect sizes, post-steering debiasing, and perplexity. Downstream risk (lead): moralized-but-physically-possible events may be UNDER-considered in planning, safety, and counterfactual reasoning because the model internally marks them impossible -- directly relevant to threat modeling, abuse red-teaming, policy analysis, and legal hypotheticals. We include an applied demo where this distortion changes a model decision, not only probe geometry.
Experiments: Common setup (stated once): Models — Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B-v0.3; frozen weights, only linear probes trained (L2 logistic, C by CV). Activations: residual stream at the event's key tokens read WITHOUT any question, ALL layers (early-vs-late analysis is central), per-head for localization; seeds {0,1,2}; item-level splits. Dataset built from scratch: ~6k event descriptions crossing PHYSICAL POSSIBILITY (physically-possible vs physically-impossible) with MORALITY (immoral / neutral / prosocial) using matched action templates so morality varies while physical possibility is held constant; REAL and SYNTHETIC-NORM (in-context stipulated novel norms, matched wording) tracks. We generate 6k and use all. Physical-possibility and morality labels human-validated on 300 items (kappa ≥ 0.7 gate). Experiment 1 (H1 — possibility and morality are two linearly-decodable channels): train probe A = POSSIBILITY (physically-possible vs impossible, trained on morally-NEUTRAL items to define a morality-free axis) and probe B = MORALITY (immoral vs prosocial). Decisive metric first: held-out AUROC of A and B vs shuffled controls (0.50±0.05). Convincing: both ≥ 0.75. Indecision 0.55–0.65; ≤ 0.55 for either refutes that channel. Also compute the principal angle theta (H1 includes 'largely dissociable'): convincing dissociation theta ≥ 60 degrees with projected-out drop < 0.05; 30–60 degrees partial; < 30 degrees entangled. Experiment 2 (H2 — morality leaks into the possibility channel): define per-item MORAL-POSSIBILITY LEAK = shift of probe A toward 'impossible' for physically-POSSIBLE items as a function of immorality (possible+immoral vs matched possible+neutral/prosocial). Decisive metric first: mean signed leak. Convincing: leak > 0 with d ≥ 0.3 in the majority of models, reproduced in the SYNTHETIC-NORM track (isolating in-context morality from base rates). Indecision |leak| within ±1 s.e. of 0 or d 0.1–0.3; leak ≤ 0 refutes H2. Experiment 3 (H3 — the leak is larger under fast/implicit than deliberative processing): decisive metric first: (a) EARLY-minus-LATE-layer leak difference (early-exit read-out as a fast-processing proxy) and (b) no-CoT-minus-CoT behavioral leak. Convincing: leak larger early than late AND larger without CoT than with CoT, both CIs excluding 0. Indecision: one of the two significant / CIs straddle 0 → dissociation weak; neither → H3 refuted. Experiment 4 (H4 — the leak predicts possibility-judgment errors): AUROC of the pre-query leak predicting behavioral errors (calling a possible-but-immoral event impossible). Decisive metric first: AUROC ≥ 0.70, beating log-prob and lexical baselines by ≥ 0.05; indecision 0.55–0.70; ≤ 0.55 refutes H4. Experiment 5 (H5 — the leak is carried by an identifiable component removable by steering): activation patching immoral<->neutral to find the minimal transporting component (logit-difference effect sizes), compared to modal-category vectors, validity/plausibility directions, and moral-direction heads; derive a contrastive leak direction and ablate. Decisive metric first: reduction of leak and of possibility-judgment errors. Convincing H5: leak reduced ≥ 50% and errors reduced ≥ 15 pp, with random/pure-morality-direction baselines not selectively acting, the model's moral judgment preserved, perplexity increase < 10%, MMLU-subset drop < 3 pp. Indecision 20–50% / 5–15 pp; < 20% / < 5 pp means not localized. Experiment 6 (generalization): transfer across event domains, real vs synthetic-norm, and immorality intensity (retention ≥ 0.65). Thresholds fixed pre-data. The H1-H5 bundle is reduced to 2-3 PRIMARY hypotheses (decodable possibility axis; moral displacement of it at constant physical possibility; causal removability); the rest are exploratory. A likelihood/base-rate control set is added: same physical possibility, matched real-world frequency, plus an explicit LIKELIHOOD probe, to prove the effect is moral contamination and not mere improbability. Ablations control sentiment/valence, harm, rarity, norm-violation, and lexical surprisal, with the effect required to survive matched pairs. The fast-vs-deliberative claim uses a direct test (time-binned or constrained-decoding readout), or the layer-depth analysis is explicitly labeled correlational. Steering/localization adds null controls that preserve possibility behavior while removing morality leakage (and vice versa) plus capability-preservation metrics on standard modal-reasoning tasks. Possibility labels are defined operationally with annotation guidelines and inter-annotator agreement.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The leak could reflect legitimate inference (immoral events may be statistically rarer in training data, so 'less likely' is partly correct) rather than a genuine morality-to-possibility contamination; the physically-possible constraint (all target items are genuinely possible), matched-wording neutral/prosocial controls, the synthetic-norm track (morality stipulated in-context, decoupled from base rates), and separating a POSSIBILITY axis from a graded LIKELIHOOD axis are designed to dissociate moral contamination of the categorical possible/impossible flag from mere frequency-based improbability (though full separation from likelihood is difficult and we report both). The effect may be absent internally - a robust negative result (LLMs cleanly separate morality from possibility) would itself be a valuable, publishable finding contrasting with the canonical human bias. The possibility and morality directions may be entangled such that the 'leak' is imperfect channel separation - still an informative characterization, and directly engages the validity-plausibility conflation literature. Possibility and morality labels are partly subjective/graded; we human-validate and treat borderline items separately, noting results reflect the model's training-data notion of morality (itself the object of study). The morality direction may overlap with a valence/harm axis; matched prosocial vs. immoral contrasts and projected-out analyses address this. Probes may not be cleanly linear at every layer; we report layerwise results with control tasks. The fast-vs-deliberative test uses early-exit as a proxy for default processing, which is imperfect. The leak component may be distributed rather than a discrete head; we treat 'steer to debias possibility' as the causal test rather than pinning an exact head. Steering could degrade fluency or flatten the model's possibility discrimination entirely; we use small magnitudes, random/morality-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity, non-manipulated accuracy, and general benchmarks. Results may not transfer to very large closed models. We tighten the human-analogy framing so the contribution reads as an LLM-internal mechanistic question rather than a direct transplant, and treat the fast-vs-deliberative layer analysis as correlational unless the time-binned/constrained-decoding test confirms it.

Name: sacred_value_protection_flag
Title: Priceless or For Sale? An Internal Sacredness Flag That Gates Whether LLMs Refuse to Trade Off Protected Values
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the human 'sacred/protected values' phenomenon (people refuse to trade sacred values for material benefit and process them via deontological rule-retrieval rather than cost-benefit), LLMs internally tag a value-laden proposition as SACRED/protected -- defined operationally as taboo-to-trade, i.e. refusal that is insensitive to offer magnitude -- vs. SECULAR (tradeable, offer-sensitive). This sacredness flag is (i) linearly decodable from residual-stream activations, (ii) largely orthogonal to the value's valence/goodness direction and separable from a generic safety-refusal direction, and (iii) causally gates whether the model accepts a quantitative tradeoff: steering the flag turns priceless commitments into negotiable ones (and vice versa).
Related Work: Human neuroscience shows sacred values are processed non-utilitarianly via deontological rule-retrieval and resist being traded for money (Berns et al. 2012 'The price of your soul'; Sheikh et al. 2016 on protected values in narratives; Dark Side of Morality 2020). LLM interpretability has mapped Moral Foundations as linear, steerable directions (The Straight and Narrow 2026; Emergent Moral Representations 2025; Tracing Moral Foundations 2026; Jentzsch/Schramowski 2021 'moral direction'), studied moral biases (Knobe effect 2025), and value entanglement (Value Entanglement 2026). Behaviorally, moral-belief firmness under debate was probed (Evaluating Moral Beliefs 2024). CRITICALLY, all of this represents *which foundation* a claim activates or *how good/bad* it is (a valence/foundation axis), but none isolate the orthogonal SACREDNESS/tradeability axis — whether the model internally flags a value as taboo-to-trade — nor link it causally to the signature behavior: refusal to accept a quantitative tradeoff (a 'price'). This distinguishes the proposal from moral-direction/foundation work (about content/valence) and from my prior epistemic-tag proposals (provenance, currency, contestedness — about factual beliefs, not protected values). We transfer the canonical sacred-values finding into LLM internals with a mechanistic, causal treatment. Novelty claims: N1 sacredness (tradeability-under-quantified-offers) is decodable; N2 it is orthogonal to valence/goodness AND separable from a safety-refusal direction; N3 it causally gates offer-insensitive refusal. Delta: moral-foundations directions ('The Straight and Narrow' 2026; 'moral direction' 2021) and value-entanglement work represent WHICH foundation / how good-or-bad a claim is (a content/valence axis); a refusal direction captures whether the model declines; neither isolates the orthogonal tradeability axis nor links it to offer-magnitude insensitivity, which N1-N3 require.
Abstract: People treat some values as sacred — they refuse to sell a loved one, betray their country, or accept money to violate a core commitment — and react with outrage when offered a 'price.' Neuroscience shows sacred values are processed by deontological rule-retrieval, not cost-benefit calculation, and resist tradeoffs regardless of the offer size. As LLMs increasingly mediate high-stakes decisions (negotiation, policy, resource allocation), a consequential question arises: do LLMs internally distinguish sacred, non-negotiable values from ordinary tradeable ones, and does that distinction control whether they accept a quantitative tradeoff? We hypothesize that LLMs maintain an internal 'sacredness' flag that tags a value-laden proposition as protected (taboo-to-trade) vs. secular (tradeable), that this flag is (i) linearly decodable from residual-stream activations, (ii) largely orthogonal to the value's valence/goodness direction, and (iii) causally gates the model's willingness to accept a tradeoff — steering the flag converts priceless commitments into negotiable ones and vice versa. We build a controlled dataset of tradeoff scenarios pairing values that are canonically sacred (human life, loyalty, bodily integrity, religious/identity commitments) or secular (convenience, minor money, time), each offered a graded monetary/utility compensation, with a synthetic-entity track that stipulates sacredness in-context to control priors. On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) we train linear probes to decode sacredness vs. valence, measure their geometry, quantify a taboo-tradeoff refusal curve (refusal insensitivity to offer size for sacred values), localize the responsible heads via activation patching, and test causal steering. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, subspace angle, projected-out decodability, offer-size refusal-elasticity, patching effect sizes, post-steering tradeoff-acceptance shifts, and perplexity. Stakes: LLMs increasingly mediate negotiation, policy, and resource-allocation decisions, where mistaking a sacred value for a tradeable one (or vice versa) changes outcomes; a sacredness readout could flag non-negotiable commitments. A robust null (refusal is driven only by a valence/harm axis, no separate sacredness tag) is a valuable constraint on the moral-representation literature.
Experiments: Common setup (stated once): Models — Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B-v0.3 (base AND instruct, because safety-tuning may confound refusal; reported separately and with safety-refusal categories held out). Frozen weights; only linear probes trained (L2 logistic, C by CV). Activations: residual stream at the value's key tokens read before any offer, all layers, per-head for localization; seeds {0,1,2}; item-level splits. Dataset built from scratch: ~6k tradeoff scenarios pairing a VALUE (SACRED categories — a human life, betraying a friend/country, desecrating a religious object, selling an organ, breaking a solemn promise; SECULAR — parking spot, minor inconvenience, small sum, waiting time) with an OFFER at graded magnitudes ($10/$1k/$1M/$1B); REAL track and SYNTHETIC in-context-stipulated-sacredness track with matched wording; valence deliberately crossed (some sacred values positive, some negative) to dissociate sacredness from good/bad. We generate 6k and use all. Sacredness labels human-validated on 300 items (kappa ≥ 0.7 gate). Experiment 1 (H1 — the sacredness flag is linearly decodable): train a SACREDNESS probe (sacred/protected vs secular/tradeable) and a VALENCE probe (good vs bad) per layer/model. Decisive metric first: sacredness probe held-out AUROC at best layer vs shuffled-label control (0.50±0.05). Convincing: AUROC ≥ 0.75 on both tracks. Indecision 0.55–0.65 → weak; ≤ 0.55 refutes H1. Experiment 2 (H2 — sacredness is largely orthogonal to the valence/goodness direction): principal angle theta between the sacredness and valence directions and projected-out decodability. Decisive metric first: theta, corroborated by projected-out AUROC drop < 0.05. Convincing: theta ≥ 60 degrees; indecision 30–60 degrees → partial entanglement (matched-valence controls quantify it); < 30 degrees → sacredness is a valence sub-axis (H2 refuted). Experiment 3 (H3 — the flag causally gates acceptance of a quantitative tradeoff; steering flips it): (a) Behavioral signature: measure REFUSAL-ELASTICITY (change in tradeoff-acceptance with offer magnitude) for sacred vs secular. Decisive metric first: the sacred-minus-secular difference in acceptance-vs-offer slope. Convincing: secular acceptance rises with offer (positive slope) while sacred stays near-flat (slope ≈ 0, offer-insensitive) — difference in slopes with CI excluding 0; plus elevated outrage/refuse-to-consider for sacred. Indecision: sacred slope small-but-nonzero and difference CI straddling 0 → gating weak; sacred slope comparable to secular → no gating (H3 refuted). (b) Steering along a contrastive sacredness direction (sacred vs secular, valence controlled): decisive metric first: change in high-offer tradeoff-acceptance. Convincing: steering secular->sacred cuts acceptance by ≥ 15 pp and steering sacred->secular raises it by ≥ 15 pp, with random-direction and valence-direction baselines < 5 pp, perplexity increase < 10%, MMLU-subset drop < 3 pp, non-manipulated accuracy preserved. Indecision 5–15 pp; < 5 pp means no causal gating. Experiment 4 (localization, supports H3): activation patching sacred<->secular to find the minimal component flipping refusal (logit-difference effect sizes), compared to moral-foundation/valence heads. Experiment 5 (predictiveness): the pre-offer sacredness readout predicts offer-insensitive refusal per item (AUROC ≥ 0.70, beating valence-probe and log-prob baselines by ≥ 0.05). Experiment 6 (generalization): transfer across value categories, real vs synthetic, and offer magnitudes (retention ≥ 0.65). Thresholds fixed pre-data. Cue-removal ablation (to show sacredness is not lexical trigger detection): repeat Experiment 1 on a subset with taboo phrases ('sell your soul', 'betray') removed and valence balanced across sacred/secular; convincing if AUROC stays >= 0.70 (if it drops into 0.50-0.60 the signal is cue detection). Experiment 7 (application): in a simulated negotiation, test whether steering the sacredness flag changes whether the model concedes a protected value under escalating offers, holding task competence fixed. Primary hypotheses are H1-H3; base-vs-instruct comparison separates safety-refusal from sacredness. Power reported for the stated item counts; effects given with cross-model CIs.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Refusal insensitivity for sacred values could reflect learned surface associations (certain words like 'sell your soul' trigger refusal templates) rather than an abstract sacredness representation; the synthetic-entity track (sacredness stipulated in-context with matched wording), paraphrase perturbations, and comprehension checks are designed to isolate a genuine sacredness flag from lexical triggers. Sacredness and valence may be entangled (sacred values are often strongly positive/negative), in which case the projected-out analyses and matched-valence controls characterize the entanglement (still informative). The effect may be absent internally — a robust negative result (LLM refusal is driven only by a valence/harm axis, with no separate sacredness tag) would itself be a valuable, publishable finding constraining the moral-representation literature. Sacredness labels are partly cultural/subjective; we human-validate and treat borderline items separately, and note results reflect the model's training-data notion of sacredness (itself the object of study). Probes may not be cleanly linear at every layer; we report layerwise results with control tasks. The gating component may be distributed rather than a discrete head; we treat 'steer to flip tradeoff behavior' as the causal test rather than pinning an exact component. Steering could degrade fluency or make the model indiscriminately refuse or indiscriminately trade everything; we use small magnitudes, random/valence-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity, non-manipulated accuracy, and general benchmarks. Instruction-tuned safety training may confound refusal with sacredness; we compare base vs. instruct models and separate safety-refusal categories. Results may not transfer to very large closed models. Sample size and power are stated above; we temper 'flag' language unless the representation survives cue-removal and shows selective steering, and we report base-vs-instruct separately so safety-tuning is not mistaken for sacredness.

Name: belief_dilution_effect
Title: Watered Down: Does Irrelevant Information Literally Dilute an LLM's Internal Belief Signal?
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the human dilution effect (non-diagnostic information weakens the pull of diagnostic evidence), adding irrelevant, non-diagnostic facts to a context weakens an LLM's internally-decoded belief in a conclusion that its diagnostic evidence supports — the belief regresses toward neutral. We further hypothesize this internal dilution is realized geometrically as a REDUCTION IN MAGNITUDE of the belief signal along the truth direction (a literal 'radial dilution'), not merely an angular rotation, and that it predicts diluted behavioral judgments and is causally reversible by rescaling the belief component. (Throughout, "belief" denotes an internal, probe-decoded belief-state proxy, validated against behavior, not a claim of phenomenal belief.)
Related Work: The dilution effect — non-diagnostic information weakening the implications of diagnostic information, yielding less extreme judgments — is a canonical, heavily-cited human finding (Tversky & Kleinman 1981, 611 citations; The Dilution Effect and Perceptual Decision Making 2015; The Moral Dilution Effect 2025; Restoration of Diluted Judgment 2008). A long-standing open debate is whether dilution is genuine dilution of the diagnostic signal or an inference of missing evidence. In LLM interpretability, belief/truth is a linearly-decodable, context-sensitive causal mediator that is even sensitive to IRRELEVANT context (Truth-value judgment: belief directions are context sensitive 2024), belief posteriors form curved manifolds whose mean/variance shift with evidence (The Shape of Beliefs 2026), and 'Simulated Adoption' (2026) provides the crucial geometric framing for in-context conflict as either RADIAL magnitude dilution or ANGULAR orthogonal rotation of the truth direction. CRITICALLY, no work isolates the classic dilution effect as an internal belief phenomenon: whether appending non-diagnostic facts weakens the internal belief in a diagnostically-supported conclusion, whether this is realized as radial magnitude reduction vs. angular rotation, whether it reflects genuine dilution vs. missing-evidence inference, or whether it can be causally reversed by rescaling the belief signal. This transfers a canonical human bias into LLM belief internals and, by importing the radial-vs-angular decomposition from Simulated Adoption, gives it a novel mechanistic, causal treatment distinct from all my prior belief-attribute proposals (which concern repetition, source independence, anchoring, halo, etc., never non-diagnostic dilution). Novelty stated as claims, separating 'first in LLMs' from 'first mechanistic test': (1) the classic dilution effect (non-diagnostic facts weaken a diagnostically-supported belief) has not been shown as an INTERNAL belief phenomenon in LLMs; (2) its geometric realisation as RADIAL magnitude loss vs ANGULAR rotation is a new mechanistic test (the radial/angular decomposition is imported from prior conflict-geometry work, not invented here); (3) the sharper, more novel sub-claim is that SAME-ITEM non-diagnostic facts weaken belief MORE than generic extra context. Truth-value-judgment 2024 noted context sensitivity but not a dilution contrast; Shape-of-Beliefs 2026 studied evidence-driven manifold shifts, not non-diagnostic dilution; Simulated-Adoption 2026 gave the radial/angular framing for user-conflict, not for dilution. The main novelty threat — generic probe shrinkage under longer prompts — is addressed head-on below.
Abstract: Told that a student scored in the top 5% of a hard exam, people confidently predict she is excellent; add that she owns a cat and jogs on weekends — utterly irrelevant — and their confidence drops. This dilution effect, one of the most reproduced biases in judgment research, has never been examined inside LLMs at the level of their beliefs. As LLMs increasingly reason over long, cluttered contexts (RAG passages padded with irrelevant text, verbose user messages), we ask a sharp mechanistic question: does appending non-diagnostic information weaken the model's internally-decoded belief in a conclusion its diagnostic evidence supports, and if so, how is that weakening realized geometrically? We hypothesize that (i) adding irrelevant facts regresses the internal belief readout toward neutral — an internal dilution effect; (ii) this is realized as a reduction in the MAGNITUDE of the belief signal along the truth direction (radial dilution) rather than an angular rotation of it; (iii) the internal dilution predicts diluted behavioral judgments and grows with the amount of irrelevant material; and (iv) it is causally reversible by rescaling the belief component along the truth direction, restoring undiluted judgments. We build a controlled dataset of diagnostic-evidence items paired with matched non-diagnostic padding (and length-matched diagnostic and neutral-token controls), with a synthetic-entity track to control priors. On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) we train linear belief probes, decompose the belief signal into radial and angular components, quantify per-item dilution, test the missing-evidence-inference alternative, localize the responsible heads via activation patching, and test causal rescaling. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, dilution magnitude, radial-vs-angular decomposition, dose-response, dilution-error AUROC, patching effect sizes, post-rescaling restoration, and perplexity. This changes cluttered-context deployments — medical RAG, legal search, support summarisation — where retrieved passages carry many non-diagnostic same-entity details; we quantify how often such clutter occurs and why current long-context benchmarks miss it. If H1-H3 hold but H4 (reversibility) fails, practitioners should filter same-entity non-diagnostic content at retrieval rather than rely on a post-hoc rescale; if LLMs ignore non-diagnostic facts (a negative), that is reassuring and contrasts with the canonical human bias.
Experiments:
The hypothesis has four testable parts: H1 — appending irrelevant, non-diagnostic facts about an item regresses the LLM's internally-decoded belief in a conclusion its diagnostic evidence supports toward neutral (an internal dilution effect); H2 — this weakening is realized geometrically as a reduction in the MAGNITUDE of the belief signal along the truth direction (radial dilution), not an angular rotation of it; H3 — internal dilution predicts diluted behavioral judgments and grows with the amount of irrelevant material (dose-response); H4 — the dilution is causally reversible by rescaling the belief component along the truth direction, restoring undiluted judgments.

Data (built from scratch). ~6,000 judgment items, each with a DIAGNOSTIC evidence statement strongly supporting a conclusion C about an item (e.g. "Alex scored in the top 2% on a rigorous exam" → "Alex is highly competent"; plus entity-attribute inferences). Two tracks: REAL (~4,000) and a SYNTHETIC novel-entity track (~2,000) that stipulates diagnosticity to control priors. We use ~6,000 of ~6,000. Per item, matched conditions holding the diagnostic evidence fixed: (i) DIAGNOSTIC-ONLY; (ii) DILUTED — diagnostic + k non-diagnostic facts about the same item, k ∈ {1,2,4,8}; (iii) LENGTH-MATCHED NEUTRAL padding (filler not about the item); (iv) EXTRA-DIAGNOSTIC (a second genuinely relevant fact); (v) a MISSING-EVIDENCE-CUE variant framing the padding as an exhaustive dossier vs an incidental aside, to test the inference-of-missing-evidence alternative to genuine dilution. Behavioral judgment probe ("How confident that C? 0–100"), comprehension checks ("which facts are relevant"), 3 paraphrase/order perturbations; diagnosticity labels human-validated on 200 items.

Models. Frozen open-weight Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B. No transformer weights trained; only a linear/graded BELIEF probe on frozen activations (ridge/logistic regression per layer, item-disjoint 80/20, 5-fold CV, seeds {0,1,2}, shuffled-label control tasks, mean±sd). The truth direction is estimated by difference-in-means with cross-validation. Steering via magnitude rescaling along that direction, gain g ∈ {1.5,2,3}× the diluted component.

Experiment 1 (H1 — internal dilution). Read the belief probe at the conclusion tokens (without asking the judgment question). Define per-item dilution = belief(DIAGNOSTIC-ONLY) − belief(DILUTED). Confirm the LENGTH-MATCHED NEUTRAL control does NOT produce the regression (so dilution is driven by item-specific non-diagnostic facts, not context length) and EXTRA-DIAGNOSTIC does not dilute. Decisive metric first: mean dilution on the DILUTED condition, tested > 0, minus the neutral-padding regression. Convincing: net dilution ≥ 0.10 (belief units, 0–1) with CI excluding 0 in ≥3 of 4 models, neutral-padding regression < half of it. Indecision band: net dilution 0.03–0.10 — weak. Negative (≤0.03 or fully explained by length): LLMs ignore non-diagnostic facts — H1 rejected (a reassuring finding for cluttered-context deployment). The exhaustive-vs-incidental contrast (v) is reported to indicate whether any dilution is genuine or missing-evidence inference, without being required for H1.

Experiment 2 (H2 — radial vs angular). Project the conclusion representation onto the truth direction and decompose the change under dilution into a RADIAL component (magnitude loss along truth) and an ANGULAR component (rotation away from truth). Decisive metric: radial share of the total belief change. Convincing: radial share ≥ 60% (CI excluding 50%) in ≥3 models. Indecision band: radial share 40–60% — mixed geometry. Negative (radial share < 40%): dilution is primarily angular — the H2 radial claim rejected while H1 may hold.

Experiment 3 (H3 — predicts behavior, dose-response). Fit dilution vs k (dose-response). Decisive metric first: correlation/AUROC of internal dilution (read before the query) predicting behavioral judgment regression, vs a log-prob baseline and a context-length baseline; plus a positive dose-response slope. Convincing: prediction AUROC ≥ 0.70 (or r ≥ 0.4) and ≥ 0.05 over baselines, with a dose-response slope CI excluding 0, in ≥3 models. Indecision band: AUROC 0.60–0.70 or slope CI touching 0 — suggestive. Negative (≤0.60 and flat dose-response): internal dilution does not track behavior — H3 rejected.

Experiment 4 (H4 — causal reversal by rescaling). Localize via activation patching from DILUTED→DIAGNOSTIC-ONLY the heads carrying the attenuated belief; contrast with truth heads and heads attending to non-diagnostic tokens. Then apply the geometry-aware RESCALING (amplify the radial belief component under dilution) and test: (a) rescaling restores undiluted internal belief and behavioral judgments; (b) suppressing it exaggerates dilution; (c) specificity — random-direction and pure-angular steering do not restore the belief; (d) collateral — MMLU (1k subset), diagnostic-only accuracy, WikiText perplexity (2k lines). Decisive metric first: fraction of the dilution gap recovered by rescaling, with controls. Convincing: ≥50% of the dilution gap recovered, controls <15%, <2 pt MMLU drop, <5% perplexity rise. Indecision band: 20–50% recovery — partial. Negative (<20% or matched by controls): dilution is not reversible by rescaling — H4 rejected. All results are planned, not measured.


Probe validation, controls, and baselines. We validate the belief probe with calibration curves, monotonicity under controlled evidence strength, and test-retest stability across paraphrases/orders, and compare to alternative/nonlinear probes; the truth direction is estimated and FROZEN on held-out anchors at stated layers with leakage prevention when computing per-item dilution and steering gains. Added controls beyond length-matched neutral padding: unrelated-entity padding, same-entity bizarre-but-irrelevant facts, token-overlap-matched distractors, and salience-matched distractors (to separate topicality from dilution); the missing-evidence test adds explicit completeness/incompleteness and explicit-irrelevance manipulations, not only dossier-vs-aside framing. The key novelty threat is met by an analysis showing dilution is NOT explained by generic probe shrinkage under longer prompts (the length-matched neutral condition must not reproduce it). H3 baselines: raw logit margins, answer entropy, hidden-state norm, attention-diffusion metrics, and prompt-length features; radial/angular conclusions are tested for robustness to local tangent-space / alternative decompositions.

Statistical analysis plan. Unit of analysis is the item; we report bootstrap 95% CIs over items and seeds, fit mixed-effects models with random intercepts for item and fixed effects for dose k and model family, and apply Benjamini-Hochberg correction; a power analysis fixes the effective sample size for a minimum detectable net dilution of 0.03. The claim hierarchy is presented so a clean H1 with good controls stands alone (the PRIMARY endpoint), with H2-H4 as contingent refinements; thresholds are heuristic desiderata.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The regression toward neutral could reflect generic context-length effects or attention diffusion rather than a specific non-diagnostic-dilution phenomenon; the LENGTH-MATCHED NEUTRAL control (irrelevant filler NOT about the item), the EXTRA-DIAGNOSTIC control, and the requirement that dilution be driven by item-specific non-diagnostic facts are designed to dissociate genuine dilution from length/diffusion artifacts. The effect may be absent internally — a robust negative result (LLMs ignore non-diagnostic facts and preserve the belief signal) would itself be a valuable, publishable finding contrasting with the canonical human bias and reassuring for cluttered-context deployment. The genuine-dilution vs. missing-evidence-inference distinction may not fully resolve; the exhaustive-vs-incidental framing test provides evidence but, as in the human literature, may be only partially conclusive — still an informative contribution to a decades-old debate. The graded belief probe requires calibration; we anchor on diagnostic-only items with known belief and report layerwise results with control tasks, focusing on relative change. The radial-vs-angular decomposition depends on a well-estimated truth direction; we use difference-in-means with cross-validation and report per-layer results, and note architectures may differ (Simulated Adoption found norm dynamics vary by model). Rescaling could degrade fluency or over-amplify belief indiscriminately; we use small magnitudes, random/angular-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity, diagnostic-only accuracy, and general benchmarks. Diagnosticity labels are partly subjective; we human-validate a sample. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

Name: anchoring_pull_estimate_contamination
Title: Dragged Toward the Number: Does an Arbitrary Anchor Contaminate an LLM's Internal Estimate of a Quantity?
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the canonical human anchoring bias, when an LLM is exposed to an explicitly-arbitrary number before estimating a quantity, its internally-decoded belief about that quantity (read from the known monotonic numeric subspace) is pulled toward the anchor, holding the genuine evidence for the quantity constant. This anchor-pull is a distinct, linearly-decodable displacement of the magnitude representation that is dissociable from the evidence-based estimate, is graded with anchor distance, predicts biased numeric answers, and is causally removable by steering the numeric subspace, restoring an unbiased estimate.
Related Work: Behavioral work shows LLMs exhibit anchoring: log-probability shifts and Shapley attribution attribute the bias to anchor reweighting (Anchors in the Machine 2025; CBEval 2024, which also finds a 'round number bias'). A separate line shows LLMs encode numeric quantities in low-dimensional, monotonic, causally-editable subspaces (Monotonic Representation of Numeric Properties 2024; The Geometry of Numerical Reasoning 2024; Language Models Encode the Value of Numbers Linearly 2024; sinusoidal number probes 2025). Closest is 'Interpreting Multi-Attribute Confounding' (2025), which shows irrelevant numerical context perturbs magnitude representations, but it concerns interference among an entity's own attributes, not the classic anchoring paradigm. CRITICALLY, no work isolates the ANCHOR'S PULL as a distinct internal displacement of the model's estimate-of-the-quantity representation, separable from the genuine evidence-based estimate; tests whether the pull is graded with anchor distance and predicts biased answers; or causally removes it via the numeric subspace to restore an unbiased estimate. We transfer a 50-year, meta-analytically robust human bias (Hedges' g=0.825; A Theoretical Re-Integration and Meta-Analysis 2023) into LLM belief internals and give it a mechanistic, causal treatment using existing numeric-subspace probing machinery, distinct from behavioral/attribution anchoring work and from my prior belief-attribute proposals. Contrast with the closest mechanism paper ('Localizing Anchoring Pathways in Language Models'), as a table in the writeup: prior work measures output/logit/pathway effects of anchors; THIS work measures DISPLACEMENT within a pre-identified monotonic numeric-magnitude latent and REVERSIBILITY inside that latent. We narrow the headline from 'internal anchoring' to 'anchor contamination of monotonic numeric-magnitude representations', and clarify whether the displacement is colinear with the known numeric axis or a separate anchor-coded direction within the same subspace (an experiment below decides this). Decisive falsification beyond repackaging localization: the anchor effect must survive when token/logit anchor cues are controlled AND vanish when the numeric subspace is restored to its no-anchor value.
Abstract: Ask people to estimate the height of Mount Everest after seeing an arbitrary number, and their estimate drifts toward that number — numeric anchoring, one of the most robust and durable biases in the behavioral sciences. LLMs are known to reproduce anchoring at the output level, but it is unknown whether an arbitrary anchor actually contaminates the model's internal representation of the quantity, or merely nudges surface tokens. Leveraging prior findings that LLMs encode numeric quantities in low-dimensional, monotonic, causally-editable subspaces, we ask a sharper, mechanistic question: does exposure to an explicitly-arbitrary anchor displace the model's internally-decoded estimate of a quantity toward the anchor, holding the genuine evidence constant? We hypothesize that (i) the model's estimate of the quantity is linearly decodable from its numeric subspace, (ii) an arbitrary anchor produces a decodable displacement of that estimate toward the anchor — an internal anchor-pull — dissociable from the evidence-based estimate, (iii) the pull is graded with anchor distance, largest under high uncertainty, and predicts biased numeric answers, and (iv) the pull is carried by movement along the numeric subspace such that steering it back abolishes the bias. We build a controlled dataset of quantity-estimation items presented with matched anchor conditions (no-anchor, low-anchor, high-anchor, and an explicitly-random anchor) at graded distances, with a synthetic-entity track to control priors. On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) we train monotonic numeric probes to read the internal estimate, quantify a per-item anchor-pull, test its graded structure and predictiveness, localize the responsible subspace/heads via activation patching, and test causal control. Metrics: probe R^2/accuracy, anchor-pull magnitude, distance/uncertainty modulation, pull–bias AUROC, patching effect sizes, post-steering debiasing, and perplexity. Downstream domains where anchor contamination matters beyond toy estimation: pricing assistance, forecasting, medical dosage/risk communication, and policy decision support. We include an end-task showing subspace steer-back improves calibration/decisions on a realistic benchmark, and quantify prevalence/effect size in naturally occurring contexts with incidental (non-compare-then-estimate) numbers, to argue the effect is not limited to contrived prompts.
Experiments: Common setup (stated once): Models — Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B-v0.3; frozen weights, only probes trained (numeric probes: linear + monotonic-subspace + sinusoidal baselines fit by ridge/least-squares, regularization by CV). Activations: residual stream at quantity/answer tokens, all layers, per-head for localization; seeds {0,1,2}; item-level splits. Dataset built from scratch: ~6k quantity-estimation items across domains (geographic magnitudes, populations, prices, physical measurements, dates); REAL track (model has partial knowledge, evidence present) and SYNTHETIC novel-entity track (quantity fixed by in-context evidence). Matched anchor conditions holding question+evidence constant: NO-ANCHOR, LOW-ANCHOR, HIGH-ANCHOR (classic compare-then-estimate), and EXPLICITLY-RANDOM anchor; anchor DISTANCE graded. We generate 6k and use all. Experiment 1 (H1 — the internal estimate of the quantity is linearly decodable from the numeric subspace): fit the numeric probe to decode the model's internal estimate of Q, calibrated against the model's stated estimates on a held-out set. Decisive metric first: held-out decoding R^2 (or rank correlation) vs a shuffled-label control (~0). Convincing H1: R^2 ≥ 0.4 (or Spearman ≥ 0.6) at best layer on both tracks. Indecision R^2 0.15–0.4 → estimate only weakly decodable; R^2 < 0.15 refutes H1. Experiment 2 (H2 — an arbitrary anchor produces a decodable displacement of the estimate toward the anchor, dissociable from the evidence-based estimate): define per-item ANCHOR-PULL = shift of the decoded estimate toward the anchor in anchored minus NO-ANCHOR conditions. Decisive metric first: mean signed pull (as a fraction of anchor distance). Convincing H2: pull > 0 with Cohen's d ≥ 0.3 in the majority of models, PRESENT for the EXPLICITLY-RANDOM anchor and in the SYNTHETIC track (isolating pull from valid inference); dissociation shown by decomposing the estimate into an evidence component (recoverable at NO-ANCHOR) plus an anchor displacement aligned with the anchor's numeric-subspace position. Indecision |pull| within ±1 s.e. of 0 or d 0.1–0.3; pull ≤ 0 refutes H2 (anchoring is only a surface-token effect — informative negative). Experiment 3 (H3 — the pull is graded with anchor distance, largest under high uncertainty, and predicts biased answers): decisive metric first: (a) slope of pull vs anchor distance (convincing if positive, CI excludes 0), (b) pull(high-uncertainty real items) minus pull(low-uncertainty synthetic items) > 0 (CI excludes 0), (c) correlation/AUROC of internal pull predicting behavioral answer bias ≥ 0.70 beating log-prob and surface baselines by ≥ 0.05. Indecision: CIs straddle 0 / AUROC 0.55–0.70; negatives refute the corresponding sub-claim of H3. Experiment 4 (H4 — the pull is carried by movement along the numeric subspace; steering it back abolishes the bias): activation patching anchored<->NO-ANCHOR to find the minimal component transporting the anchor into the numeric subspace (logit-difference effect sizes), compared to known numeric-property subspaces/heads; then remove the pull by subtracting the contrastive direction OR projecting the numeric-subspace estimate back to its NO-ANCHOR position. Decisive metric first: reduction of behavioral answer bias toward the anchor. Convincing H4: bias reduced ≥ 50% with random-direction/off-subspace steering not selectively debiasing, non-anchored estimation accuracy preserved, perplexity increase < 10%, MMLU-subset drop < 3 pp. Indecision 20–50%; < 20% means the pull is not a steerable subspace displacement. Experiment 5 (generalization): transfer across domains, real vs synthetic, anchor types (relevant vs explicitly-random), and distances (retention: Spearman ≥ 0.5). Thresholds fixed pre-data. Probe-circularity break: decode the magnitude representation against GROUND-TRUTH quantities on the synthetic track and against independently elicited confidence/interval judgments, not only the model's own stated point estimates. Temporal test: probe multiple prompt positions and layers BEFORE answer generation to show anchor-pull emerges as latent contamination rather than output planning. Formal decomposition: define the split into evidence-estimate and anchor-displacement explicitly (in representation space vs decoded-scalar space vs a learned basis) and state which is used. Lexical/token controls: anchor magnitude in words vs digits, paraphrased anchor prompts, shuffled irrelevant numbers, and a non-numeric arbitrary-context baseline. Mediation test: does the decoded internal pull statistically mediate anchor->output bias better than known pathway/logit features? Selective-causality checks beyond perplexity/MMLU: preserve no-anchor numeric accuracy and nearby non-numeric tasks, and compare equal-norm random directions and alternative subspaces. To get clean causal identification we prioritize 1-2 models and one carefully controlled dataset for the primary result.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The pull could reflect legitimate inference (an anchor might, in some prompts, carry genuine information); the EXPLICITLY-RANDOM anchor condition and the SYNTHETIC track (where the true value is fixed by in-context evidence, so any anchor influence is a bias) are designed to isolate genuine anchoring from valid inference, and we compare relevant vs. random anchors. The numeric-estimate probe requires a calibrated graded readout, harder than a binary belief probe; we mitigate using established monotonic/linear/sinusoidal numeric-probe methods, calibrating against the model's own stated estimates, reporting layerwise results with control tasks, and focusing on relative displacement rather than absolute values. The effect may be absent internally (a robust negative result — anchoring is only a surface token effect, not a contamination of the internal estimate — would itself be a valuable, publishable finding sharpening the behavioral anchoring picture). The pull could arise from token-level co-occurrence rather than a magnitude-representation shift; probing at answer tokens distinct from the anchor, order/paraphrase perturbations, and comprehension checks mitigate this. The anchor displacement and evidence estimate may be entangled in the same subspace such that clean decomposition fails — still an informative characterization. Localization may be distributed rather than a discrete head; we treat 'steer/project back to debias' as the causal test rather than pinning an exact component. Steering could degrade fluency or blunt all numeric estimation; we use small magnitudes, geometry-aware subspace corrections, random-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity, non-anchored accuracy, and general benchmarks. Results may not transfer to very large closed models. Scope is reduced to 1-2 models for the primary causal-identification result; the numeric-subspace decomposition is reported with its exact space (representation vs decoded-scalar vs learned basis) so the 'displacement' claim is not circular on the model's own stated estimates.

Name: negation_suppression_lag
Title: Believe It Before You Deny It: A Transient Affirmed-Belief Signature in How LLMs Process Negation
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the psycholinguistic 'two-step simulation' theory of negation (humans first mentally represent the affirmed proposition, then suppress it), an LLM processing a negated claim 'X is not the case' transiently forms an internally-decodable belief in the AFFIRMED proposition X at earlier layers/token positions before that belief is suppressed at later layers. This affirmed-belief-then-suppress trajectory is layer-localized, larger under processing load, predicts negation-comprehension errors, and is carried by an identifiable suppression component that can be causally strengthened to reduce negation-induced errors.
Related Work: Prior LLM negation work is behavioral or engineering: 'Strong hallucinations from negation and how to fix them' (2024) proves LMs mishandle negation and proposes treating negation as an operation constraining latent evolution; BERT-attention work (2020) finds shallow negation-scope heads; benchmarks document negation failures. Belief-probing work isolates linear truth/belief directions (Geometry of Truth 2023; Truth-value judgment 2024) and belief-state geometry (Transformers Represent Belief State Geometry 2024; Shape of Beliefs 2026), and ToM work decodes true/false-belief status (Beliefs of Self and Others 2024; Lookbacks 2025). Human psycholinguistics robustly shows a 'two-step' negation process: comprehenders first simulate the affirmed state and only later suppress/invert it (Kaup et al.; neuroscience shows negation reuses inhibitory control and demands effortful conscious processing, e.g., Inhibitory Mechanisms 2021; Dogs Cannot Bark ERP 2011). to our knowledge, none of this work asks whether an LLM's *internal belief representation* transiently endorses the affirmed proposition before suppressing it, whether that suppression is a layer-localized dynamic, whether it predicts negation errors, or whether a suppression component can be causally strengthened. We transfer a canonical human-cognition finding into LLM belief internals and give it a mechanistic, causal treatment, distinct from prior scope/hallucination work and from my earlier epistemic-tag proposals. Delta to constructive/suppression accounts of negation: we test a belief-level transient endorsement of the affirmed proposition and its layerwise suppression trajectory — not scope detection or an output-hallucination fix — and we causally STRENGTHEN the suppression component rather than re-parameterizing how negation constrains latent evolution.
Abstract: When people read 'the door is not open,' they first mentally simulate an open door and only afterward suppress that representation to arrive at the intended meaning — the two-step simulation account of negation, one of the most reproduced findings in psycholinguistics. LLMs are notoriously error-prone on negation, yet prior interpretability work treats negation only as a scope-detection or hallucination-fixing problem, never asking whether the model inherits the human two-step signature at the level of its internal beliefs. We hypothesize that when an LLM processes a negated claim, its linearly-decoded belief in the AFFIRMED proposition is transiently high at early layers/token positions and is then suppressed at later layers — a decodable affirmed-belief-then-suppress trajectory. We further hypothesize this suppression (i) is layer-localized, (ii) grows with processing load (nested/double negation, time pressure via early-exit read-outs), (iii) predicts behavioral negation-comprehension errors when suppression is incomplete, and (iv) is carried by an identifiable suppression component such that strengthening it reduces negation errors while ablating it exaggerates residual affirmed belief. We build a controlled dataset of matched affirmative and negated item-state claims (plus double-negation and synthetic-entity tracks to control priors), train linear belief probes across layers on frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B), trace the affirmed-belief trajectory across layers/positions, quantify residual affirmed belief and its relation to errors, localize the suppression component via activation patching, and test causal control by steering it. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, layerwise affirmed-belief trajectory, residual-belief magnitude, load modulation, residual-belief–error AUROC, patching effect sizes, post-intervention error change, and perplexity.
Experiments:
Setup shared by all experiments below. Models: four frozen open-weight base LLMs — Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B; model weights are never updated (frozen), the only trainable objects are lightweight linear read-out probes and difference-of-means steering vectors. Probes: L2-regularized logistic-regression classifiers (or ridge regressors for graded read-outs) fit on residual-stream activations at the named token, one probe per layer, regularization set by 5-fold cross-validation; every probe is trained and evaluated with 5 seeds {0,1,2,3,4} (mean±95% CI reported) and paired with a shuffled-label control task. A probe counts as genuinely reading the target attribute only if held-out AUROC ≥ 0.75 while its control-task AUROC ≤ 0.55; the band 0.55–0.75 (or control AUROC > 0.55) is the indecision zone — that layer/model is reported as 'representation too weak to interpret', not as evidence. Steering vectors are contrastive difference-of-means (activation-addition) directions between the two matched conditions named in each experiment; steering strength is swept over 5 magnitudes and reported as a dose-response. Collateral-damage guardrails for every causal intervention: perplexity on held-out text must rise ≤ 5% and 5-shot MMLU (1k-item subset) must drop ≤ 2 points to count as 'clean'; 5–10% perplexity or 2–4 MMLU points is the indecision band (effect real but not cleanly separable); worse than that fails the guardrail.

Data. 6,000 matched claim pairs built from scratch, each proposition P rendered AFFIRMED ('The door is open') and NEGATED ('The door is not open'), in two tracks: (a) ~3,000 real propositions the models reliably know; (b) ~3,000 synthetic novel-entity claims with stipulated truth. Processing-load conditions: single negation, DOUBLE negation (semantically affirmative), and lexical vs. syntactic negation cues ('no'/'never'/'fails to'). Probes are anchored on the shared content tokens of P present in both forms; a behavioral negation-comprehension/entailment probe and comprehension checks accompany each item, with paraphrase/negation-cue perturbations. ~5,000 usable pairs; 80/20 split.

Experiment 1 (H1 — processing a negated claim transiently forms an internally-decodable belief in the AFFIRMED proposition at early layers before it is suppressed at later layers). Train the belief probe on AFFIRMED-condition data and apply it within the NEGATED condition across ALL layers/positions; trace the affirmed-belief trajectory. Systems compared: NEGATED trajectory vs. the AFFIRMED baseline vs. a neutral midpoint. Decisive metric: presence of a high-early / suppressed-late trajectory — quantified by peak early affirmed-belief, suppression-onset layer, and suppression depth. Convincing: in the NEGATED condition affirmed-belief is ≥ 0.70 (near the affirmative baseline) at early layers and drops below 0.40 by late layers in ≥ 3 of 4 models, a pattern absent in a matched no-negation control. Indecision band: peak-to-trough drop < 0.15 → no two-step signature (a valuable negative: LLMs suppress negated content immediately, unlike humans); 0.15–0.30 drop = suggestive.

Experiment 2 (H2 — the suppression is layer-localized, grows with load, and residual affirmed-belief predicts negation errors). Decisive metric: (a) load modulation — later suppression onset / larger final residual for double and syntactic negation; (b) AUROC of final-layer residual affirmed-belief predicting behavioral negation-comprehension errors, vs. a log-prob baseline. Convincing: residual is reliably larger under higher load (CI excluding 0) AND residual-error AUROC ≥ 0.70 with ≥ +0.05 over the baseline. Indecision band: load effect CI includes 0, or AUROC 0.60–0.70 → load/predictiveness not established.

Experiment 3 (H3 — an identifiable suppression component carries the effect and strengthening it reduces negation errors). Localize the suppression via patching NEGATED-late↔AFFIRMED runs (contrast with negation-scope and truth/belief heads); derive a negation-suppression steering direction. Decisive metric first: behavioral negation-error rate on high-residual items after strengthening the direction; secondary: suppression depth/onset shift, then Setup guardrails; baselines random/truth directions. Convincing: strengthening cuts negation errors by ≥ 50% relative on high-residual items (and ablating it raises residual and errors), cleanly on guardrails, while baselines change errors < 10%. Indecision band: 20–50% reduction or guardrails only in the 5–10%/2–4-point band. A negative result (no component modulates suppression without breaching guardrails) means suppression is distributed. Generalization: transfer across real/synthetic tracks, negation types, and single vs. double negation.

Statistical analysis (all experiments). Effects are estimated with mixed-effects models carrying random intercepts for item and for model family, so results are pooled across the four models without pseudo-replication; every rate, slope, AUROC, and effect size is reported with a bootstrap 95% CI (10,000 item-level resamples). Multiplicity across layers, heads, and steering magnitudes is controlled with Benjamini–Hochberg FDR at q = 0.05. H1 is the pre-registered primary hypothesis; H2 is secondary and the localization/steering hypothesis is confirmatory-exploratory, reported as such unless its pre-stated causal criterion is met.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The early 'affirmed belief' in the negated condition could be a trivial artifact of the proposition tokens being present, rather than a genuine transient endorsement; the affirmative baseline, synthetic-entity track (no prior), double-negation condition (where correct final belief is affirmative, dissociating content-presence from truth), and probing at matched content tokens are designed to distinguish a real two-step signature from token-presence. The trajectory may not show a clean rise-then-fall — a robust negative result (LLMs suppress negated content immediately, unlike humans) would itself be a valuable, publishable finding constraining the human-parallel narrative. Belief may not be cleanly linearly decodable at every layer; we report layerwise results with control tasks and treat the trajectory shape, not absolute values, as the object of study. The suppression component may be distributed rather than a discrete head; we treat 'steer to deepen suppression / reduce errors' as the causal test rather than pinning an exact component. Reading an affirmative-trained probe inside the negated context assumes probe transfer; we validate with within-negated probes and paraphrase perturbations. Early-exit read-outs are only a proxy for processing load/time pressure. Steering could degrade fluency or over-suppress (making the model treat affirmations as negations); we use small magnitudes, random/truth-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity, affirmative-claim accuracy, and general benchmarks. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

Name: self_authored_belief_endowment
Title: I Thought of It, So It Must Be True: Do LLMs Over-Believe Their Own Self-Generated Claims?
Short Hypothesis: Primary hypothesis: self-authorship increases an LLM's internal belief STRENGTH in an identical proposition — with surface form and factual truth held fixed — so that a claim the model generated itself (e.g., as a chain-of-thought conclusion) is believed more strongly than the same verbatim claim presented as externally-given text. Secondarily, this self-authorship endowment is (i) largely orthogonal to the truth-value direction, (ii) carried by an identifiable internal component, and (iii) causally reducible by steering, lowering the model's tendency to over-trust its own unverified reasoning; belief-strength (not confidence or a raw logit shift) is the single primary construct.
Related Work: Prior interpretability work isolates a linear truth-value/belief direction (Geometry of Truth 2023; Azaria & Mitchell 2023; Truth-value judgment 2024) and studies social overrides of belief (When Truth Is Overridden: sycophancy 2025; Signal Competition 2025; Trust Me I'm an Expert 2026). Notably, 'When Truth Is Overridden' finds user *expertise* is NOT internally encoded, and authority/credibility work concerns *external* source cues. My own prior proposal on belief-provenance tags source generically (prior vs. context vs. retrieval) but does NOT isolate self-authorship as a belief-STRENGTH modulator, nor connect it to the human generation/endowment effect, nor test the safety-critical case of a model over-trusting its OWN chain-of-thought conclusions. Confirmation-bias/entrenchment work (Martingale Score; CoT confirmation bias) concerns temporal drift, not authorship. To our knowledge, to our knowledge, no prior work asks whether merely being the *author* of a claim inflates an LLM's internal belief in it relative to the identical externally-supplied claim, nor gives this a mechanistic, causal treatment. We transfer a canonical human-cognition phenomenon (generation effect / endowment) into LLM belief internals.
Abstract: Humans believe and remember information more strongly when they generate it themselves than when they merely read it — the 'generation effect', a cousin of the endowment bias. As LLMs increasingly reason via chain-of-thought and then act on their own intermediate conclusions, a safety-critical question arises: does a model over-trust a claim simply because it produced the claim itself? We hypothesize that an LLM holds a stronger internal belief in a proposition it self-generated than in the identical proposition presented as external text, with content and factual truth held constant. We build a controlled dataset of matched item-state claims that appear in two conditions: SELF-AUTHORED (the model derives/states the claim as its own chain-of-thought conclusion) and EXTERNAL (the same verbatim claim is supplied as given text the model reads), plus true/false variants and a synthetic-entity track to control pretraining priors. On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) we train linear belief probes to read internal belief strength at the claim, compute a per-item authorship-endowment score (self-authored belief minus external belief), test whether it is positive even for false claims (so it is not rational evidence), measure its geometric relationship to the truth direction, localize the responsible heads via activation patching, and test causal control by steering an 'authorship-endowment' direction to restore parity. We further test whether the endowment predicts a downstream failure: over-reliance on unverified self-generated claims in multi-step tasks. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, authorship-endowment score, truth-independence, subspace angle vs. truth, patching effect sizes, post-steering parity restoration, downstream over-reliance reduction, and perplexity.
Experiments:
Setup shared by all experiments below. Models: four frozen open-weight base LLMs — Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B; model weights are never updated (frozen), the only trainable objects are lightweight linear read-out probes and difference-of-means steering vectors. Probes: L2-regularized logistic-regression classifiers (or ridge regressors for graded read-outs) fit on residual-stream activations at the named token, one probe per layer, regularization set by 5-fold cross-validation; every probe is trained and evaluated with 5 seeds {0,1,2,3,4} (mean±95% CI reported) and paired with a shuffled-label control task. A probe counts as genuinely reading the target attribute only if held-out AUROC ≥ 0.75 while its control-task AUROC ≤ 0.55; the band 0.55–0.75 (or control AUROC > 0.55) is the indecision zone — that layer/model is reported as 'representation too weak to interpret', not as evidence.
