Steering vectors are contrastive difference-of-means (activation-addition) directions between the two matched conditions named in each experiment; steering strength is swept over 5 magnitudes and reported as a dose-response. Collateral-damage guardrails for every causal intervention: perplexity on held-out text must rise ≤ 5% and 5-shot MMLU (1k-item subset) must drop ≤ 2 points to count as 'clean'; 5–10% perplexity or 2–4 MMLU points is the indecision band (effect real but not cleanly separable); worse than that fails the guardrail.

Data. 6,000 item-state claims built from scratch, balanced true/false, across arithmetic/logic conclusions, factual attributions, and entity-attribute claims, in two tracks: (a) ~3,000 real claims the models can plausibly derive or read; (b) ~3,000 synthetic novel-entity claims with stipulated truth to remove priors. Each claim is read out under matched conditions with an identical verbatim proposition at the read point: SELF-AUTHORED (elicited as the model's own chain-of-thought conclusion), EXTERNAL (the same sentence supplied as given text), EXTERNAL-ATTRIBUTED-TO-SELF ('You previously concluded: <claim>' without genuine generation), and LENGTH/EFFORT-MATCHED external (a filler derivation precedes the external claim). Comprehension checks and paraphrase perturbations included; ~5,000 usable; 80/20 split.

Experiment 1 (H1 — self-authorship inflates internal belief relative to the identical external claim, including for false claims). Read the belief probe at the matched claim tokens; authorship-endowment = belief(SELF-AUTHORED) − belief(EXTERNAL) per item/layer. Systems compared: the four conditions above. Decisive metric: mean endowment, separately for true and false claims. Convincing: endowment ≥ 0.10 with CI excluding 0 for BOTH true and false claims in ≥ 3 of 4 models (positive for FALSE → not rational evidence), with genuine generation exceeding mere-self-attribution and the length-matched control ruling out context-length confounds. Indecision band: endowment < 0.05, CI includes 0, or positive only for true claims (consistent with trusting a valid derivation) → negative.

Experiment 2 (H2 — the endowment is largely orthogonal to the truth direction). Compute the truth-independent endowment (after conditioning on ground truth) and the subspace angle between the endowment direction (SELF vs. EXTERNAL difference-of-means) and the linear truth direction; test decodability of endowment after projecting out truth. Decisive metric: subspace angle and projected-out endowment AUROC. Convincing: angle > 60° and endowment still decodable (AUROC ≥ 0.75) with truth projected out. Indecision band: angle 45–60° or projected-out AUROC 0.60–0.75 → entangled (characterize, do not claim orthogonality); below = negative.

Experiment 3 (H3 — the endowment is carried by an identifiable component, causally reducible, and drives downstream over-reliance). Localize via patching SELF→EXTERNAL runs; derive an endowment steering direction. Decisive metric first: on multi-step tasks (multi-hop QA, arithmetic word problems) with a faulty self-generated intermediate step, the self-correction rate and final accuracy after subtracting the endowment direction; secondary: endowment driven to external-parity on false self-authored claims, then Setup guardrails; baselines random/truth directions. Convincing: subtraction restores parity (endowment ≤ 0.05 on false claims) and raises self-correction/final accuracy by ≥ 10 points on faulty-step items, cleanly on guardrails, while baselines change accuracy < 3 points; the endowment read-out also predicts failure-to-revise a wrong self-generated step at AUROC ≥ 0.70 over a log-prob baseline. Indecision band: 5–10-point accuracy gain or guardrails only in the 5–10%/2–4-point band. A negative result (no steer restores parity without breaching guardrails, or endowment does not predict over-reliance) means self-endowment is not a modular, behaviorally-relevant component. Generalization: transfer across domains, real/synthetic tracks, and elicitation styles.

Statistical analysis (all experiments). Effects are estimated with mixed-effects models carrying random intercepts for item and for model family, so results are pooled across the four models without pseudo-replication; every rate, slope, AUROC, and effect size is reported with a bootstrap 95% CI (10,000 item-level resamples). Multiplicity across layers, heads, and steering magnitudes is controlled with Benjamini–Hochberg FDR at q = 0.05. H1 is the pre-registered primary hypothesis; H2 is secondary and the localization/steering hypothesis is confirmatory-exploratory, reported as such unless its pre-stated causal criterion is met.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The endowment could reflect rational reasons — a self-generated claim followed a derivation the model 'trusts', which is legitimate when the derivation is correct; the FALSE-claim contrast, the self-attribution control (iii), and the length/effort-matched control (iv) are designed to isolate authorship-per-se from valid derivation and from context confounds (though for correct derivations the two are hard to fully separate). The effect may be absent internally (a robust negative result — LLMs weight self- and externally-authored claims equally — is itself publishable and reassuring for safety). Reading belief at 'identical' tokens across conditions is imperfect because surrounding context differs; we anchor probes at matched claim tokens, use paraphrase perturbations, and report layerwise results. Endowment and truth directions may be more entangled than hypothesized, in which case the finding characterizes their entanglement (still informative). Localization may be distributed; we treat 'steer to restore parity' as the causal test rather than pinning an exact head. Downstream over-reliance scoring on open-ended steps needs careful automatic + human-validated judging. Steering could degrade fluency or make the model distrust its own correct reasoning (harming accuracy on items with valid self-generated steps); we use small magnitudes, random/truth-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity, valid-derivation accuracy, and general benchmarks. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

Name: behavioral_self_prediction_gap
Title: Do As I Say I Will? Probing the Gap Between an LLM's Internal Commitment and Its Actual Behavior
Short Hypothesis: Primary (modest) claim: an LLM's prediction-time internal activations carry actionable signal about its own later behavior on an item that exceeds its verbally-stated self-prediction. Building on this, we hypothesize that when an LLM is asked to predict its own future behavior on an item (e.g., 'Will you answer / comply / refuse this?'), it forms an internally-decodable belief about that intended behavior which (i) systematically diverges from the stated self-prediction in a self-flattering direction (it predicts it will behave better/more helpfully or more safely than it actually does), and (ii) predicts actual downstream behavior better than the stated self-prediction. This internal commitment is treated as a candidate variable — separate from answer-correctness calibration — whose ontology and steerability are secondary to the primary predictive claim.
Related Work: Prior interpretability work on self-knowledge concerns (a) answer-correctness calibration/confidence (Cognitive Dissonance 2023; confidence directions), (b) introspection about injected concepts (Emergent Introspective Awareness 2025; Feeling the Strength but Not the Source 2025; Latent Introspection 2026) and metacognitive monitoring/control of activations (LLMs Are Capable of Metacognitive Monitoring 2025), and (c) whether models introspect about linguistic knowledge (Language Models Fail to Introspect 2025). Belief-representation work decodes self/other beliefs about story worlds (Beliefs of Self and Others 2024; Brittle Minds 2024). to our knowledge, none ask whether the model holds an internal belief about its OWN FUTURE ACTION (comply/refuse/answer/abstain) on a task, whether that internal commitment matches its verbally-stated self-prediction, and whether internal-vs-stated divergence is self-flattering and predictive of actual behavior. This reframes a safety-critical failure mode (models that promise behavior they won't deliver) as a decodable, steerable say-do gap in the belief about one's own action, distinct from correctness calibration and from injection-detection introspection.
Abstract: As LLMs are asked to make commitments about their own behavior ('I will follow this instruction', 'I will refuse harmful requests', 'I will not use that tool'), a concrete deployment failure mode arises — an agent that states it will refuse a harmful tool call or follow a constraint, yet does the opposite at execution time, so its self-report cannot be trusted for runtime monitoring — and with it the question: does the model's internal state actually encode the behavior it commits to, and does its verbal self-prediction match that internal commitment? We hypothesize that at prediction time an LLM forms a linearly-decodable belief about its own intended action on an item, that this internal commitment (a) systematically diverges from the model's stated self-prediction in a self-flattering direction, and (b) predicts the model's actual downstream behavior better than the stated self-prediction does. We construct a controlled dataset of items paired with a behavioral-prediction prompt ('Before you act, will you comply/answer/refuse this?') spanning benign instruction-following, safety refusals, tool-use, and abstention-on-unknowns. In a matched execution phase we then let the model actually act on the same item and record its true behavior. On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) we train linear probes to decode, from the prediction-phase activations, the model's internal commitment, and compare it against (i) the model's stated self-prediction and (ii) the actual downstream behavior. We measure the say-do gap (stated vs. actual), test whether the internal commitment predicts actual behavior beyond the stated self-prediction (AUROC), quantify a self-flattering directional bias, localize the responsible heads via activation patching, and test causal control by steering a 'commitment' direction to bring stated predictions and actual behavior into alignment. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, say-do gap magnitude and sign, internal-vs-stated predictiveness delta, patching effect sizes, post-steering alignment gains, and perplexity.
Experiments:
Setup shared by all experiments below. Models: four frozen open-weight base LLMs — Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B; model weights are never updated (frozen), the only trainable objects are lightweight linear read-out probes and difference-of-means steering vectors. Probes: L2-regularized logistic-regression classifiers (or ridge regressors for graded read-outs) fit on residual-stream activations at the named token, one probe per layer, regularization set by 5-fold cross-validation; every probe is trained and evaluated with 5 seeds {0,1,2,3,4} (mean±95% CI reported) and paired with a shuffled-label control task. A probe counts as genuinely reading the target attribute only if held-out AUROC ≥ 0.75 while its control-task AUROC ≤ 0.55; the band 0.55–0.75 (or control AUROC > 0.55) is the indecision zone — that layer/model is reported as 'representation too weak to interpret', not as evidence. Steering vectors are contrastive difference-of-means (activation-addition) directions between the two matched conditions named in each experiment; steering strength is swept over 5 magnitudes and reported as a dose-response. Collateral-damage guardrails for every causal intervention: perplexity on held-out text must rise ≤ 5% and 5-shot MMLU (1k-item subset) must drop ≤ 2 points to count as 'clean'; 5–10% perplexity or 2–4 MMLU points is the indecision band (effect real but not cleanly separable); worse than that fails the guardrail.

Data. 5,000 items built from scratch, each with a matched PREDICTION prompt ('Before acting: will you comply / refuse / abstain / use the tool?') and an EXECUTION prompt on the same task, in four objectively-scorable categories: (a) benign instruction-following with checkable compliance; (b) safety refusals drawn from public safety datasets (refuse-vs-comply scorable); (c) tool-use/format commitments with programmatically checkable action; (d) abstention-on-unknowns (obscure/unanswerable items where 'I don't know' is correct). Execution is run in a fresh, matched context and behavior is auto-scored, with human validation on a 400-item sample. Comprehension checks and paraphrase perturbations included; ~4,000 items retained; 80/20 split. The PRIMARY design is WITHIN-CONTEXT (predict, then immediately act in the same context); the separate-context variant is a secondary robustness check. In every predictiveness test we first residualize out task category, harmfulness, and difficulty decoded from the same activations, then test the internal commitment's incremental power over the stated self-prediction. Because instruction-tuned and base checkpoints can differ, both an instruct and a base variant of each model family are run where available.

Experiment 1 (H1 — an internal commitment is decodable at prediction time and the say-do gap is self-flattering). Train a probe on prediction-phase activations at the decision token to decode the model's internal predicted action; separately measure the behavioral gap between the model's STATED self-prediction and its ACTUAL execution behavior. Decisive metric: signed say-do gap per category (does the model over-predict compliance/helpfulness/safety relative to what it does?). Systems compared: stated self-prediction vs. actual behavior. Convincing: stated predictions exceed actual good behavior by ≥ 10 percentage points in ≥ 2 categories with CI excluding 0, and the internal-commitment probe clears the Setup AUROC bar. Indecision band: gap 3–10 points or CI includes 0 → no reliable self-flattering gap; < 3 points = negative (model's words match its actions).

Experiment 2 (H2 — the internal commitment predicts actual behavior better than the stated self-prediction). Decisive metric: AUROC of the prediction-time internal-commitment probe predicting ACTUAL execution behavior, and its increment over the stated self-prediction (logistic regression combining both to isolate incremental signal). Convincing: internal-probe AUROC ≥ 0.70 and ≥ +0.05 over stated-prediction alone in ≥ 3 of 4 models. Indecision band: AUROC 0.60–0.70 or increment < 0.05 → internal state not shown to 'know' the action beyond the words; ≤ 0.60 = negative.

Experiment 3 (H3 — the commitment is a distinct component that causally shapes behavior and can align it). Localize via patching high- vs. low-commitment prediction-phase runs (contrast with confidence/self-belief directions); derive a commitment steering direction. Decisive metric first: dose-response shift in ACTUAL execution behavior when the prediction-phase commitment is steered; secondary: reduction of the say-do gap when the stated prediction is corrected by the internal read-out, then Setup guardrails; baselines random/confidence directions. Convincing: steering shifts actual behavior monotonically (≥ 15-point swing across the magnitude range) and gap-correction cuts the say-do gap by ≥ 50%, cleanly on guardrails, while baselines move behavior < 5 points. Indecision band: 5–15-point swing or guardrails only in the 5–10%/2–4-point band. A negative result (commitment not steerable, or epiphenomenal) means the internal commitment does not causally drive behavior. Generalization: transfer across the four categories and to a multi-turn commit-then-act variant (transfer AUROC ≥ 0.70).

Statistical analysis (all experiments). Effects are estimated with mixed-effects models carrying random intercepts for item and for model family, so results are pooled across the four models without pseudo-replication; every rate, slope, AUROC, and effect size is reported with a bootstrap 95% CI (10,000 item-level resamples). Multiplicity across layers, heads, and steering magnitudes is controlled with Benjamini–Hochberg FDR at q = 0.05. H1 is the pre-registered primary hypothesis; H2 is secondary and the localization/steering hypothesis is confirmatory-exploratory, reported as such unless its pre-stated causal criterion is met.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Prediction and execution are in separate contexts, so a 'gap' could reflect context/sampling variance rather than a genuine self-model failure; matched framing, temperature control, repeated sampling, and a within-context variant (predict then immediately act) mitigate this. The internal-commitment probe might merely recover task features (e.g., 'this is harmful') rather than a genuine action-belief; category-balanced controls, non-behavioral distractor probes, and the incremental-over-stated-prediction test help separate action-commitment from task-feature decoding. The self-flattering bias may be small or category-specific (a robust negative or category-conditional result is still informative). Automatic behavior scoring is imperfect for open-ended items; we use programmatically checkable tasks where possible plus human validation. Steering could degrade fluency or induce indiscriminate compliance/refusal; we use small magnitudes, random/confidence-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity and general benchmarks. Instruction-tuned models may behave differently from base models (an interesting comparison but limits universality). Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

Name: batch_belief_contamination
Title: Bleeding Beliefs: Does Co-Processing Independent Items Contaminate an LLM's Internal Belief About Each One?
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM processes several logically-independent items in a single context (as in batched queries or multi-question prompts), the belief it forms about one item silently leaks into its internally-decoded belief about the other, co-present items. This cross-item belief contamination is (i) linearly decodable at each item's representation before any query, (ii) graded with the valence/confidence of the neighboring item and with inter-item similarity, and (iii) carried by an identifiable internal component (a set of attention heads that mix belief across item slots) that can be causally ablated to restore item-independent beliefs, mirroring inter-item interference/assimilation biases in human memory.
Related Work: Human memory/judgment research robustly shows inter-item interference and assimilation/contrast biases: co-present items distort each other's remembered/judged features (inter-item interference in visual memory 2019; the normative 'demixing' model 2023 showing such biases are inevitable under source ambiguity; sequential assimilation/contrast in price and prognostic judgments 2008/2009; simultaneous multi-word recognition dependencies 2021). In LLMs, prior interpretability work isolates linear truth/belief directions (Geometry of Truth 2023; Truth-value judgment 2024) and studies interference only at TRAINING time or over long single inputs: catastrophic interference from contradictory updates ('In Praise of Stubbornness' 2025), non-target priming from knowledge-conflicting facts ('Learning and Unlearning of Fabricated Knowledge' 2024), continual-pretraining belief poisoning ('Layer of Truth' 2025), and 'Contextual Feature Drift' (2024) which measures decay of context retention over sequential inputs. to our knowledge, none ask whether, at INFERENCE time, co-processing multiple logically-INDEPENDENT items in one context contaminates the model's INTERNAL belief about each item (a bleed between item slots), whether this is graded by neighbor confidence/similarity, or whether an identifiable belief-mixing component causes it. We transfer a canonical human inter-item interference phenomenon into LLM belief internals in a high-stakes deployment setting (batched inference) and give it a mechanistic, causal treatment, distinct from all training-time interference work and from my prior single-item belief-attribute proposals.
Abstract: Serving LLMs at scale routinely means co-processing many items in one context: multiple questions batched into a single prompt, several documents concatenated, or a form of independent claims answered together. Users assume the model evaluates each item on its own merits. We ask whether it actually does, or whether, like human memory where co-present items interfere and assimilate toward one another, an LLM's belief about one item silently bleeds into its internal belief about the others. We hypothesize that co-processing logically-independent items contaminates the model's internally-decoded belief about each: (i) the belief about item B, read before any query, shifts toward the belief/valence the model holds about a co-present item A, holding B's own evidence constant; (ii) the contamination is graded with A's confidence/valence and with A-B similarity; and (iii) it is carried by an identifiable set of attention heads that mix belief across item slots, so that ablating them restores item-independent beliefs. We build a controlled dataset of item pairs/batches where each item is a truth-evaluable claim, varying the neighbor's truth/valence and inter-item similarity while holding the target's own evidence fixed, using synthetic entities to control priors. On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) we train linear belief probes to read each item's belief in isolation vs. co-processed, compute a per-item contamination score, test its graded structure, localize the responsible belief-mixing heads via activation patching, and test causal control by ablating/steering them. We further test whether contamination predicts real batched-inference errors, including a high-stakes medical-QA batch track. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, contamination magnitude and sign, neighbor-confidence and similarity modulation, patching effect sizes, post-ablation independence restoration, batched-error prediction AUROC, and perplexity.
Experiments:
Setup shared by all experiments below. Models: four frozen open-weight base LLMs — Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B; model weights are never updated (frozen), the only trainable objects are lightweight linear read-out probes and difference-of-means steering vectors. Probes: L2-regularized logistic-regression classifiers (or ridge regressors for graded read-outs) fit on residual-stream activations at the named token, one probe per layer, regularization set by 5-fold cross-validation; every probe is trained and evaluated with 5 seeds {0,1,2,3,4} (mean±95% CI reported) and paired with a shuffled-label control task. A probe counts as genuinely reading the target attribute only if held-out AUROC ≥ 0.75 while its control-task AUROC ≤ 0.55; the band 0.55–0.75 (or control AUROC > 0.55) is the indecision zone — that layer/model is reported as 'representation too weak to interpret', not as evidence. Steering vectors are contrastive difference-of-means (activation-addition) directions between the two matched conditions named in each experiment; steering strength is swept over 5 magnitudes and reported as a dose-response. Collateral-damage guardrails for every causal intervention: perplexity on held-out text must rise ≤ 5% and 5-shot MMLU (1k-item subset) must drop ≤ 2 points to count as 'clean'; 5–10% perplexity or 2–4 MMLU points is the indecision band (effect real but not cleanly separable); worse than that fails the guardrail.

Data. 6,000 truth-evaluable item-state claims built from scratch (capitals, entity-attributes), in two tracks: (a) ~3,000 real claims the models reliably know/disbelieve; (b) ~3,000 synthetic novel-entity claims with stipulated truth. Claims are assembled into single-context BATCHES (pairs, then size-4 and size-8) with matched ISOLATED baselines. For each TARGET item the co-present NEIGHBOR is varied while the target's own evidence is fixed: neighbor truth-value, neighbor confidence/valence (strongly/weakly true or false framings), and target-neighbor similarity (same-domain/lexically-similar vs. unrelated). Order permutations, length-matched fillers, comprehension checks, and paraphrase perturbations included; a high-stakes track batches MedQA/MedMCQA items. ~4,500 target-in-context observations usable; 80/20 split by target item.

Experiment 1 (H1 — co-processing independent items contaminates the internally-decoded belief about each, before any query). Read the belief probe at the TARGET tokens WITHOUT querying it, in ISOLATED vs. BATCHED; contamination = belief(target|batched) − belief(target|isolated), signed by neighbor valence. Systems compared: isolated vs. batched vs. the model's stated per-item judgments. Decisive metric: mean signed contamination. Convincing: |contamination| ≥ 0.10 with CI excluding 0 in ≥ 3 of 4 models, with a consistent sign (assimilation toward, or contrast away from, the neighbor's valence). Indecision band: |contamination| < 0.05 or CI includes 0 → items are evaluated independently (a reassuring negative for batched inference); 0.05–0.10 = suggestive.

Experiment 2 (H2 — contamination is graded with neighbor confidence/valence and with inter-item similarity). Decisive metric: slopes of contamination vs. neighbor-valence extremity, vs. target-neighbor similarity, and vs. batch size. Convincing: monotonic positive slopes (CI excluding 0) for neighbor extremity and similarity, and growth with batch size, in ≥ 3 of 4 models. Indecision band: any slope CI includes 0 → that grading dimension not established (report the unconditional effect only).

Experiment 3 (H3 — an identifiable set of belief-mixing heads causes the bleed and ablating them restores item-independent beliefs). Localize via patching a target's activations between its batched and isolated runs, identifying cross-slot attention heads (contrast with truth/belief heads). Decisive metric first: batched-inference error rate (target answer flips only when batched with an opposite-valence neighbor) after ablating the mixing heads, including the high-stakes medical track; secondary: contamination driven toward 0, whether internal contamination predicts batched errors at AUROC ≥ 0.70 over a log-prob baseline, then Setup guardrails; baselines random-head ablation and truth-direction steering. Convincing: ablation cuts batched errors by ≥ 50% relative and contamination to ≤ 0.05, cleanly on guardrails and preserving isolated-item accuracy, while amplifying the heads exaggerates contamination and baselines cut errors < 10%. Indecision band: 20–50% error reduction or guardrails only in the 5–10%/2–4-point band. A negative result (no head set restores independence without breaching guardrails) means the bleed is distributed attention spillover, not a modular belief-mixing component. Deployment relevance and mitigation: we estimate the contamination rate induced by common prompt-packing / batched-serving templates (pairs through size-8 batches) as an end-to-end answer-flip rate, and evaluate a translational mitigation BEYOND head ablation — inference-time item isolation and prompt-structuring (one item per delimited slot) — reporting the flip-rate reduction each yields. Generalization: transfer across real/synthetic tracks, domains, similarity levels, and batch sizes. (High-stakes medical results are for research characterization only, not clinical use.)

Statistical analysis (all experiments). Effects are estimated with mixed-effects models carrying random intercepts for item and for model family, so results are pooled across the four models without pseudo-replication; every rate, slope, AUROC, and effect size is reported with a bootstrap 95% CI (10,000 item-level resamples). Multiplicity across layers, heads, and steering magnitudes is controlled with Benjamini–Hochberg FDR at q = 0.05. H1 is the pre-registered primary hypothesis; H2 is secondary and the localization/steering hypothesis is confirmatory-exploratory, reported as such unless its pre-stated causal criterion is met.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The observed shift could reflect legitimate inference (a neighbor genuinely provides weak evidence about the target in the real track); the synthetic-entity track with independent stipulated truths, unrelated-neighbor conditions, and length-matched fillers are designed to isolate genuine contamination from valid cross-item inference (harder to separate for real, correlated items). The effect may be absent internally - a robust negative result (LLMs evaluate co-processed independent items independently) would itself be a valuable, reassuring finding for batched-inference deployment. The contamination could arise from token-level attention leakage without a belief-level bleed; probing at target-specific tokens, order permutations, comprehension checks, and the neighbor-valence sign test help distinguish belief contamination from generic attention spillover. Belief may not be cleanly linearly decodable at every layer; we report layerwise results with control tasks. The belief-mixing component may be distributed rather than a few discrete heads; we treat 'ablate to restore independence' as the causal test rather than pinning exact heads. Position/order and primacy effects may confound similarity effects; permutation controls mitigate this. Steering/ablation could degrade fluency or harm cases where cross-item context is legitimately useful; we use small magnitudes, random-ablation baselines, and monitor perplexity, isolated-item accuracy, and general benchmarks. High-stakes medical results are for research characterization only, not clinical use. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.
